# Engineering journal

Decisions, findings and dead ends — the things a `git log` cannot carry.

The rule for an entry: record what a future reader would otherwise have to
rediscover. A change that speaks for itself in the diff does not need an entry;
a change that looks wrong until you know why does.

**Order.** The entries from "The gates, spread over threads" down to
"Print and reparse works" run newest first; from "The 109 that were never
looked at" on, they run oldest first and carry their dates in the title.
New entries go at the end, dated. Search by title; the index below names
the entries whose decisions still bind.

Written before the repository was published (2026-10-11), mostly by AI
coding agents for the maintainer: commit hashes and "`main`" in those
entries name the unpublished pre-publication history, "the owner" is the
maintainer, and `CLAUDE.md` is today's `AGENTS.md`
([`README.md`, "About the record"](README.md#about-the-record)).

## The gates, spread over threads

*2026-09-17. No scoreboard number moved; every report below is byte-identical
to the one it replaced, which is the whole claim.*

The full gate run was nine minutes and the inner loop two, and the
2026-09-08 entry below had already taken the build profile and the oracle
spawns off the table. What was left was measured stage by stage on a quiet
machine, and it was **one `Db` walking the corpus one file at a time** —
five times over, in five drivers that each had a good reason to share a
`Db` across files (the base library parsed once, not 2,922 times) and no
reason to share it across *threads*.

| stage | one at a time | spread | how |
|---|---|---|---|
| `xtask conformance` | 100.5 s | **14.0 s** | a `Db` per thread, consecutive chunks of assertions |
| `xtask conformance --strict` | 97.9 s | **13.8 s** | the same |
| `xtask errors`, our side | 18.1 s | **3.0 s** | the same; the oracle side was already fanned out |
| `xtask ir`, the instances census | 27.6 s | **3.7 s** | a `Db` per thread, one file per slot |
| `xtask ir`, the count gates and the twins | 90.4 s | **14.7 s** | the loop body became `grade_root`, per-thread `CountGrades`, merged and sorted |
| `xtask ir`, whole | 129 s | **25 s** | |
| `xtask repoint` | 51.1 s | **7.4 s** | one `syntax-test.py` per thread, each in its own working directory |
| `kg-db` `tests/query.rs`, each corpus walk | 40 s | **15–17 s** | eight threads sharing the one `Db` |
| `cargo test --workspace --profile quick` | 68 s | **34 s** | |

**The shape is the same everywhere, and it is a driver, not a grade.** A
thread owns a `Db`; work is handed out through an atomic counter; every
result lands in a slot indexed by its assertion or file; and the report is
built from the slots in corpus order, exactly as the sequential loop built
it. `check_snippet`, `score`, `judge`, the ledgers and the gates are called
as before and were not edited. `conformance.rs` is the scoreboard and
off-limits by `CLAUDE.md`; what changed in it is which thread calls the
grade, and the owner sanctioned that change on this date.

**Consecutive chunks, not one snippet per fetch.** Assertions arrive grouped
by test file, and a settings change re-roots the `Db`; a chunk of ~90
consecutive snippets switches settings a few times at most, where a
snippet-per-fetch would switch on nearly every one. `--jobs 1` is the old
loop, one `Db` in corpus order, and it is the reading to fall back to: a
snippet whose verdict differs between `--jobs 1` and the default would mean
the verdict depends on what the `Db` checked before it, which is a bug in
the memo, not in the fan-out. Measured: identical.

**The count loop was the one refactor.** 400 lines of body, 73
accumulators, all of them sums, unions or lists keyed by root — so the body
moved into `grade_root` unchanged but for three top-level `continue`s that
became `return`s, the accumulators into a `CountGrades` a thread owns,
`merge` folds the threads and `sort` puts every failure list back in corpus
order (a stable sort by root, since a root's own entries were pushed in body
order by one thread). The "first disagreement" strings are per-root locals
and never crossed the loop boundary, which is what made the merge a fold
with no order in it.

**`repoint` runs upstream's runner, and the runner's temp files are relative
to its working directory** — a subfolder per test-file stem, plus a `.done`
and a `.error` beside it. Two registrations sharing a test file under
different options would share that subfolder, so every registration now gets
its own working directory under the one temp root, and the verdicts print in
registration order after the last runner returns.

**Two things that were not the problem.** `kg-lsp` read as 15.8 s in the
first per-crate timing and is 0.1 s: the rest was compiling its test
binaries in a profile that had never built them. And builds are not the
loop — a release rebuild of `xtask` and `kg-cli` after an edit to `kg-db`
is 8.8 s, a quick-profile rebuild plus one test is 1.0 s.

**Left where it was.** `kg-fmt`'s `tests/corpus.rs` walks the corpus in
5.5 s and names the reference by an absolute path under one user's home,
which is a portability defect before it is a speed one. The shared-`Db`
walks in `query.rs` scale 2.5× on eight threads rather than eight; a `Db`
per thread would likely do better and was not tried, since 15 s a test is
under the rest of the suite.

## A higher-order function is a template (Stage B, first half)

Every silence left in `closures.k` and `higher-order-functions.k` had the
same root: the reference never types a function-typed parameter as
written. `higherOrderFunctions` (`Function.hs:313-361`, frontend pass 2)
makes an inline function with such parameters a template — a capture
typename and a closure function type per parameter, the parameter
retyped `Closure<(Do$capture, …) -> R, Do, Do$capture>` — and every call
then deduces `Do$capture` and `Do` from the closure it is given, `Do` by
*name* (`TNameArg`, `Type.hs:1562-1564`). `decltype(Do) x = 10` inside the
copy, `x(10)` on a `decltype(Do) x`, the `Do` mismatch messages that
spell both function types with the capture: all of it is what the copy
says once it exists.

**The rewrite** is `kg_hir::rewrite::higher_order`, modelled on the
abbreviated-template pass: the template parameters wear the parameter's
note, the closure function type rebuilds the written one with the
capture consed in front, `mergeTemplateParams` folds a function that was
already a template. Three unit tests print the result and compare it to
the reference's shape; an alias-typed parameter is left as written
(`resolvedFuncParams` is not read here). It runs first in
`rewrite::pipeline`, and in `Db::body_ir` — the census counts a
template's parameters on the lowering, and a two-argument `Go<uint32,
bool>` against a four-parameter template is a copy with `Do` unbound.

**Three things the twin needed to decide such a call.** A deduced call
may bind a parameter by name, and the rewrite half mints that name back
(`deduce_rewrite`, an `ArgShape::Function`). The base run's rewrite half declines a higher-order callee
altogether — the written declaration undercounts its parameters and the
twin decides the call. And `templateTypeCheck`'s clause for a
function-typed parameter (`TypeCheck.hs:269-275`) is checked where the
binding is made, `name_bound_mismatch`, because the twin never prints the
instance the reference checks it on: a mismatch is the pass-8 message at
the call and declines the rewrite, one report and no copy; an undecidable
one — `(Do$capture, S<uint32>) -> uint32`, an instance type this table
cannot spell — declines the rewrite and says nothing
(`higher-order-functions.k::132,133`, the symbolic-instance item).

**What the gate taught, in order.** Thirteen must-accepts turned red:
every one a generic lambda, `[](auto x)`, whose closure the port built
and converted. The reference never builds it: the hoisted function is an
abbreviated *template*, `tIsFunction` fails on it, no `TClosure`, the
instance stays unresolved, and `templateTypeCheck` lets the name through
(`tIsTemplate $ typeOf argExp`, `TypeCheck.hs:266`). `closure_instance`
declines a template — and an `auto` parameter, since the twin's leftover
abbreviated function is what the table keeps under the name. Then five
snippets that had agreed went silent, all one shape: a *function* passed
where the closure parameter is. The reference wraps it in a lambda first
— `addLambdaWrappers` (`Function.hs:363-421`), `$wrapper$F`, the segments
of the resolved name joined by `$` — and `elaborate::wrappers` now does,
reading the callee's signature off the base table and minting the
parameters as a deduced argument is minted; `rewrite::pipeline` split
around it, since it is the one rewrite of pass 8's list that reads types.
Where no wrapper can be made — a name inside a copy, a template instance,
a member function — the deduction takes the closure the wrapper would
have passed (`wrapped_closure`, the function behind the empty capture,
or `make_capture1` over the class for a member) and the rewrite half
declines; the verdicts are the reference's, the copies are not made.
Then twenty-four more must-accepts: a captured lambda at home against a
helper module's template read through its twin (the closure with its
captures, `lambda_closure`), a member function named as an argument,
a function-typed constant, an `optional<T>` inside the closure's
function type (ported only as far as the plain rule says), and one that
took the longest: `Foo<DoIt>` with a member `DoIt` inside `Foo`. The
sorted lowering had resolved the argument to the helper's chain and the
printer spelled it by its leaf inside the copy, where the member won.
Written or resolved, an imported function argument is now spelled by its
module through an alias, as a foreign spec's is. The `dropped` set does
not see it — the pairing refuses a chain against a bare name — which is
why a first attempt to read `Whole::dropped` in pass 4 was inert, and is
gone.

Gates: conformance 2486 → 2489/2489 decidable, errors 549 → 552 agree,
68 → 65 silent, 24 disagreements unchanged — `closures.k::1,9,15` from
silence to agreement; ten tests in `elaborate::higher_order_tests`, each
red with its arm cut. Two arms the first cut carried were inert and are
gone: a minted `Closure<…>` instance as a reason for a next round (the
minted `Closure` *name* already is) and a member-function exemption from
the name-bound check. Two arms no unit test can reach are proven by the
gates instead: with the undecidable name-bound check deciding the call,
the errors gate reads 26 disagreements, `higher-order-functions.k::132,
133` converting where the reference judges `Do`; and with the rewrite
half deciding a call whose closure parameter is given a bare function —
one no wrapper was made for — eleven must-accepts convert `() -> void`
to the closure inside the copy (`extern-class.k::53`,
`template-argument-deduction.k::157`), which `xtask ir`'s instance diff
never sees and the conformance gate does; that decline was removed on the
ir gate's word and restored on conformance's. A proof script that
removed text and could not put it back graded five proofs on a cut tree
before it was caught — the scripts now refuse an empty replacement. Not done: wrappers inside copies (a lambda or a
function argument in a template body, `higher-order-functions.k::116`),
`closureCalls`, the symbolic `S<T>` spelling, a member access on a
reference as an argument, attributed function types.

## A constant is keyed by where it is declared

The sharper `type agreement` line left five roots, and three were one
defect: `const auto c = a * b` typed `const uint14` where the reference
folds it to the literal 4096 and says `uint13` — in a copy of a template
class (`wide_to_narrow.k`'s `NumScalarIterations`), in `float32.k`'s
`log2_internal<1, 0>` (`fractionFbit + BaseFbit`, `uint7` for 48), in
`helper/constexpr.k`'s `C<2>` (`uint34` for a `uint32 * 2` the reference
reads as `uint33` through the literal rule). Walked down from silence
with the oracle (scratchpad/l9/w3.k–w9.k), the defect was not in the
twin: a plain class at home did it too, as soon as the member's name was
not unique in the file.

**`FileScope` keyed constants by unique simple name.** `unambiguous_names`
counted every item's leaf and kept the ones seen once; a member `c`
beside a `static C c;` in another function was dropped, and two copies
of a template class — `__kg_m0::NumScalarIterations`,
`__kg_m1::NumScalarIterations` — dropped each other. A dropped
declaration never folds, its uses stay names, and `inferType`'s width
algebra answers for the expression the reference had already replaced
with a literal. Every twin with two instances of one template lost every
member constant of both.

**Keyed by qualified name now, looked up from the use's own scope.** The
item tree already has each declaration's `declScopeName ++ [name]`
(`Symbols.hs:70-71`), module namespace dropped: `["C", "c"]`, `["f",
"$", "c"]`. A declaration's initializer is folded in its own scope
(`["C"]`, so `a * b` finds `["C", "a"]`), and a use is looked up from
`getScopeQualifier` at the use — the enclosing class's key, or a function
body's with `"$"` behind it — walked outward as `lookupSymbol` walks
(`Symbols.hs:83-87`). The evaluator asks its environment for that scope
(`ConstEnv::scope_of`, defaulted to "the caller's") at the one place a
name is looked up, so no caller changed. One old assertion changed with
it: `const auto N = 1; inline void f() { const auto N = 2; static
assert(N == 9); }` was pinned as silence — "two declarations of one
name: no answer rather than a guess" — and is "static assertion failed"
now, which is the reference's answer (scratchpad/l9/n1.k). Two new
tests, one red with the scope answer cut, one red with the qualified
keys cut.

**And the type a folded node has is the literal's.** The gate still read
`const uint14` at the copies after that, because the *declaration's* type
— `const auto c = a * b` — is `inferType`'s, and `inferExpType` there
sees a `BinaryF` over two names typed `const uint11` and `const uint3`:
the width algebra, `uint14`. The reference's `inferExpType` never sees
that node: `evaluateConstexpr` runs first at every node, bottom-up
(`Inference.hs:47,50`), so both names are `IntLiteral`s and the product
is the folded literal by the time its parent is typed, and its type is
`inferIntLiteralType` of the value (`Type.hs:485-491`). `SymbolEnv` gained
`folded_value` — `folded_int` with the literal's own type kept — and
`infer` returns the literal's type for a path, a binary, a unary or a
paren the environment folds to an integer, except at an assignment's
target (the parser rejects a `const` there by symbol, `Parser.hs:800`,
and pass 19 reads the declared type for it). A folded operand counts as
the literal it became in the binary rules too, which is how `uint32 x`
times a folded `2` is `uint33` and not `uint34`. The conversion sites had
been masking all of this by folding on their own; `decltype(c)` is where
the table's own answer shows, `uint13` now and `uint14` before.

The first cut of that rule took every fold's type at its word and the
gate said no twice. The file-scope fold cannot type a product of *typed*
literals — its `binary_op_type` answers `None`, so `const uint32 a`
times `const int16 b` folds to an untyped `-200`, `int9`, where the
reference's `inferBinaryOp` says `int48` (`literal-operand.k::8`); and
it cannot cast through an alias template, so `const MyInt<2> x = 0` folds
untyped and `bitsizeof x` read 1, not 2 (`using.k::7`). An untyped fold
is trusted only where the reference's is untyped too: at a name whose
declaration is the literal's own type, and at an expression whose every
leaf is untyped. A typed fold is always its type. And a folded operand
counts as a literal in the binary rules only untyped, since two typed
literals still take the algebra. `bitsizeof` of a `const auto` stays
silent on both sides of the port — the size-operand rule declines `auto`
declarations and could now trust a folded one; noted, not done.

**A folded name keeps its `const`.** With the widths right the gate still
read `uint6` against the reference's `const uint6` at every use of a
folded name: `inferExpType` typed the `NamedValue` `const T` before the
fold replaced it, and a resolved type is never revised (`resolveTypeOf`,
`Type.hs:1037-1048`), so the literal that stands there wears the
declaration's `const`; the folded *expression* is the bare literal, which
`const auto c = a * b` wraps in `tConst` itself. A name is
`Const(literal)`, an expression `literal`. `type agreement` reads 26/28,
and the two roots left are the method-name nodes the reference types
`undefined` (`o.next(…)`, `stage0.execute(…)`) where this table holds the
method's function type — a convention to settle, not a width.

**And the one environment that wraps another must forward the scope.**
`xtask ir`'s differential counted 287 resolved instances before this
entry and 280 after it — a number no other gate moved, now printed per
file under `--verbose` so the next such slip has a name. Six were
`trace.k`'s `horizontal<width>` and `right<margin>` in a `box` nested in
`print_memory_map`, one `float32.k`'s `exp2_translate<23,
translatedMantissaFbit>`: template arguments folded through `WidthEnv`,
which delegates `lookup_const` to the file scope but had `scope_of`'s
default, "the caller's scope" — the module's, where a qualified key is
not. Forwarded, the count is 292: the seven back and five the old
simple-name key never had. A test pins the nested-local shape, red with
the forwarding cut.

## A captured lambda is its closure

Two absences, found by walking `uint8 z = fn` on `[y](uint32 x) -> uint32`
down from silence to the reference's conversion (scratchpad/l6/u3.k,
`kg-oracle --errors` 2026-09-08).

**The elaborated lookup stopped at a module's direct imports.** A call to
`make_capture1(y)` decides `make_capture1<uint32>`, whose copy is
materialised in `data.closure` — a module nothing in the file imports by
name: `base.k` re-exposes it (`module data.closure` in its export list), and
`visibleSymbols` is `exposed ∪ reExposed ∪ diffs` (`SymbolTable.hs:148`).
`Imports::elaborated_hit` asked only the direct target's namespace, so a
plain `uint8 z = make_capture1(y)` in a file importing only the base
library was silent where an explicit `import data.closure` beside it
converted. It walks every namespace an import's interface carries now,
each answered by the module that declares it; the test imports a stub
`base` that re-exposes the closure module and is red with the walk
narrowed to the target's own namespace.

**A rewrite's own mention of a template was not a reason for a next
round.** `desugarLambdas` writes `make_captureN(…)` for a lambda with
captures (`Function.hs:146-159`), a call the module's text never made and
the base run's deduction never saw; the round-two trigger counted
mentions inside *copies*, and a module whose only rewrite was a lambda
stopped after round one with the call undeduced. A minted (`Donated`)
node naming a template counts as a copy's mention now, the round after
decides the instance, hands it to `data.closure` as a foreign spec, and
the home twin reads the copy back through the walk above. Three probes
fell in line at once: the captured closure's spelling to the character
(`Closure<(data.closure::make_capture1<uint32>::$::Capture, uint32) ->
uint32, Go@?lambda0, …Capture>`); `[y](uint32 x) { return {0, 1}; }` is
the `decltype` report, not pass 17's line; and `lambdas.k::22` — a
capture naming a type alias — is the reference's own verdict at last,
"Invalid conversion from `type uint32` to `uint32`" at the capture, the
twin's conversion check meeting the minted argument once the parser's
rule leaves it alone. The silence booked in the entry below is gone.

The capture-list note is the token it lands on — the first capture, or
the `]` — rather than the list's tail from there; a position in the
reference, a range here.

**What the extra round did to `xtask ir`'s type agreement.** The gate reads
the reference at `--template-iterations 1`, where a nested instance inside
a copy — `fork_join<uint32, 2, 32, 32> _fj;` in a copy of a template class
— is still `unresolved`; the round this entry adds had already decided it,
and the gate counted the decided type as "absent from the reference":
18/28 became 17/28. A decided type against an undecided one grades
nothing either way, so those are counted now, not failed — 124 of the
2301 compared — and `--verbose` lists every absent key beside what the
reference holds there. Read that way the line is 23/28, and the five
roots left are real disagreements to look at: a `const uint7`/`const
uint14`/`const uint34` where the reference has another width
(`float32.k`, `wide_to_narrow.k`, `helper/constexpr.k`) and a `() ->
uint8`/`() -> uint32` function type (`schedule.k`, `test_cases_18.k`).

## The testing loop, measured

A full gate run took 25 minutes and the assumption was that the oracle
and the release rebuilds were why. Timed stage by stage on the built
binaries (scratchpad `timing1.sh`, 2026-09-08), it was not:

| stage | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `cargo test --workspace` (dev profile) | 818 s | 68 s under `--profile quick`, cold build included |
| `xtask ir` | 468 s | 128 s with the oracle cache warm |
| `xtask conformance` / `--strict` | 99 s + 100 s | run together, 100 s |
| `xtask errors` | 33 s | 20 s warm |
| `cargo test --release -p kg-db -- <one test>` after an edit | 10 s | 2 s under `quick` |

**The dev profile was the cost.** `profile.dev.package."*"` optimises the
dependencies but leaves the workspace crates at opt-level 0, and
`kg-db`'s `tests/query.rs` walks the corpus through the frontend — 37 s
optimised, most of the 818 s not. `[profile.quick]` inherits `dev` (so
`debug_assert!` and overflow checks stay, which is why the workspace
tests run there at all — `kg-ty`'s fixpoint monotonicity assertion has
caught a real bug) and sets opt-level 1 with incremental on.

**The oracle cache** (`xtask/src/oracle_cache.rs`) keys a run on the
oracle binary's bytes, every `.k` file under the reference's `library/`
and `test/` by path and content, the arguments, the working directory
and the file's text; it stores the raw `stdout`/`stderr` and nothing this
port reads into them, so every parse of the oracle's output still runs
fresh and only the spawn is skipped. Cold and warm `errors` and `ir`
runs diff to zero lines. Each gate prints its replayed/spawned counts so
a run that graded nothing fresh says so; `KG_ORACLE_CACHE=0` bypasses it.
The store is `target/oracle-cache/`, 3216 entries and 681 MB — the
`--tree` and `--typed` lines are the payload — and can be deleted. FNV-1a
over 128 bits, written in place: the inputs are local, and no crate in
the workspace has a stronger digest.

**`scripts/gates.sh` and `scripts/quick.sh`** are the two loops: the
full suite (build, quick-profile tests, clippy, then fmt-check,
conformance, strict, errors and corpus together on the release binary,
then `ir`, then `bench` alone) and the inner one (one test filter, then
conformance and errors together). What was not worth doing: parallel
mutation proofs (each needs its own tree and target directory, and the
rebuild they would share is 10 s), and merging the plain and strict
conformance passes, since `conformance.rs` is the scoreboard.

---

## A `decltype` with no written form, and where a lambda's capture list is

**The pass-6 rule the port did not have.** `eval (DecltypeF _ x) =
fromMaybe (illegalDecltype x) $ expFromType x $ typeOf x`
(`Constexpr.hs:304-305`): once a `decltype`'s operand type is resolved,
the folder replaces the node with that type's written form, and where
`expFromType` has none (`Type.hs:1612-1642` — an initializer list, an
array of no extent, a function whose return or parameter has none) the
node becomes ``"Argument of type `T` is illegal for `decltype`"``. `kg-ty`
had carried the message for months (`illegal_decltype_message`) with no
caller; `static assert(bitsizeof(decltype({0})) == 1)` compiled clean,
and `using T = decltype(f)` on an `auto` function returning `{0}` said
"Could not deduce function return type" — pass 17's report, which the
reference never reaches, because this error exists by the pass-8
checkpoint (`hasErrors'`, `Template.hs:55,84`). Pass 4's `spellable` was
already `expFromType`'s `Just`; the new `pass_6_illegal_decltype` reads
it, and the checkpoint does the rest.

**Two things about where it lands, both learned from the gate.** The
first cut turned four `type-constexpr.k` snippets red — `static
assert(!(decltype({}) < uint1))` is "static assertion failed", not this.
`inferExpTree` is bottom-up (`Inference.hs:53`), so the `decltype` is
judged first; but `evaluateConstexpr` keeps the judged node's *note* —
its type included — on whatever it rewrites the node to
(`Constexpr.hs:122`, `NotedExp n $ eval e`), so the error node still
answers `tIsType`, and the type comparison one level up folds over it to
a boolean (`Constexpr.hs:236-250`), discarding the error with the rest
of the subtree. No other clause folds over a type-typed operand
(`bitsizeof` asks `tWidth`, `clog2` a natural, a cast a literal), so the
one swallowing parent is a comparison `compare_type_operands` would
decide, read through parentheses. And the report is at the outermost
enclosing paren when there is one — `parens expr` renotes at the `(`,
the convention pass 10 already follows: `bitsizeof(decltype({0}))` is
rejected at the `(`.

**A lambda's capture list is noted after its `[`.** `brackets (noted
capture `sepBy` comma)` with `brackets = between (symbol "[") (symbol
"]")` (`Parser.hs:441`, `Lexer.hs:278`): the `Seq`'s note is taken once
the bracket and the trivia behind it are consumed — at the first capture,
or at the `]` of an empty list. Every node `desugarLambdas` mints wears
that note (`new = flip newNote lambdaCaptures`, `Function.hs:206-214`),
which is where `Closure<decltype(fn), fn, capture>` is, which is where
`[](uint32 x) { return {0}; }` is rejected: `(…Capture, uint32) ->
{uint1}` is illegal for `decltype`, at column 18 for `[]` and 21 for
`[   ]`. The lowering allocates the list's `Seq` at the `CAPTURE_LIST`
node, so the twin's report came home one column early. The first cut
moved the `Seq` itself to the content range, `Donated`; `xtask ir`
rejected it on 127 files — every IR head, own or donated, is a CST
node's range, and no node starts after the bracket — and two `kg-hir`
tests hold the list `Own` for `captureThis`'s rebuild. So the shift is
the seam's: `carry_home` moves a diagnostic that lands on a
`CAPTURE_LIST` head to after the bracket, from the module's own tree,
and `lambdas.k::6` agrees to the character, the twin's own checkpoint
keeping pass 17 off the hoisted function.

**What the twin's pass 0 must not say.** `lambdas.k::22` captures a type
alias — `[a]` on `using a = uint32` — and the twin's parser rule rejected
`make_capture1(a)` as "Invalid use of a type as an expression". The
reference's parser never sees that call: `makeCapture` builds the argument
itself (`Function.hs:146-157`), and the verdict is the argument check's,
"Invalid conversion from `type uint32` to `uint32`" — `T0` deduced to
the type named, the argument typed `TType` of it. `Whole::minted` — the
twin ranges of every paired node the IR marks `Donated` — now exempts a
minted argument from the parser's rule, which is silence there rather
than a wrong rejection. The conversion itself is not yet said: a
capture is inside the lambda subtree inference postpones
(`Inference.hs:55`, `go (NotedExp n e@LambdaF{}) = Note n e`), so a
home-side arm over `CAPTURE` nodes reads no type and was cut as dead; the
twin-side conversion needs `make_capture1<uint32>` decided and
materialised in the twin, which no captured lambda gets today — `uint8 z
= fn` on `[y](uint32 x)` is silent, and `[y](uint32 x) { return {0, 1};
}` still says pass 17's line where the reference says the `decltype`.
That is the next family: `make_captureN` instances in the twin.

**A limit worth knowing.** `Db::instances`' error gate reads the *base*
check, and "errors from passes 9-19 gate too" (`db.rs`): a program with
an independent later-pass error elaborates nothing, so the twin's
pass-6 error never exists and the later-pass error is shown where the
reference gates it. `inline auto f(uint32 x) { return {0}; }` beside a
lambda returning `{0}` reports `f`'s "Could not deduce function return
type"; the reference reports the lambda's `decltype` and gates `f`. No
corpus snippet has the shape; noted, not fixed.

**An arm that looked inert, and the test that was.** `deduce_type` in
`kg-ty` meets a closure against a written `(T) -> R` parameter with its
function shorn of the capture; the closure test meant to pin it — `Go(fn)`
on `(T) -> uint32 Do` with `T` from nowhere else — stayed green with the
arm cut, and so did the higher-order path's own classification cut, since
silence is what both give. The arm was removed on that evidence and the
gate put it back: `static-if.k::44` and `::45`, `Go([](uint32 x) ->
uint32 {…}, 10)` on `(T) -> T Do, T x`, are the reference's clean
compiles, and without the arm `T` is the literal's `uint4` alone and the
closure is rejected against it. That shape is the test now — two sources
for `T`, the closure's winning — and it is red with the arm cut. The
first test's shape became the mismatch it can see: `[](bool b) ->
uint32` against `(uint32) -> uint32 Do` is "Invalid argument for
template parameter `Do`", both function types spelled with the capture,
at the call, red with the subtype check forced; and the cast's
classification is pinned by the higher-order silence test, which says
"Could not deduce all arguments" once the cast falls through to "not a
function".

Gates: errors disagreements 26 → 24 (both lambda verdicts), agree
547 → 546, silent 68 → 69 (`lambdas.k::22`, booked as above); the
numbers are `docs/status.md`'s. Five new tests and the stage's two
reshaped ones, each red with its arm cut — after one proof script
failed to restore a cut and had three proofs re-run against the whole
tree; the scripts now check their own restores.

## A lambda is typed through its twin

**Where the reference types a lambda.** `infer LambdaF{} = TUnresolved`
(`Type.hs:1231`): a written lambda has no type. `desugarLambdas` turns it
into an alias for its capture (`decltype(make_captureN(…))`), a hoisted
function taking the capture first, and a `cast<Closure<decltype(f), f,
capture>>(make_captureN(…))` where it stood; *that* is typed —
`TType (TClosure fn F C …)` off the three arguments of the `Closure`
instance (`:1176-1177`), the instance kept as the type's face (`tIsClosure
(TInstance _ x _) = x == data'closure'core'Closure`, `:617`). This port's
desugar lives in the route, so everything a module says about a lambda,
it says through its twin — and a module with a lambda and no template
had no twin. Three things, each proven by mutation against the tests
below:

* **A lambda is a reason for a twin** (`writes_a_lambda`, beside
  `declares_a_template`, and past the route's "decided nothing, holds no
  spec" early return). Every library module with a lambda is elaborated
  now; the bench moved 376 → 378 ms, inside the machine's band.
* **The twin resolves a bare alias by its one declaration.** The hoisted
  lambda function sits at module scope and its parameter type is the
  capture alias declared inside the function the lambda came from; the
  printer spells a resolved name by its leaf, so the twin reads `__kg_m1`
  where the reference reads `Go::$::?lambda0$capture`, and the table's
  scope walk missed. An alias names exactly one declaration:
  `Declarations::alias_leaves` indexes every `__kg_mN` the map declares by
  its leaf, and `lookup_walking` falls back to it where the walk and the
  imports both miss.
* **`Closure<F, fn, C>` types as the closure instance.**
  `infer_path` had returned `Unresolved` for every written template
  instance; `closure_instance` now recognises the one instance the table
  can type as written — the leaf `Closure` naming a template, three
  arguments of the right kinds — and returns `Type(Instance { template:
  data.closure.core::Closure, args, concrete: Closure { func, func_ty,
  capture } })`. `function_params` already read a closure's parameters past
  the capture and `return_ty` its return, so `fn(false)` is checked against
  `(uint32)` and `uint32 z = fn` against the instance, once the conversion
  pass's two "an instance is left alone" guards learned that a closure's
  is not.

**What the first gate run said, and the four rules it cost.** Ninety-eight
must-accepts failed, every one "Could not deduce all arguments for
template …": pass 4's higher-order path classifies a lambda argument
(`closure_of_argument`) and had two answers for the twin's cast — not a
lambda, not a function, so "not a function", where the base run's
unresolved lambda had been "unknown", silence. The cast is the closure
it stands for: its function shorn of the capture, its captured types
read off the capture struct's fields, and the `const` of a closure
*variable* unwrapped first (the oracle accepts `Go(fn, x)` on `const
auto fn = […]`; the first cut said "Could not deduce" for it). An
abbreviated lambda — `[](auto x)` — is a template the twin hoists as one,
its function type says `auto`, and the written-lambda path answers
`Unknown` for it; the cast path now does too. A lambda with no return
type is `-> auto`, and the hoisted function's `return` was converted
*to* `auto` ("Invalid conversion from `uint4` to `auto`", `lambdas.k::2`):
`auto` is deduced from a conversion, never a target of one. And a closure
against a written `(T) -> R` parameter is judged by its function past
the capture (`Type.hs:532,576`) — in pass 4's `closure_of_argument`,
the one place that reads it; a second arm for it in `kg-ty`'s
`deduce_type` was inert and is gone (next entry). Conformance closed at
2486/2486, five more decidable than before the stage.

`lambdas.k::4` now says "Invalid conversion from `bool` to `uint32`" at
`false`, and a closure variable is spelled `const data.closure.core::
Closure<(data.closure.core::make_capture0::$::Capture, uint32) -> uint32,
main@?lambda0, data.closure.core::make_capture0::$::Capture>` — the
reference's spelling to the character, the hoisted lambda by its hoisted
name through the seam's unrenaming. Six tests in
`elaborate::closure_tests`, over a stub `data/closure/core.k` that is the
library's text verbatim, each rule red with its arm cut.

What the stage does not reach: every closure snippet that passes a lambda
to a *higher-order function* (`closures.k::1,9,12,13`, `higher-order-
functions.k`), because `higherOrderFunctions` (`Function.hs:313-361`) —
the rewrite that makes such a function a template with a capture type and
a closure function per function-typed parameter, and `addLambdaWrappers`
beside it — is not ported; and `closureCalls`, the rewrite that passes the
capture to the hoisted function, which the reference runs after inference.
Those are the next stage.

## A copy as a function-typed argument

`F2<Foo, F1<Foo>>(bar)` (`local-structs.k::10`): the reference materialises
`F2<|@main@$@Foo@@helper@local_structs@F1<|@main@$@Foo|>|>` and reports
the call's `bar` against the copy's `Foo`. This port declined the
instance twice over, and the batch is the two refusals in order.

**The census could not shape the argument — in round one.**
`ArgShape::Function` wants a bare name whose table type is a resolved
function; `F1<Foo>` is a template instance. But once round one resolved
it, `main`'s twin spells it `__kg_m1` — a bare name the twin's table
types as the copy's function — which is exactly the shape wanted, one
round later; and that round runs, because the census *postponed* the
candidate in round one and a postponement is already a reason for the
next round. (A trigger for "an alias among an instance's arguments" was
written, proved inert by mutation against the end-to-end test, and
removed.) **The guard could not form the expected function type.** `resolve_guard` binds a typename parameter, for the function
types that mention it, to a built-in written as the argument and nothing
else; `(T) -> uint32 Fn` with `T = Foo` — a struct — had no binding and
the candidate was postponed forever. A named type the table resolved
binds now. **The owner spelled the argument bare.** Minted from the spec,
the function argument was `__kg_m1` and mangled, once aliases mangle as
their originals, `@F1<|@main@$@Foo|>` — while `main`'s mention, resolved
through the helper's namespace, mangled `@@helper@local_structs@F1<|…|>`,
and the reference agrees with `main`: a name is mangled with its
namespace ahead, an empty root segment then one per component, even a
one-component `h` (`@@h@F1<|…|>`, `kg-oracle --tree --template-iterations
3` over the unit test's program). So `ArgShape::Function` carries the
qualifier a resolved mention brought, `mint_shape` finds a copy's
template's namespace in the program's template index otherwise, and the
argument is minted as a fresh alias for the *qualified* spelling —
`.helper.local_structs::F1<|@main@$@Foo|>`, a leading `.` marking the
namespace, since a scope path (`main::$::Foo`) mangles with no root
segment and text cannot tell the two apart — which the mangler reads
back segment by segment and `unrename_message` strips before spelling.

**And a function-local function names itself by its hoisted name.** The
first gate run with the binding failed two must-accepts
(`local-functions.k::5,6`): `Foo<Capture, bool, Do>` with `Do` declared
inside `Go` was now decided, and the copy called `Do` — a name no module
declares, since `moveFunctions` hoists it under `Go@Do`, and the
reference mangles the argument as exactly that
(`Foo<|@Go@$@Capture$bool@Go@Do|>`, `kg-oracle --tree`). The census
shapes a function-local argument by its hoisted name (`hoisted_name`:
every `$`-free segment of the declaring scope, then the name); the owner
mints it as written, and the renamer aliases the unlexable name at
print, as it does every mangle, typed through `leaves` under the original
(an arm minting it as an alias up front was written, proved inert by
mutation, and removed). Both modules now hold
`Foo<|@Go@$@Capture$bool@Go@Do|>` for it, the reference's name to the
byte.

Two tests, red with either mechanism cut; the accept test red with the
hoisted name gone. Open beside it: a
non-spellable *type* leaf's original is `show_unmangled`'s pretty text
(`h::S<uint32>`), not a mangle, so a copy whose argument is a foreign
instance from a namespace the owner does not import is still named
differently on the two sides — no corpus snippet reaches it yet.

## A copy's argument mangled as what it stands for

**Two modules named the same instance differently, and neither could
see the other's copy.** `F2<Foo, F1<Bar>>(foo)` over two function-local
structs (`local-structs.k::9`) was silent: `main`'s twin mentioned
`F1<|@main@$@Bar|>` — the mangle of the scoped name, which is what the
reference writes (`kg-oracle --tree --template-iterations 2`) — while
the helper's twin, which cannot spell `main::$::Bar` and prints a leaf
alias `__kg_m0` for it, declared its copy `F1<|@__kg_m0|>`: the alias
mangled as itself. Nothing resolved the mention to the copy, the call's
callee stayed `Unresolved`, and pass 8 had no function type to hold
`F1<Bar>` against. `From<S<uint32>, FromS<S<uint32>>>(x)`
(`function-template-param.k::30`) was the same one level down:
`FromS<|@@helper@function_template_param@__kg_m0|>` where the reference
writes `FromS<|@@helper@function_template_param@S<|$uint@32|>|>` — and
there the seam did raise the verdict in a second round and then dropped
it, because the message spelled a type by an original that itself named
an alias, which `unrename_message` declines.

**The mangler now reads an alias as its original.** `mangle_args` takes
the pool's `Renames`; an `Identifier` the pool minted mangles as what it
stands for — each `::` segment its own `@` (`@main@$@Bar`), a dotted
namespace opened by an empty segment (`@@helper@function_template_param@
…`), and an alias inside the original unaliased in turn
(`unalias_deep`), since an original minted from a type read off a twin
names that twin's copy by the alias the twin declared it under. Both
rewrite passes carry the map from the elaboration (`with_renames`);
`xtask ir`'s own route, at one iteration and alias-free, passes none and
is unchanged (resolve diff 0 DIFF, instance diff 0 DIFF). One rule fell
out of the first gate run: the renamer must **leave a lexable name
alone** whatever the pool decided for it elsewhere. A leaf alias minted
for another module's twin had been renaming `struct S` in its *own*
module's twin, where the seam then compared `Struct([__kg_m0])` against
the copy's `Struct([S])` and said "Invalid conversion from `S` to `S`";
`foreign_leaf_tests` caught it, red before the rule.

**And the unmangler reads nested and qualified mangles.** `unmangle_text`
finds the `|>` that closes its `<|` with nesting counted; `unmangle_leaf`
reads a run of `@segment`s as one name — `main::$::Bar`, and, opening
with an empty segment, `helper.function_template_param::S` — with a
nested copy's arguments after the last segment. `local-structs.k::9`,
`function-template-param.k::30,34` now read as the reference prints
them, to the character (`(helper.function_template_param::S<helper.
function_template_param::S<uint32>>) -> void`). `local-structs.k::10`
stays silent: its `F1<Foo>` is a copy *as a function-typed argument*,
which the census still declines (`ArgShape::Function` wants a bare
name) — the next family.

Tests: `kg-hir`'s `an_aliased_argument_mangles_as_what_it_stands_for`,
`kg-ty`'s `nested_and_qualified_mangles_unmangle_as_the_reference_spells_
them`, and two end-to-end in `template_type_check::written_parameter_type_
tests`; each red with its mechanism cut, and the renamer rule proven by
the pre-existing foreign-leaf test.

## Two shapes `deduceAuto` gives up on

Pass 17 reports "Could not deduce variable type" and "Could not deduce
function return type" for shapes it can name, not for every initializer
the table left unresolved — the table leaves more unresolved than the
reference does, and the general rule would invent errors. Two shapes the
oracle pinned join the list (`scratchpad/da/`, `kg-oracle --errors`
2026-09-17):

* **A `static for` over a runtime value.** `static for (const auto x :
  y)` with `y` a parameter, or a local the loop cannot fold, has nothing
  to deduce `x` from — `unrollStaticFor` evaluates the limit — and the
  reference says so at the `auto`, past the `const` (`auto-placeholder.k
  ::7`, 5:19); over a `const` local, or in a plain `for`, nothing is
  said. `facts::certainly_runtime` on the limit is the whole test; the
  induction-variable exclusion that kept every loop out of the variable
  arm now excludes only the loops that deduce.
* **A first `return` under a `static if` the fold could not decide.**
  `inline auto Fn(uint32 y) { static if (y > 1) { return true; } else {
  return 10; } }` cannot be given a return type — `deduceReturnType`
  reads the first top-level `return` and finds a `static if` — and the
  reference reports that first, at the `auto`, and the predicate second
  (`type-constexpr.k::37` is the same with a `decltype` the fold declines,
  still silent: pass 16 says nothing there either, and this arm reads
  pass 16's verdict from the sink rather than deciding the predicate
  twice). A decided `static if`, or a runtime `if`, deduces.

Two tests in `deduce_auto::tests`, each red with its condition cut.

## A member the class lacks, and a written `this`

`f.Bar()` on a class with no `Bar` was silent (`basics.k::184`); the
reference says "Symbol name not in scope: `Bar`" at the member, and the
same for `f.z` read as a field and for a class another module declares
(`scratchpad/mm/{a,c,d}.k`, `kg-oracle --errors` 2026-09-17). Pass 9's
member arm was ready for it since 2026-09-10 — it fires when the receiver
resolved and the table typed the member `Undefined` — and
`Declarations::method` never said so: a miss on a class that has members
was `Unresolved`, because the map could not tell a missing member from an
untyped one. It can. The walk keys `$this` for every named class it saw
and every member beside it, dead branches gone, so a class the map (or an
import's map) declares at all is declared in full, and a missing key is a
missing member. One catch: the walk did not key member templates — a
`template` node has no name of its own, the wrapped declaration has it —
so every `c.Foo<bool>(x)` became "Symbol name not in scope: `Foo`" on the
first try. Now the template is keyed by that name with the table's type
for the node, `TTemplate` (`Type.hs:227`), which is what
`lookupSymbolByName (class ++ [member])` finds in the reference too
(`Type.hs:1358-1362`); a template-typed callee's call is `Unresolved` by
`return_ty`, as the miss used to be, so nothing downstream moved.

A written `this` was rejected everywhere; the reference rejects it in an
expression — `return this.x` — and accepts it as the receiver of a method
call — `this.Go()` — where the parser reads `FunctionSpecifierF (Just This)
Go` (`Parser.hs:730-734`) and looks nothing up (`scratchpad/mm/e2.k`: one
report, at the second). `is_call_receiver` is the whole rule.

**Where the miss is a receiver, the reference says nothing — and where
it is under a template argument list, its parser speaks first.** The
first gate run with the member rule raised one disagreement:
`member-function-template.k::22`, `c2s[1].c[0].Foo<uint32>(x)` with no
`c` on `C2`, where this port now said "Symbol name not in scope: `c`" and
the reference says "`Foo`: undefined template" at the head of the callee
— a `PARSE-ERROR`. Nine probes (`scratchpad/pt/`) drew the lines. A
missing member read as a value, or as the base of another *field*
access, is reported (`c2s[1].zz`, `c2.zz.ww`: "`zz`"); the receiver of a
*method call* is not (`c2.zz.Go(x)`, `c2s[1].c[0].Go(x)`): the specifier
is typed through `method` on the receiver's `TUndefined`, which is
`TUnresolved`, and the reference's only report is a conversion from
`unresolved` downstream — silence here, since that family is not ported.
A member named with template arguments and no `template` keyword is the
parser's: it finds `Foo` among the receiver's class's member templates
(`Parser.hs:668-680`), and a class with none of that name (`c.Nope<
uint32>(x)`), or a chain with a member the class lacks so there is no
class to look into, is "`Foo`: undefined template" at the callee's head,
and the frontend is never entered; `parse_time_find_symbol` now has that
rule beside `findSymbol`'s two, source only, returning early. The
question is put to the class's *own declaration* — found through the
symbol map and the declaring module's tree, its `template` members
scanned by name, prototypes included — not to `Templates::member`, whose
answers are hedged for the census's purposes: a prototype in an `extern`
class is not indexed and a class name the helper shares is "ambiguous",
and the first gate run failed three must-accepts on exactly those
(`extern-class.k::39,40`, `type-check.k::62`). The third also showed a
receiver the table types `Undefined` for a reason of its own — a `c`
shadowed by a `static Z c` in an inner block — so the non-class arm asks
only whether a *member* down the chain is missing. An
*array* receiver parses — nothing to look into, nothing to reject — and
`unresolvedTemplates` then says "Undefined template `Foo`" at the member
(`Frontend.hs:431`), which was `::20`'s pre-existing disagreement: pass
12's keyword-only arm learned the no-keyword form on a resolved
non-class receiver, and pass 9's member arm leaves every template-argument
member alone.

Five tests across `undefined_symbols::tests` and
`unresolved_templates::tests`, each red with its arm cut (the receiver
skip, the parser rule, the chain walk, pass 12's arm); the class half of
`a_member_the_receiver_does_not_have`, which had asserted the silence as
silence with the reference's verdict in its own comment, now asserts the
verdict.

## A constant where a type was expected, and the type it becomes

`Foo<10, 10>` for `template <typename T, T X> class Foo` was silent; the
reference says two things (`type-check.k::19`): "Invalid argument for
template parameter `T`. Expected a type" at the first `10`, and at the
second, "Invalid argument for template parameter `X`. Expected a constant
expression of type: Expected a type but the argument type is: uint4". The
second message is the first one's error *as a type*: `tType _ = TError
"Expected a type"` (`Type.hs:465`) is what `resolveTemplateParamType`
makes of `T` when its argument is not a type, and the generic value check
(`TypeCheck.hs:289-294`) then spells `showUnmangled (TError m)` as `m`.

Pass 8 had the first message and never reached it: `Instance::substitute`
binds each typename parameter to the node its argument names, and a
later parameter whose declared type mentions an *unbound* one made
`resolve_kind` fail and the whole instance's validation return `None` —
both reports lost. Now a typename parameter whose argument is a resolved
constant that is not a type (a literal, or what the fold decided; an
argument the table cannot type is the reference's `templateResolved`
postponement and stays silence) resolves every mention of itself to
`Kind::Resolved(Ty::Error("Expected a type"))`, and the value arm does
the rest: `is_subtype(uint4, TError)` is false by clauses 1-2, and
`show_unmangled` of an error type is its text. One test in
`template_type_check::tests`, red with no argument counting as a
constant.

## An instance's arguments, read off its name

**`Go(Second<bool, uint32>)` was silent where the reference says
"Conflicting template argument deduction results for parameter `T1`. Could
be `bool` or `uint32`."** The argument is a function-template instance
used as a value; the elaborated table types it `(Tuple2<|$bool|$uint@32|>)
-> uint32`, and pass 4 hands that to `deduce_type` against `(Tuple2<T1,
T2>) -> T1 fn`. The return type binds `T1` to `uint32`; the parameter
should bind it to `bool` — clause 3, `deduceType (TypeIdentifier _
(TemplateInstance a b)) (TInstance _ a' b')` (`Type.hs:1532`), reads the
instance's arguments beside its concrete type. This port has no
`TInstance` for a copy: the census materialises `Second<|…|>`, the
read-back types the copy's parameter as the *struct* `Tuple2<|$bool|$uint
@32|>`, and every `Ty::Instance` in `kg-ty` is a test fixture. So the
port's clause 3 never fired on a copy, `T1` kept its first binding, and the
conflict was never made. (Measured with one `eprintln!` in pass 4's
driver: `actuals=[Function { params: [Struct([…, Tuple2<|…|>])] }]`,
`deduced=[(0, uint32), (1, None)]`.)

**The template identity a copy carries is its mangled leaf, and the
mangle is readable for what the corpus actually passes.** `Mangle.hs:29-60`
concatenates the arguments with no separator: `$bool`, `$uint@32`,
`$int@8`, `@10`, `@-3` for the compiler's types and integer literals; `@Foo`
for a user name, `$array…`, `$fun…` for the rest. `infer::mangled_instance`
splits a `Struct`/`Class`/`Union`/`Enum` leaf at `<|…|>` and reads the
scalar and literal forms into `TArg`s, in order; a user name or anything
structured ends the read with `None`, and then nothing is deduced — the
old behaviour, silence, since the mangle has no separators and what such an
argument spans is not decidable from the text. `deduce_type` gets one arm
between clause 3 and the initializer clause: formal a template instance,
actual a readable mangle of the same template, `deduce_arg` per position.
The reconciliation is untouched and gives the reference's order: `bool`
(new, from the parameter under `DeduceSubtype`) against `uint32` (old,
from the return type) is neither a subtype of the other, so clause 12's
message, new first. `::8` — `Go1(First<bool, uint4>, MakePair(false,
100))` — comes out "Could be `uint7` or `uint4`" the same way.

This is a deliberate stand-in, not the port of `TInstance`. The faithful
shape is a `Ty::Instance { concrete, template, args }` written by the
read-back for every copy's declared type, which would also spell messages
as the reference does (`Pair<bool, uint7>` keeps the alias name where this
port says `Tuple2<bool, uint7>`, a message disagreement still booked) and
let `is_instance()` mean what it says. That is a change to the type layer's
whole view of the copies, and the deduction was one clause away; the
stand-in is one function with one contract and can be deleted when the
instance type lands.

Two tests: `kg-ty`'s `a_mangled_leaf_spells_its_template_and_scalar_
arguments` (the reader, including the negative literal and the refusal of
`@S`) and `kg-db`'s `a_copy_typed_argument_deduces_through_its_mangled_
leaf` (the conflict, end to end, over a two-file program); the latter is
red with the reader returning `None`.

## Pass 9 over the twin

**Three silent snippets, one cause: the copies were never asked whether
their names exist.** The passes after `instantiateTemplates` walk the twin
(`Frontend.hs:55-80`), and this port ran them there through
`passes::run` — the single-file door, which by design has no pass 9
(`undefinedSymbols` needs the whole program's symbol map, and the door is
`check_source`'s contract). So `obj.Do()` on `static Method<false> obj;`
stayed quiet although `staticControl` had deleted `Do` from the copy
(`static-if.k::42`), `[x]` in the copy of `Foo<2>` captured a name only a
dead branch declared (`::61`), and `T x = T::B2;` copied for `C<E>` named
an enumerator `E` does not have (`enum.k::58`).

**The twin now gets a `Whole` of its own.** `Whole.twin_tree` is the
twin's item tree (`kg_resolve::lower_file_named` over the twin's parse),
standing in for the module's own in `Whole::tree` while the program —
every other module's tree, the graph — is shared, not copied;
`symbols::overlay` is the twin's map: the twin module's own symbols built,
layered over the program's memoized map minus that module's base entries
(the first cut rebuilt the whole program's map and cloned every tree per
module, which the release timings forgave and a debug build of the rooted
library test did not — its minutes became tens of them); `Whole.file` is
the twin's synthetic id, since the twin's table is keyed by it and the
seam translates the ranges home. `run_whole_program` then runs the same list the base run
runs — the parse-time table's two rejections, passes 0–8, pass 9, 10–19,
pass 13's imported-class half — and `carry_home` frames what was inside a
copy. Two fixed points along the way:

* **A minted name is known by construction.** The twin spells what the
  elaboration decided by its `__kg_mN` — `static __kg_m0 obj;` — declared
  in the twin of the module owning the template (not in this module's
  program) or held as a leaf no tree declares (`mint_leaf`). Pass 9 asked
  the map and reported "Type name not in scope: `Method<false>`" — the
  alias unrenamed, the verdict wrong. `Templates::is_alias` short-circuits
  `known_globally`; the reverse map `Templates::original_of` lets
  `qualified_member` judge `__kg_m0::B2` under `E` itself, which is how
  `enum.k::58` says "Symbol name not in scope: `B2`, Perhaps you meant:
  `B1`" at the member with the site as its frame — the oracle's report,
  to the character.
* **`this` is a name in the twin, and only there.** `captureThis`
  (`Frontend.hs:66`) makes it an argument, and the twin prints
  `make_capture2(this, x)`; the base text only ever has the keyword, and a
  *written* `this` is the rejection `a_written_this_is_not_in_scope`
  grades — the first gate run had it green in the base run too, and red.
  Two "Symbol name not in scope: `this`" were raised in every copy with a
  capturing lambda and declined at the seam (a rewrite-minted node pairs
  with nothing), harmless to the output and fatal to the run: pass 9's
  checkpoint gated passes 10–19 over that twin. `Scoped::aliases` holds
  it beside the intrinsics when `Whole.file` is not the module's own.
* **A name the printer spelled by its leaf is not pass 9's to judge.** The
  first gate run also failed eight must-accepts — `template.k::38,39`,
  `using.k::39`, `enum.k::51,56`, `auto-placeholder.k::19`,
  `decltype.k::10`, `local-functions.k::14` — and the reference library
  test with them, all one shape: the copy of `T::X x;` for `C<Foo>` prints
  as `X x;`, `Bar::Zero` as `Zero`, `bar_t::foo_t` as `foo_t`. A sorted
  name's prefix reaches the twin's text only through a source slice
  (`kg_hir::pretty`), and a copy has none; the twin's own tree declares no
  `X`, and pass 9 said so. The twin is not a self-contained program for
  name resolution, and that is the printer's contract, not a bug to fix
  here. So every side-map pair whose IR side is a qualified `ScopedName`
  (or an `EnumConstant`) and whose parsed side is bare marks a range
  (`Whole.dropped`), and the `PATH` arm skips it — unwrapping
  `TypeIdentifier`/`QualifiedIdentifier`/`EnumValue` on both sides first,
  since the pair sits at the wrapper and the leaf under it is unpaired,
  and chained through the rounds by the range the next round's IR was read
  from, since `auto-placeholder.k::19` drops its qualifier in round one and
  pairs bare with bare in round two. What pass 9 judges in a copy is
  spelled as the user spelled it: a bare `x`, or `__kg_m0::B2` under an
  alias the printer does keep. `static-if.k::42`'s `obj.Do()` is a seam
  verdict of the *member* arm, which reads the twin's table and is
  untouched by any of this.
* **Outside the copies, the twin is nobody's text to judge for scope.**
  With the dropped leaves handled, `test/library/processor/risc-v.k` still
  said "Type name not in scope: `Opcode`" at a lambda parameter: the
  rewrite had hoisted the lambda's body to module scope (`moveFunctions`),
  where the class's nested enum is out of reach, and the pair for that
  name did not exist to mark it dropped. The general rule is the right
  one: the seam is the rewrites' spelling of the user's text — hoisted
  functions, desugared captures, the aliases the twin declares — and the
  base run judged that text in its own scopes already. `Whole.copies`
  holds the twin ranges of every paired node the IR keeps inside an
  expansion, merged; the path, capture and string-hole arms judge only
  inside one. The member arm is type-driven and keeps the seam:
  `static-if.k::42`'s `obj.Do()` still comes from there.
* **The closure alias is the rewrite's, too.** `test/library/data/fifo/
  wide_to_narrow.k` then reported `total_count` and `actual` inside a
  copy: the lambda rewrite prints `using __kg_m2 = decltype(make_capture3(
  this, total_count, actual));` at the top of the enclosing function,
  above the `if` block that declares both, and pass 9 read the spelling.
  The `cast<Closure<…>>(make_capture3(…))` at the lambda's own position
  names them where they are and stays judged; a path under an
  `ALIAS_DECL` in a twin is skipped. A unit test cannot hold either of
  these — a capturing lambda needs `data.closure` — so the rooted test
  over every `test/library/` program (`the_rooted_door_agrees_with_the_
  reference_on_every_test_library_program`, 55 programs, the oracle's
  four `HARTS` rejections in `mmio.k` and nothing else) is the proof:
  `copies` handed as `None` reddens it on `risc-v.k`, the alias skip
  removed reddens it on `wide_to_narrow.k`.
* **A qualifier leaf the pool already aliased must be renamed too.** The
  renamer skips a prefix `ScopedName`'s leaf on the premise that it never
  prints — true when the printer prints, false when it slices: `E::A` in
  `main.k` kept its `E` while `enum E` had become `enum __kg_m1`, because
  another module's twin had minted `E` as a leaf for a foreign copy, and
  pass 9 over main's twin reported the `E` the twin no longer declared.
  `survey` now keeps a leaf the pool has decided out of the skip set
  (`ident_is_aliased`); `foreign_leaf_tests` is the proof, red before.

**A `static if` declares for the class, function or file holding it —
not for the file.** `Scoped::static_if_names` was a file-wide set: a name
any `static if` declared counted everywhere, because only the taken branch
survives and the predicate is pass 16's. Over the twin that hedge covered
the copy: the template `Foo` beside `__kg_m0` still holds `static if (N >
10) { uint32 x; }`, undecided, and the copy's `return x;` was "seen".
Each name now carries the range of its holder (the nearest enclosing
`CLASS_DECL`, `FN_DECL` or the file), and a use is covered only inside it.
The oracle confirms the rule in the base run too, where it was a lost
rejection since 2026-09-10: `class A { static if (true) { uint32 x; } }
class B { … return x; }` is "Symbol name not in scope: `x`" at the use
(`scratchpad/sc/leak1.k`, and `leak3.k` with the predicate undecided).
Still toward silence: a `static if` inside a nested block is covered by
the whole function.

Seven tests in `elaborate::twin_names_tests`, each proven load-bearing by
mutation: the twin back on `passes::run` (three red), `is_alias` false,
`original_of` dropped, the holder widened to the file (two red, the
"seen from its own class" one green), `dropped` handed as `None` and the
round chain cut (one red each), and `this` removed — that last one
proven on `kg dump twin` over `scratchpad/sc/lam1.k`, whose declined
count goes 0 → 2, since a capturing lambda needs `data.closure` and the
unit harness loads no base library.

**Seventeen declines, all one finding, left open.** The `ir` gate's
carried-home line went from `9 raised, 9 carried, 0 declined` to `10, 8,
17`. Every decline is pass 9 over a twin reporting a *template parameter
name* — `U` fifteen times in `test/library/data/array.k`'s second round,
`TestDiscard` twice in `data/fifo/wide_to_narrow.k` — at a node no pair
aligns, so nothing reaches the output. What it says about the twin is the
point: somewhere in a copy's desugared parts (a hoisted lambda body, a
member template's copy) a parameter survives unsubstituted, and every type
under it is what the twin's table makes of an undefined name. Not this
batch's; it needs the copies read, not the seam.

One process note. `cargo test -p kg-db` rebuilds the library and not the
`kg` binary, and an hour went into "the holder rule does nothing" against
a stale `target/release/kg`. Probe with the binary the change was built
into, or build it first.

## A report at the parentheses the twin printed

*2026-09-16, later. Conformance **2467 → 2468/2468**, strict **138 →
137**, `errors` **530** agreeing at 25 disagreements, 86 silent; `xtask
ir`'s `carried home` reads 9 of 9, none declined.*

`{.x = false, .y = -10}` into a foreign copy's struct member was raised
in the twin — the target had its fields, the designator its slot, the
narrowing its hint — and never arrived: `carried home … declined 1`. The
printer parenthesises operands, so the twin's text reads `(-10)`, the
pass reported at the parentheses, and a range that starts at `(` is
start-aligned with no node the module's own text has. The reference's
note is the operand's (`checkConversion`'s `a`, `TypeCheck.hs:152-157`),
so the pass now reports at the innermost expression the parentheses wrap
(`unparen`), which is also where the reference puts it
(`template-instance-identifiers.k::37`; `scratchpad/sc/p_b.k` 3:54).

A probe first: three cross-module shapes, of which the positional one
was silent on both sides — a positional narrowing continues with the
outer continuation, a warning, where a designator switches to
`errorNarrowingConversions` (`:157`) — and the direct struct template
reported fine, which is what put the difference at the printer and not
the pass. The callback-field pair (`dependent-template.k::12,15`) stays:
its element is a dependent template instance *as a value*, a function
the twin has yet to type.

## An alias to an instance

*2026-09-16. Conformance **2465 → 2467/2467**, strict **140 → 138**,
`errors` **529** agreeing at 25 disagreements, 87 silent.*

`using Bbool = B<bool>;` then `Bbool::A<uint32>::A3_t`. The census read
`Bbool` as a namespace — a leading qualifier naming no class — stripped
it, and decided the *top-level* `A<uint32>`, which exists in the same
helper and has no `A3_t`: a wrong copy, then silence. The reference's
`resolveTypeName` (`Parser.hs:736-757`) replaces an alias prefix with its
target for the segments after it, so `Bbool::A<uint32>` is
`B<bool>::A<uint32>`, a member of an instance, postponed until the copy
exists.

Three pieces, all on the census and the type table; two more on the CST
index were written and deleted for pinning nothing:

* every top-level `using X = …;` is a class-like qualifier to the census,
  whatever it names, and one whose target is not yet a bare class name
  defers its member to the next round (`Candidate::deferred` again);
* the twin's `using Bbool = __kg_m0;` names a plain copy, read through
  whatever the lowering wrapped a bare name in — a value, a qualified
  identifier, a type identifier — and `IrTemplates::member` resolves the
  alias to the class;
* the declaration map expands an alias qualifier to its target's own
  qualified name and asks the imports for the rest
  (`Declarations::type_of_symbol`), which is how `Bbool::__kg_m1::A3_t`
  reaches a foreign copy's member.

`::38,40` report where the reference does; `::37` is a designated
initializer's narrowing, a different family. The CST index learnt the
same aliases first, for the validation of `Bbool::A<uint32>` in the base
run — and the base run has nothing to validate there: the reference
postpones the whole member until the copy exists, and so, now, does this
port. Both additions went green when broken and are gone.

---

## `a.template b<…>` is one name

*2026-09-15, later. Conformance **2463 → 2465/2465**, strict **142 →
140**, `errors` **527** agreeing at 25 disagreements, 89 silent.*

`obj.template Go<uint32>()` with no `obj` anywhere is, to the reference,
"Undefined template `Go`" at `Go` — never "Symbol name not in scope:
`obj`". The parser reads the whole access as one `TemplateInstance` over
the scoped name `obj::Go`; pass 9 does not judge a template instance's
name, and pass 12's `lookupSymbol` on `obj::Go` fails whole
(`unresolvedTemplateErrors e _`, `Frontend.hs:431`). The same verdict
comes from a receiver the table *does* know whose `Go` is a plain
function: the lookup finds something that is not a `Template`, and that
is the `_` arm too. So pass 9 now leaves the receiver of a
`.template` access alone, and pass 12 reports the member where the
receiver has no class the table can name, or a class the index knows
with no member template of that name — and only there: a class the
index cannot answer for (two of that simple name) is its silence, not an
absence. Both `dependent-template.k` copies report at the helper's line
with the instance as their frame (`::1,5`; `scratchpad/fn/f1.k` 13:18).

Small, and mostly a note on shape: three probes in a row of the same
family — the keyword before a bare name, the keyword after a dot, and
the dot on a known class — were three different arms, and the second
was silenced by the very early exit the first had relaxed, since a
member access carries its `template` keyword as a token of the
`FIELD_EXPR`, not of a path segment. And the gate caught the arm's
first width: a receiver the table leaves *unresolved* — declared under
a `static if` inside a function, which the fold does not reach — is a
hedge, not an absence; only the table's `Undefined` is one
(`dependent-template.k::10,12`, one `expected:0` and one verdict the
arm had displaced).

## A dead branch declares nothing

*2026-09-15. Conformance **2457 → 2463/2463**, strict **148 → 142**,
`errors` **525** agreeing at 25 disagreements, 91 silent; `bench` keystroke
370 ms against 366 interleaved. `static if`, decided.*

`staticControl` (`Constexpr.hs:41-47`) runs *inside* pass 6, so every pass
from 9 on sees a decided `static if` as its live branch, spliced into the
enclosing scope (`removeNestedScope`), and nothing of the other. This port
kept both branches as hedges — every name a `static if` declares counted
everywhere, which turned the `expected:1` half of each static-if pair into
a lost rejection. Now the predicate of every *top-level* `static if` is
folded once per file, with the constants the file can see
(`facts::dead_static_if_branches`), and the dead branch is:

* nothing to the declaration map the inference resolves names in
  (`types::Walk` files nothing under it), and nothing to the inference's
  own walk, which visits a decided `static if`'s live branch in full as
  the spliced declarations it becomes rather than its condition alone —
  so `static if (Cond) { using T = uint32; } else { struct T {…} }` files
  one `T`, the struct, and `const T x = 10` is the conversion the
  reference reports (`static-if.k::72`);
* nothing to pass 9's hedge: a name declared only in a dead branch is
  undefined at its use, with the reference's hint (`::31,33`).

The last was the surprise of the day. Four filters were written for pass
9 — the scope tables, the whole-program map, the file's own name set, and
a skip for uses inside the dead branch — and only the hedge's exclusion
went red when broken. The item tree never files a `static if`'s
declarations at all: the hedge *is* their only route into this pass, and
a use inside a branch was never judged before elaboration to begin with.
Three filters and a whole-program `alive` check were deleted for pinning
nothing; the note is here because the next reader will reach for them
again.

Inside copies the reference's fold is the twin's: `static_control`
(`kg_hir::rewrite`) runs over each round's output, keeping the live branch
of a `static if` whose predicate a substitution made a literal — and
folding first the one comparison a substitution leaves behind, two integer
literals under `<`, `>` and their kin (`N > 10` under `N = 1`). So
`auto_Fn<false>` returns `10` into a `bool` (`::3`). A copy's parameter
also prints bare again: the resolved-instance qualifier arm of 2026-09-11
now excludes a *function* copy's name, since `__kg_m0::x` resolves but
names no runtime value to any pass that looks for a bare name — which is
what kept `static if (x != 0)` over a `const T x` silent (`::26`), together
with the folder's silence on a name it cannot fold, which the reference's
"did not evaluate to a boolean constant" does not share.

The gate caught one thing the probes had not: `template Go<bool>()` where
the only `Go` sits under `static if (false)` moved from silent to
*disagreeing*. Pass 9 reported "Symbol name not in scope" where the
reference says "Undefined template `Go`" — pass 12's message
(`unresolvedTemplateErrors e _`, `Frontend.hs:431`), because pass 9 does
not judge a dependent template's name at all. Now it leaves the `template`
keyword's name alone, and pass 12 reports it where no template the keyword
could reach exists (`dependent-template.k::8`). "Could reach" took two
tries: the first version asked the top-level index and invented "Undefined
template" for every `template Go<…>` whose `Go` sits under a live `static
if` or is a member of the enclosing class — three `expected:0` assertions
and a fourth snippet, caught by the gate, never by a probe. The keyword
exists precisely for the declarations the parse-time table cannot see, so
the question is now asked of every `template <…>` in the program's text:
in scope when it is top level (through any `static if`) or a member of a
class enclosing the use, and not in one of this file's dead branches
(`Templates::is_named_live`). Without the keyword the reference's parser
rejects first (divergence #7), so that form is untouched.

The tripwire fired, and was worth its name. The gate run read `bench`
keystroke at **450 ms** against the 363–366 of the last three commits;
an interleaved A/B against the previous commit, built in its own
worktree and target directory, confirmed +84 ms on `risc-v.k`. Twelve
single toggles of everything this batch added each left it at 450 — and
so did all twelve at once — because the one toggle that mattered was
wrong: it filtered *after* the walk it meant to disable. `Templates::of`
had grown a `descendants()` over every node of every root to find the
`template <…>` declarations the keyword can reach, and it is built once
per twin round. A descent that enters only where a declaration can sit
— a class's list, a `static if`'s branches, a block — reads 370. The
lesson for the next time is the second one: prove a toggle disables what
you think it does before you read anything into its number.

Left in the family: `obj.Do()` on `Method<false>` and a capture of a
member a dead branch took (`::42,61`). Both are undefined names *inside a
copy* — the twin's table now reads a copy's missing member as `Undefined`
(a materialised class declares every member it has) — and pass 9 does not
run over a twin: it needs the whole program's symbol map, which the twins
do not yet have. That is the next piece.

## A deduced call on a receiver

*2026-09-14, later. Conformance **2448 → 2457/2457**, strict **157 →
148**, `errors` **519** agreeing at 25 disagreements, 97 silent; `bench`
keystroke 364 ms, in the slow mode's band.*

`deduced_calls` declined every `FieldExpr` callee with a note that the
census and the minting "do not spell" a member's key. Both do now — the
receiver form of the morning gave the census `prefix.Class.Fn`, and
`with_deduction` had resolved the member through the receiver's class all
along (`Type.hs:1390-1391`) for the diagnostic half. The site records the
class, the rewrite keys a member template by its class's simple name and
its own (`by_member`), phase one hands a foreign member deduction to the
class's module the same way, and `o.Fn_T_10(x)` over `uint4[9][4]` reports
the conversion the reference reports: deduction binds `T` from the
element, the outer dimension disagrees, and the call says so
(`template-argument-deduction.k::101,119,124,138`).

Two things the twin prints that are worth knowing about. A copy's
parameter mention prints as `Class::__kg_m0::x[0]` — the resolved-instance
qualifier arm of 2026-09-11 — and resolves, since a parameter is a table
entry under its function (`Parser.hs:378`); it is not wrong, only
verbose. And the written-qualifier rule of the morning needed an adjacency
test: a decl-scope prefix `makeQualified` mints wears the declaring
class's *name* range, which spells itself from across the file, so a
written `C::W` is now one whose prefix sits just before its leaf with
`::` between.

Two more shapes fell in the same sitting. A partly explicit deduced call
— `Fn_T_T_N<bool>(10, fs)` — is `explicitArgs <> deducedArgs`
(`Type.hs:1407`): the rewrite keeps the written list as written and mints
the deduced tail after it, and a foreign owner is handed the written
arguments as shapes too. And `o.Fn_uint_N_M(x)` on `static Template_N<5>
o`, where the receiver has no class until its copy lands: the base table
holds nothing for `o` (or, once elaborated, a class by a mangled name no
source declares), so such a call opens the next round outright; the
twin's deduction then reads the copy's `uint<5>[M]` and binds `M = 2`; the
rewrite's index learns the finished twins' own templates (a copy's member
is one); and a minted instance of a template the twin does not own is a
`TwinDecision` like a written one, made by the owner on the next pass. A
mistake along the way is worth its line: restricting the by-leaf map to
one-segment paths, to keep members out of it, silently declined every
*foreign* deduced call — a foreign template's path carries its namespace
— and the cross-module integration test caught it in the gate run.

The four `template-argument-deduction.k` shapes that stay silent all use
`Fn_T_T_N<Enum[4]>(es, fs)`-style explicit *array* arguments of an
imported enum, or a closure — the next families.

## A member template named through a receiver

*2026-09-14. Conformance **2441 → 2448/2448**, strict **164 → 157**,
`errors` **510** agreeing at 25 disagreements, 106 silent; `bench`
keystroke 363 ms, in the slow mode's band. `c.Foo<bool>(x)` and everything it needed.*

The census read `Exp::Path` and nothing else, so a member template named
through a receiver — `c.Foo<bool>(x)`, a `TemplateInstance` under a
`FunctionSpecifier` whose class the lowering could not know
(`$unresolved`) — was never a candidate, and the copy the reference makes
inside the class never existed here. The receiver's *type* names the
class (`MemberAccessF`, `Type.hs:1390-1391`); the candidate's site is the
name's own range, which the sorted lowering's node for the callee wears.
A receiver typed as an instance no round has materialised yet
(`static T2<uint32> c`) defers the call to the round whose twin declares
the copy (`Candidate::deferred`, another postponement).

Four consequences, each found by the next probe:

* **A function-typed value parameter.** The guard's IR reading declined
  any kind that mentions a parameter inside a larger type; the CST side
  had `function_type_written` all along. `(S) -> T Fn` on the copy is now
  read position by position — a parameter's mention is the lowering's
  `TypeParam` node where it resolved it, a bare path where it did not.
* **A function named as an argument.** The mangler declines `NamedValue`,
  rightly: a named constant is folded before the reference mangles
  anything. But a function *is* mangled, `@Go` (`Mangle.hs:53,56`), and
  the copy's body calls it by name (`kg-oracle --tree`, `scratchpad/fn/
  r2.k`, `Bar<|$bool@Go|>`). The census records the shape
  (`ArgShape::Function`), the mention sheds its wrapper before `resolve`
  (`canonical_args`, which the specs now read their lists from — the
  first version took them off the twin *before* the unwrap, and resolved
  a mention to a copy nobody made), and a foreign owner mints the bare
  name and tells its twin the type (`Imports::with_foreign`), declined
  where the owner declares that name itself.
* **`check` before `instantiate`.** With the receiver form deciding
  `c.Bar<uint16, 6>` on a `bool x` parameter, the copy was made and its
  body and call failed conversions the reference never reaches: `check`
  replaces the rejected instance with an `Error` node first
  (`Template.hs:58`, `TypeCheck.hs:223-229`). Every twin round now asks
  pass 8 what it rejects (`rejected_instance_lists`) and drops those
  occurrences (`InstanceSet::reject`). Round one needs no such filter —
  the census gate already refuses a program the home run rejects — and
  the one written for it pinned nothing and was deleted.
* **`null (errors a)`.** `return c.Foo<bool>(x)` with a rejected argument
  is one error at `x`; the return's conversion is silenced because the
  argument is already an `ErrorF` (`TypeCheck.hs:162`). Two things had
  to change: the conversion pass visits children before parents (the
  sink is what `poisoned` reads), and the home run's sink is *seeded*
  with the twin's carried verdicts (`Db::frontend_diagnostics`), which
  also gives the reference's program-wide `hasErrors` its cross-twin
  reach.

Left in the families this touched: deduced member calls (`o.Fn_T_10(x)`,
`deduced_calls` declines a `FieldExpr` callee — the shape is now the
census's, the deduction half is not), a receiver reached through an
index (`c2s[1].c[0].Foo<uint32>`, a parse-time verdict), and `Do<uint32,
A<uint4>::A1_t>` as a function argument.
