## Fields are items, never symbols

*2026-09-06, the first DX slice under the new queue. Tests 1258 → 1262;
conformance, strict, corpus, formatter and the errors gate unchanged.*

The reference files a `Struct` or `Union` with `const mempty`
(`Symbols.hs:48-49`) and parses a field with `uninitVar`, never `symbol`
(`Parser.hs:465`): a field is in no symbol map and no scope. That is why
aggregate bodies were never lowered — and why goto-definition, hover,
highlight and references all declined on `s.x`, which is most of what a
hardware programmer points at.

The two facts are separable. A field is now an **item** in the tree —
`Variable(DeclareMember)`, keyed under the struct's `$quasiN` scope, with the
struct as its `parent` — and it is *still* never declared into a scope and
never a global symbol: `in_config` skips `Item::is_field()`, and so do the
three other consumers that mean "what `getSymbols` files" (`unambiguous_names`
for constant folding, `declared_by_last_component` for import attribution,
and `shadowed_declaration`, which already excluded members). Two
`kg-resolve` tests that pinned the item list as *evidence* of the symbol
rule now assert both halves separately; pinning the tree alone had said
nothing about the symbols.

`definition_at` answers `a.b` off `a`'s **type** — `tLookupField`'s own
route (`Type.hs:961-971`) — looking through `Const` and `Instance`, finding
the aggregate's item by qualified name and the field among its children.
Class members resolve the same way, which is also the reference's
(`Type.hs:1232-1235`). Hover shows a field as `S::x`, the one place the
`$quasiN` key is edited for display, because that key identifies nothing to
a user and, unlike every other key hover prints, no map holds it.

Three LSP tests that asserted "declines rather than answering textually"
were corrected to the positive answer: the declaration and `p.x` light up,
and the `const auto x` above the struct — the look-alike a textual match
would find — stays dark. That last clause is the property the old tests
were protecting, and it survives.

## The errors gate, and 88 disagreements that no green number had ever shown

*2026-09-06. `cargo xtask errors` lands: 131 disagreements on its first run,
43 by the end of the day. `conformance` 2098/2098 and `--strict` 508 before
and after; tests 1253 → 1258; every other gate at baseline. Two decisions
recorded in `roadmap.md`: the backend goes through the ParseTree C ABI, and
DX slices are interleaved from here on.*

`xtask conformance` compares exit codes and the first `Error N` and never a
position or a message (`docs/spec/conformance.md` §1.7). The review of this
date found two bugs of the class that leaves invisible — a missing import
reported at the wrong `import`, and a `TypeKey` collision — by running
`kg-oracle --errors` on a probe file by hand. This gate is that probe run over
every must-reject snippet: the reference's own frontend, with the snippet's
own ctest flags translated to the driver's spelling, against our first error
by position. **Containment**, not first-against-first — the reference lands a
circular import once per file in the cycle, and its output order is a tree
traversal — so the question is "is the first thing we say something the
reference says anywhere, at that place, in those words".

### What the first run said

131 disagreements, and the categorisation is the reusable part. Sorted by
message shape with names blanked, the top rows were whole *families*, not
snippets:

* 13 × `symbol redefinition. See previous declaration` — the reference
  appends ` at <path>:<line>:<col>` (`symbolLoc`, `Error.hs:108-112`), and
  we never had the path. `kg-resolve` now takes a display name
  (`lower_file_named`), and every `Item` records `decl`, where the reference
  *reports* a declaration, beside `range`, which is its name.
* 10 + 5 + 3 + 2 × a type error with the type missing: `Invalid operands to
  binary expression` where the reference says ``… : `uint8` and `bool` ``.
  The width algebra had no interner to render through, so it had omitted the
  operand — with a comment saying the text was "ours to improve". It now
  takes `names: Option<&Interner>` through twenty functions, and
  `Ty::element`/`field`/`field_at` likewise. `basics::199` printed
  ``Types `?` and `?` `` on the way, which is what an unthreaded interner
  looks like.
* 10 + 9 + 6 × a message that agreed and a position that did not.

### Four rules about *where*, each measured against the oracle

**A declaration is reported at its first token, after `static`.**
`err x e = NotedExp (note (unfix x) <> n)` (`Frontend.hs:388`) reports at
the member's own note, and a `Variable`'s note begins at its type — the
oracle prints `9:1` for `uint32 x;` and `11:8` for `static Foo f;`. We
reported at the *name*. Five sites moved (exportable-class members, the two
function-type variable checks, template-parameter redefinition, symbol
redefinition).

**The node range is not the declaration.** The tree attaches a comment to the
node that follows it, so `VAR_DECL@24..50` begins at `// a comment`. Every
one of those five sites would have pointed at the comment; `kg_syntax::
trimmed_range` is the one place that knows, and `Item::decl` is computed
through it. `static assert(false)` under a comment was the visible case
(`basics::42`, reported on line 2, a comment, against the reference's 3:15).

**The reference has no paren node.** `parens expression` returns the inner
expression with a note taken before the `(`, so an error on `(a << b)` is at
the paren. Pass 10 now climbs every enclosing `PAREN_EXPR` before reporting.

**A parse error lands on the next token, not on the trivia before it.**
`Event::Error`'s offset was `raw`'s text start, and `raw` may still point at a
blank line or a comment; megaparsec's offset is taken after `whitespace`. One
loop in `output.rs` took the parse-position class from 36 to 18 and moved no
test. `basics::25` had reported `static` misplaced at 1:1, an empty line.

Two rules about *what*, both from the same instrument. The parser twin of
`checkConstLValue` names the **base** symbol (`symbolError s`,
`Parser.hs:794-801`) — `` `s` `` for `s.x = 1` on a `const s` — and only
`checkConstLValue` itself, reached for a `const` member of a mutable object,
spells the lvalue. And an array-dimension error wears the *literal's* note
when one was written and the *bracket's* when the parser substituted the
value (`uint32[0]` at the `0`, `int32[3.14]` and an enum value at the `[`);
the first reading of that rule was wrong in both directions until the second
example appeared, which is the argument for a corpus-wide gate over a probe
file.

### What the gate books, and why each booking is keyed to a mechanism

* **Parse-time table, 28.** The reference's *parser* rejects `static a1<10>
  x;` with `unexpected '<'` because its symbol table says `a1` is not a
  template (`Parser.hs:668-680`); ours has no table at parse time and name
  resolution reports the name two columns earlier. That is divergence #7 by
  construction, so the verdict is booked, not failed — but only when *every*
  error the reference reports is a grammar error (`unexpected …`). The
  reference routes its symbol table's and import loader's verdicts through
  the same parse-error channel with messages of their own (`Circular
  dependency`, `Can't find file`), and those compare like any frontend
  error. The first draft booked all of them and hid eight real agreements
  and one real disagreement.
* **Hint lists compare as sets** (divergence #29): the reference's order is
  `HashMap.toList`. Which names are offered is still graded, and five
  snippets still differ there — the reference's `inScope` needs the
  referring scope, and it filters by *inferred* type, so an `auto` whose
  initialiser is the undefined name is never offered as a hint for itself.
* **Nested `In imported file:` bundles** (`Error.hs:60`) are parsed to their
  innermost location, because we report an error where it is.
* **Skipped, 92, counted by reason**: the driver takes no `--define`,
  `--target-device` or `--Werror`.

### What it cannot see, stated

Only the first error per side. The 433 snippets we compile cleanly are
"ours silent" and `--verbose` prints the reference's message for each —
which is the attribution the strict-failure surveys used to do by hand with a
shell loop. A message that agrees at a wrong *second* error is invisible
until the first is fixed. And `check_snippet` is the graded route on our
side, so a `kg check` that rendered differently from the harness would not
show here.

---

## Two bugs the scoreboard cannot see, found by driving the binaries and the debug build

*2026-09-06, review session. Conformance 2098/2098 and `--strict` 508 before and
after; tests 1251 → 1253; every other gate at baseline.*

Both were found the way `CLAUDE.md`'s last rule says to look — run the thing a
user runs — and neither could have moved a conformance number, which is the
point of writing them down together.

### A missing import was reported at the wrong `import`

`kg check` on a file whose *second* import cannot be found pointed the error at
the *first* one — or, on a library file run without `-I`, at the copyright
comment on line 1. The reference reports `parseFileFailure offset err` at the
failing import's own keyword (`Parser.hs:195-201`; `docs/spec/diagnostics.md`
example 4 shows `2:1` for exactly this shape), and `kg-oracle --errors`
confirms it in one invocation.

The cause is a lookup that could never succeed: `program.rs` looked the failed
import up in `ModuleGraph::imports`, and a failed import is precisely the one
the loading loop `continue`s past without adding to the graph. The fallback,
`importer.start()`, is offset 0, so every such error landed there. The item
tree holds every written import with its range; that is where the keyword now
comes from. Pinned by `a_missing_import_is_reported_at_its_own_keyword`, which
reads offset 0 against 9 without the fix.

The conformance harness compares exit codes and `Error N` and never a position
(`docs/spec/conformance.md` §1.7), so this class is invisible to it by
construction. The oracle's `--errors` mode is the only instrument that sees it,
and its README already records one more of the same class — `nosuch()` reported
at the expression here and at the member name there — "not yet investigated".
A position-and-message differential over the `expected:1` snippets is the gate
this project does not have.

### Two `ERROR` nodes of one extent, and an assertion release never runs

`cargo run -p xtask -- bench` — the **debug** build, which the `cargo xtask`
alias never produces — panicked in `check` on `test/syntax/loops.k`:
`the maintained resolved-count disagrees with a walk of the tree`, 1631 against
1629. Eight snippet accumulators trip it; no clean parse does.

`TypeKey`'s documentation claims no two nodes of one kind share a full range,
and `TypeTable::resolved` — the counter that replaced a 38%-of-`infer_program`
walk on 2026-08-11 — depends on it: one key written resolved counts once, and a
walk that finds two nodes at that key counts twice. The claim was false on
exactly one shape, `type_()`'s fallthrough: it opened a marker, called
`err_recover` — which wraps the token it consumes in an `ERROR` of its own — and
then completed the marker as `ERROR` around it. Two `ERROR` nodes, one range,
one key, typed `Untyped` by the algebra's catch-all and therefore resolved. The
discrepancy is the number of such pairs, and it was 2 on that file.

The parser keeps the outer node — it is the type *slot*, and stays even when
recovery consumes nothing — and puts the token straight into it. Pinned by
`no_two_nodes_of_one_kind_share_a_range` over the whole corpus, accumulators
included, which names all eight files without the fix. `cargo xtask fuzz` now
has a `check` stage so a recovered tree that panics the frontend is a fuzz
failure rather than a bench surprise; it is clean at 2000 mutations.

### And two numbers nobody had re-read

`cargo xtask bench` in release, on a quiet machine, reads `check` **75.9 ms**
— byte-for-byte the documented value — and `keystroke` **211.7 ms** against a
documented 108.3. `check` holding still rules out load. The read-back landed
`Db::elaboration` on the `Db::diagnostics` path and neither commit of that day
mentions a bench run; the tripwire fired, on this reading, three weeks late.
Not fixed here — the elaboration is the feature, `float32.k` declares
templates, and the memo cannot help an edit — but a keystroke that costs
thirteen frames is now a number in `status.md` rather than one nobody held.

`cargo xtask repoint` reads **14/72**, not 13. The +1 is `doc-comments`, which
`--parse-docs` delivered on 2026-08-14 to a `target/release/kanagawa` last
built on the 13th; `repoint` does not rebuild the binary it grades
(`repoint.rs:76` says so) and nobody had. A gate that grades a stale artefact
reports the previous commit's world.

Two things worth keeping. `debug_assert` invariants in `kg-ty` run under
`cargo test` and under nothing else this repo documents, because every
corpus-wide gate is `--release`. And the counter's identity
`unresolved = nodes − resolved` is a claim about the *tree*, not the table,
which is why a parser test rather than a `kg-ty` test pins it.

## The read-back landed, and the consumers the plan named were the wrong ones

*The last piece of the print-and-reparse route: `kg_hir::readback` (the side
map and the five-field write), `kg_db::elaborate` (the production driver), and
`deduceTemplateArgs`' rewrite half. `conformance` 2087→**2088**, `--strict`
519→**518**, and the fifth `TypeKey` field has its first production caller.
Scratch in a scratch directory (not kept).*

The route as it now runs on every `kg check` and every language-server
diagnostic pass, per module that declares a top-level template:
`lower_sorted → pipeline → deduce rewrite → resolve → instantiate → rename →
pretty_with_source → reparse → lower_sorted the twin → infer the twin with the
existing engine → side map → read back`. The elaborated table is what
`frontend_diagnostics` hands the passes, so "the deduced type becomes the
call's type" is now true for same-module instances — `uint32 x = 1 <<
Hold(z);` with a local `template <typename T> T Hold(T x)` reports the
reference's exact `Invalid shift left` where it compiled clean before, with
`Hold<uint64>` deduced, materialised, printed, re-inferred and read home.

### The strict consumers the brief named do not exist yet, and that was checkable

The plan said `template-argument-deduction.k`'s 41 "now need pass 8 alone"
(`status.md`). Running the oracle over all 41 says otherwise:

* **15 are `Invalid conversion from …`** — `checkConversion'`'s *error*
  clause, which this port has never wired: `conversion.rs` reports only the
  narrowing *warning*, and its doc says so ("four of its five outcomes are
  errors and are silences here"). The **return** site is not visited at all
  (`checkReturn`, `TypeCheck.hs:77-87`). Read-back types alone move zero of
  these; the pass-19 clause is the missing half.
* **18 are deduction conflicts** whose second binding comes from
  `setTypeOfTemplateCall` (`Type.hs:1120-1129`) — and our
  `is_template_instance` guard requires a *written* argument list, because the
  reference's guard is satisfied by pass 4's rewrite having wrapped every
  deducible callee in a `TemplateInstance` first. On the CST that wrap does
  not exist, so the stamp never lands and step 3 of the deduction never fires.
* Nearly all deduce against templates in `helper/`, the cross-module boundary
  below. The handful that instantiate a *local* template (`::31`'s `Go<10>()`)
  still land on the unwired conversion clause: the read-back types their call
  today, and pass 19 has nowhere to put the answer.

One strict assertion did fall, and it is instructive about mechanism:
`function-template::20`, `Foo<uint32>()` calling a class template instance.
The twin's inference types the call `tReturn (TClass …)` = `TError "Undefined
function"` (`Type.hs:582`) — the reference's own inner-inference product — the
read-back carries the error type home, and pass 10 reports it. The reference
happens to reject the same program earlier, at parse time; the code matches.

### The cross-module boundary, measured

Same-module instances only, and the two blockers are named in
`elaborate.rs`'s module doc rather than worked around: (1)
`passes::types::Imports` resolves an imported name through the defining
module's **item tree** (`type_of_def`), and a materialised declaration exists
in no item tree — so a cross-module mangled mention cannot type-resolve
however the twin program is assembled; (2) the rename layer mints its
bijection **per module**, so two modules alias one mangled name independently
and a twin *program* cannot link. Both are program-scope naming decisions —
the next slice, not a caller trick. The journal's "the import closure is not
a problem for the synthetic file" was measured on a single-file prototype and
does not extend to the corpus's helper-module shape.

### The type-agreement gate, and what its first run caught

`xtask ir` now prints `type agreement: N/M elaborated roots` — every type the
read-back wrote at a materialised copy must be one the reference's own
`typeof` holds at that text range, read off a new `kg-oracle --typed` mode
(`--notes` plus `showPretty typeof` per note, US/RS-delimited so the scan
cannot desynchronise). Containment, not a bijection; blind spots are printed
at the line. Its first run read **0/34 with 2204 types compared** — because
`elaborate.rs` rendered with `show_pretty(ty, None)` and every name printed
`?`. A structural gate would have stayed green forever; the instrument paid
for itself before its falsification was even run.

Then it was run, and this is the measurement the whole slice rests on. **Plant
A2 — read each twin type from the *previous* pair while writing home at the
current one.** Structurally intact: every node still gets a type, every
structural gate stays green, and only the pairing is wrong. That is the exact
failure mode nothing else here can see. `type agreement` went **13/28 → 0/30**,
and the disagreements went whole-file — `fixed.k` 60 of 60, `float32/internal.k`
84 of 84, `float32.k` 314 of 335 — where the honest run's are partial. **Plant B
— skip `unrename_ty` on the way home**, so a type comes back spelling
`__kg_mN`: `an_alias_spelling_is_unrenamed_on_the_way_home` goes red with
`Struct([Symbol(9)])` against `Struct([Symbol(8)])`.

The line is therefore not a self-report. It distinguishes a right pairing from
a wrong one that survives every structural check, which is what the brief made
the condition for trusting any of this.

**13/28 is the honest number and it is not a target.** The 15 disagreeing roots
are *not* booked — no booking here names an unported pass, and inventing one
would be exactly the "predicate that holds whatever the code does" this project
has caught twice. They are unattributed, and unattributed is the correct thing
to print until someone measures them.

### Costs priced

`Db::elaboration` is memoized on program identity like `inference`, and the
early-out is "no module of the program declares a top-level template", checked
off memoized parses — most conformance snippets and every template-free file
skip the route entirely. The gates moved: `conformance` runs in about the same
time; `xtask ir` grew ~90 s of `--typed` oracle prefetch plus the per-root
elaborations.

`capture diff` and `lambda diff` graded 122 `library/` roots. `library/` holds
**119 of the corpus's 1306 lambdas** — 9% — so `lambda diff` was grading
`desugarLambdas` on a twentieth of its own blast radius while printing a clean
122/122. Extending both to `test/` costs one `collect` call and ~65 s of oracle
time, and takes the ledger to **890 rewritten lambdas across 109 roots**.

Two files disagreed immediately, and the first was the gate's fault.

**`test/library/processor/risc-v.k` — the guard was measuring an unported
pass.** The ledger drops `$wrapper$…` entries by name, because
`addLambdaWrappers` is sub-pass 1 and unported. Its `survivors` count did not.
So the reference claimed a survivor this port can never hold:
`$wrapper$CustomDecode`, at `Tests::DecoderTests::$::$quasi0::$quasi1`, minted
from `decode_instr(LUI, CustomDecode)` passing a bare function name. Every real
lambda in that file agreed. The filter has to be applied to *both* halves of a
ledger or the half without it silently measures something else.

**`test/interface/is_last_exported_class.k` — a real divergence, from a pass
five stages upstream.** Its `static for (const auto i : 2)` has a constant
bound, and `staticControl` (`Constexpr.hs:41-54`) rewrites `StaticForF` to
`UnrolledForF` — as an algebra of `inferExpTree`, i.e. **pass 6**, so it has run
long before pass 8 begins. Only `evaluateConstexpr`'s third of that is ported
here, so our tree still holds an `Exp::StaticFor` and `desugarLambdas` correctly
reverts on it where the reference, holding no `StaticFor` at all, goes ahead.
Verified directly: `StaticForF 0, UnrolledForF 1` in the reference tree.

### The booking, and the hole in the first attempt

The first relaxation was "on a file where the reference unrolled something,
require `ours.survivors >= theirs.survivors`" — one-sided, so the direction the
guard exists for still bites. It was not enough, and the failure taught the
lesson: the *entries* diverge for the same reason. That file has two nested
lambdas, `[]()` outside and `[](index_t<16> i)` inside, both named `?lambda0` in
different scopes; the reference desugars both and we desugar one, so a sorted
pairwise comparison lines our single entry up against their first and reports a
`params` mismatch that is not one.

Relaxing entries to a subset would then have admitted a port that rewrites
**nothing** — `ours >= theirs` on survivors is satisfied by doing no work at
all. What closes it is a **conservation law**, and it holds on every file,
booked or not:

> a written lambda either becomes a ledger entry or survives — never both,
> never neither.

Wrappers are excluded from both halves, so the two sides count the same
population and this is an equality rather than a bound. On the offending file:
theirs 2 entries + 0 survivors, ours 1 + 1. Both 2. With that in place the
relaxation can be "every lambda we rewrote, we rewrote exactly as they did" and
still not be free.

The general shape is worth keeping: **when an unported pass forces you to relax
a comparison, find the quantity it conserves.** A relaxation with nothing
holding it down is indistinguishable from deleting the check.

### The two lines do not detect independently

Falsified rather than assumed. `captureThis` narrowed to fire only on lambdas
that already capture something moves `capture diff` **and** `lambda diff` to
exactly **298/351** — the same 53 files. `lambda diff` sees it because the
implicit `this` is capture 0 and therefore part of every in-class lambda's
`make_captureN` arity.

So `capture diff` is not buying extra arity coverage, and saying otherwise
because two green numbers sit next to each other would be the kind of implied
claim this project keeps catching itself making. What it *does* buy is the
`--passes 3` boundary, which is independent of pass 8 entirely, and the lambdas
`desugarLambdas` never rewrites and therefore never enters in the ledger. Both
are kept for that reason and not for the count.

### And a measurement that was never real

`oracle diff` appeared to have gone from 42 s to 140 s. It had not moved at all:
one `Instant` was covering all three oracle fan-outs, so widening the other two
was billed to the first. Each has its own timer now — 23.6 s, 42.3 s, 44.5 s.
A shared timer is a shared number, and a shared number is a wrong one as soon as
anything beside it changes.

## `desugarLambdas`, and a gate technique that did not generalise

1,849 lines for 74 lines of Haskell (`Function.hs:189-262`), and **1289 of the
corpus's 1306 lambdas** rewritten. The 17 that are not are under a `static for`,
which the reference also leaves standing. Zero substrate additions — both of the
design's predictions were wrong, and so were both of its line-range citations
(`:189-202` lands mid-`lambdaRef`; `addLambdaWrappers` is `:366-423`, not
`:366-380`).

### The gate technique from the previous entry does not transfer

`captureThis` got the first whole-corpus line in this project on which a rewrite
is graded by the reference: two constructor **counts** at a pass boundary, one
minted only by the pass and one that no pass in the window touches. The obvious
move was to do the same for `desugarLambdas` at `--template-passes 1`→`2`. The
counts are there and they are beautiful:

```
             tp1    tp2   delta
LambdaF      146      5   −141
AliasF       184    325   +141
CastF        503    644   +141
FunctionF{LambdaFunction}
               0    141   +141
DecltypeF     52    296   +244   (141 + 103 non-generic)
VariableF   3157   3319   +162   (115 written + 47 `this`)
```

and they **cannot be the gate**. `addLambdaWrappers` is sub-pass 1 — inside the
window — and is not ported. It synthesizes 27 extra `library/` lambdas, so the
reference's `+141` is a number our side can only ever reach as 114; worse, a
wrapper's alias and function land inside *other* lambdas' bodies, so no per-file
total is decomposable into "ours" and "theirs" at all. The `captureThis` window
was clean by luck, not by design: nothing unported ran in it.

What replaces the counts is a **per-lambda ledger** — `(name, make_captureN
arity, param count, generic?, uncapture field indices)`. Every field is a direct
function of the source lambda, so a wrapper is simply an entry dropped by name,
and the comparison survives an unported pass minting entries we do not have.
Two details are load-bearing and both were found by running the thing:

* **Pair by adjacency, never by name.** `?lambda0` recurs — the parser's counter
  resets at every named scope (`Parser/SymbolTable.hs:183-192`) — and a nested
  lambda's declarations sit inside the outer function's subtree, so a
  name-keyed reader silently merges them. That version corrupted 9 of 122 roots.
* **`survivors` is the guard and it is not zero.** Five of `library/`'s 119
  lambdas are left standing under `static for` (3 in `data/hash_table.k`, 2 in
  `data/vector.k`). It is the one number that moves if the port desugars a
  lambda the reference leaves alone.

```
lambda diff: 122/122 library roots agree with the reference on every lambda
             `desugarLambdas` rewrites, at --passes 8 --template-passes 2
             reference: 114 rewritten across 26 roots, 5 left standing,
                        27 `$wrapper$` excluded
             make_captureN arities: 0:28 1:42 2:28 3:13 4:2 9:1
```

### What each instrument can and cannot see

Falsified rather than asserted, and the pattern is the useful part:

| plant | `lambda diff` | `lambdas:` invariant | unit tests |
|---|---|---|---|
| `xI` off by one | **98/122**, indices named | red | red |
| both `static for` stops dropped | **120/122** on `survivors` | red | red |
| capture param appended, not prepended | **122/122 — blind** | green | **red** (2 of 17) |

Position is not in the ledger, and it should not be: the ledger grades
*composition* — which lambdas were rewritten, with what arity, reading which
capture fields — and the unit tests grade *shape*. A gate that tried to do both
would be a tree comparison, which this window cannot support. Naming what an
instrument is blind to is the price of it being cheap enough to run.

### Two arms that are correct and unpinnable

`lambdaRef FunctionF{} = Nothing` (`:218`) and `lambdaDefs`' `Function{} = []`
(`:232`) both protect a nested local function's lambdas from being rewritten a
second time by the enclosing function's walk. I predicted, from a census showing
**131 of the corpus's lambdas** sit under two or more nested `FN_DECL`s, that
removing either would "not be subtle". Measured: removing either is **completely
invisible** — every gate stays green. The bottom-up cata has already emptied the
nested function of bare lambdas before any outer walk reaches it, and every
other position a `Function` could occupy relative to a lambda is a reference
`PARSE-ERROR`. Both arms are kept, as transcription and as defence against a
future traversal change, and the unpinnability is written at the code rather
than papered over with a test that would pass either way. This is the third time
this project has caught itself about to bank a vacuous test.

### A shallow protection that reads as a deep one

`static for` is where the transcription is most likely to go wrong, and the
Haskell says nothing about it locally. `lambdaDefs` stops at `StaticFor` and
`lambdaRef` reverts at it — but the **cata still visits lambdas inside the
loop**, so clause 2 still rewrites their *bodies*. A lambda nested inside a
static-for lambda is therefore desugared into the surviving lambda's body, and
only the outer one is left standing, bare, with no alias and no function.
`library/data/vector.k` has exactly that shape: three lambdas under a `static
for`, one nested inside another, and **two** survive at `--template-passes 2`.

I found this chasing a one-off disagreement between an AST census (which said 3)
and a direct oracle count (which said 2). The census was not wrong about the
syntax; it was wrong about the pass. Worth remembering the next time a corpus
census and the oracle disagree by one — the oracle is describing the pass, and
the census is describing the text.

### And a substring that reads backwards

`LambdaF` is a prefix of `LambdaFunction`, the `funcKind` this pass mints. A
substring count of `"LambdaF"` over `--tree` output therefore counts the pass's
own output as un-rewritten input: on a two-lambda fixture it reads 2 at
`--template-passes 1` **and** 2 at `2`, i.e. "nothing happened" on a tree where
everything did. `capture diff` could not have hit it — it reads `--passes 3`,
five passes before any `LambdaFunction` exists — but it is spelled with the
brace now so that it still cannot when it does.

## `captureThis`, and the first rewrite the reference grades

`captureThis` (`Frontend.hs:185-193`) is nine lines of Haskell. Three documents
in this repo described it as a detail with nothing to port and no diagnostic
behind it. All three were wrong, and the shape of the error is worth keeping,
because it is the same shape twice: a claim about the *reference* was inferred
from a claim about *this port*.

**"There is nothing left to port."** `crates/kg-db/src/lib.rs`, `passes/mod.rs`
and `docs/status.md` all said pass 3 was finished — `reifyEnums`' numbering
lives in `scope::enum_constant_value`, and `captureThis` "is read only by
`desugarLambdas`, inside pass 8, and is codegen shape". The premise is false:
`grep ThisF` over the reference finds **five** readers, and one of them is
`thisReference` (`Frontend.hs:452-456`), a clause of frontend pass **16**. The
conclusion is false for a sharper reason. `moveFunctions` rewrites a member
reference to `$this._x` from the *symbol map* (`memberAccess`,
`Function.hs:52-64`; the `:152-158` this entry cited is `makeCapture` and was
wrong), whether
or not this pass ran; the only thing that ever defines `$this` in the moved
lambda's scope is the local `desugarLambdas` unpacks out of the `This` capture.
So omitting pass 3 does not produce a slightly different tree — it produces a
tree in which `$this` is undefined, and `undefinedSymbols` (pass 9) reports it.
A missing rewrite five passes upstream manufacturing a spurious diagnostic five
passes downstream is exactly the failure mode this project books as "invented a
diagnostic about a correct program".

**"Every `this`-capturing lambda would get the wrong capture arity."**
`docs/status.md` said this, and it understates the pass twice. The rewrite is
*unconditional* — every `LambdaF` lexically inside a `ClassF` gets a `ThisF`,
whether or not it touches a member. **648 of the corpus's 1306 lambdas**, of
which **111 reference no member of their class at all**. For those 111 the
consequence is not an index slip: `makeCapture` selects its *module* on
`null lambdaCaptures` (`Function.hs:152-154`), so the emitted call is
`@data@closure@core::make_capture0` where the reference emits
`@data@closure::make_capture1`. A different function, silently.

**And "`this` is a sixth intrinsic."** `undefined_symbols::intrinsics` chained
`"this"` into the five-name set, reasoning that a `this` is a `ThisF` whose
failed lookup gives `TUnresolved`. The grammar has no `this` keyword
(`Parser/Lexer.hs:164-219`, 54 reserved words, none of them `this`); `ThisF` is
synthesized, post-parse, and is named `$this` (`Parser/Syntax.hs:267-268,739`),
a spelling no source file can produce. A written `this` is an ordinary `PATH`
and the reference rejects it — verified directly against the oracle. The
suppression hid a real error class. Fixed, pinned, and it moved no number:
no corpus assertion writes a bare `this`, which is why nothing caught it.

### The gate is the finding

`rewrite: 479/479` is a **self-report** — it says the pass ran and left the tree
sound. Nothing in it compares the 65 against the reference, and the reference
does not agree with the 65. That has been written at the call site since slice
1, and it is the weakest thing about the rewriting half.

`captureThis` gets something better, and the reason is worth generalising. The
oracle can print the reference's tree at any pass boundary, but comparing
*trees* at `--passes 3` is useless here: passes 1 and 2 have run by then and
neither is ported, so the shapes differ for reasons that have nothing to do
with this pass. Two **counts** isolate it exactly:

* `ThisF` — `captureThis` is the only producer before pass 8 (the other,
  `addLambdaWrappers`, is `Function.hs:407-409`, inside it).
* `LambdaF` — no pass before 8 adds or removes one, so this is the guard that
  stops the first count from agreeing by accident on a tree we read wrong.

```
capture diff: 122/122 library roots agree with the reference on
              `ThisF` and `LambdaF` counts at --passes 3
```

122 is every library root the oracle accepts. This is the first whole-corpus
line in the project on which a *rewrite* is graded by the reference instead of
by this port's reading of it, and the technique is not specific to `captureThis`
— any pass with a constructor it alone mints can be graded this way, for the
cost of one extra oracle run per file (+10s on the `xtask ir` wall clock).

**Both halves of the grade are load-bearing, and they see different corpora.**
Planting `Exp::Struct` where the nested-class boundary reads `Exp::Class`:

| | verdict |
|---|---|
| `capture diff:` | **122/122, unmoved** — no `library/` file nests a class inside a class |
| `capture:` (the port's own invariant) | **red on 3 `test/` files**, which the oracle cannot parse at all |

The reverse plant — fire only on lambdas that already capture something, the
plausible "surely it only matters if it captures" mistake — moves both: 648 →
367 `This` nodes, `capture diff` 122 → 114. So the reference grades the extent
and the independent walk grades the shape, and neither subsumes the other.

That independent walk is worth naming as a pattern. The pass derives "is this
lambda inside a class" by *firing* at `Class` and then *declining* at the next
one; the checker derives it by carrying a boolean down from the root. Two
derivations of one predicate, and the cheap one is the check.

### Three transcription details that are not obvious from the Haskell

**The donor is the capture list, not the lambda.** `copyNote` is
`renote . const` (`Desugar.hs:104`) applied to `lambdaCaptures`, so the `ThisF`
wears the capture-list `SeqF`'s note. Read off `--notes` for a `[]` lambda at
column 20, the `ThisF` and the `SeqF` around it print the identical
`Src {offset = 69, 6:20-6:20}` and the `LambdaF`'s is a different one. Under
`CLAUDE.md`'s house rule this is a unit test, and swapping the donor for the
lambda fails that test and nothing else in the tree.

**The scope is the lambda's, not the class's.** `l@LambdaF{..}` binds
`declScopeName` from the lambda, so a lambda in `Foo::Run` gets
`["Foo","Run","$"]` and one nested inside *it* gets
`["Foo","Run","$","?lambda0","$"]`. Substituting the class's scope turns six of
the nine unit tests red at once, which is what a genuinely load-bearing
distinction looks like.

**`Struct` and `Union` are neither triggers nor boundaries, and it does not
matter.** Both arms match `ClassF` and nothing else. A `struct` body is
`memberVariable \`sepEndBy\` semi` (`Parser.hs:299`) and cannot hold a function
or a lambda at all — the oracle rejects every fixture that tries. Recorded in
the module so a later reader does not "fix" the match to cover all three
aggregates.

### One fork, two passes, five passes apart

`captureThis` is frontend pass 3 and `abbreviatedFunctionTemplate` is sub-pass 3
of frontend pass 8. They are now composed by `rewrite::pipeline` over **one**
`ModuleIr::fork` — the arena decision from the slice-1 entry, arriving at its
first real test. `kg dump ir --rewrite` runs the pipeline; `xtask ir` grades the
two passes on separate lines over separate forks, because merging them would
break `unchanged_outside` (false the moment a lambda is rewritten) and would
make a movement in either count unattributable.

The first composed run also produced a small useful surprise. A census script
compared `kg dump ir --rewrite` against the reference at `--passes 3` and found
`library/data/function.k` with 18 lambdas to the reference's 16. Not a bug:
`abbreviatedFunctionTemplate` `deep_copy`s the leftover declaration, and that
body contains lambdas, so the pipeline legitimately holds two copies of each —
while the reference at `--passes 3` has not reached pass 8. The grade has to run
`capture_this` alone, which is what it does.

## Four passes, eight assertions, and an estimate that was wrong three different ways

Passes 18, 5, 3 and 17 were written in parallel by four agents and wired one at
a time. `conformance` 2041→**2049/2049**, `--strict` 565→**557**, and every
gate green. The interesting part is not the eight; it is that the roadmap had
predicted thirteen *from pass 18 alone*, and each of the three misses has a
different cause.

| pass | predicted | landed | attribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18 `interpolatedStringPost` | ~13, "self-contained" | **+3** | all `interpolated-string.k` |
| 5 `intrinsics` | implied non-zero | **0** | none, by construction |
| 3 `reifyEnums`/`captureThis` | unestimated | **0** | already ported |
| 17 `deduceAuto` | unestimated | **+5** | `basics.k`, `function-auto-return.k`, `lambdas.k` ×1, `initializer-list.k` ×2 |

### The estimate was a filename, not a cause

Every one of those numbers came from counting `--strict` failures in the corpus
file whose name matched the pass. `interpolated-string.k` had thirteen, so pass
18 was "~13, nearly all of `interpolated-string.k`". It has ten left, and only
six of those are pass 18's clauses at all: two are parse errors inside the
reference's `format` parser (`Parser.hs:900`), two are pass 9 `undefinedSymbols`
— which sets `hasErrors` and skips every later pass (`Frontend.hs:43-45`), so
they could never have been pass 18's.

`enum.k` is the same story told louder. It has fourteen failures and pass 3 is
"the enum pass". **Zero of the fourteen are pass 3's**: six are pass 8
instantiation, two are pass 19's `checkEnumConsts`/`checkEnumBaseType`, one wants
a whole-program `ConstEnv`, one is pass 9, and the rest are the const
environment's scope model. The pass table in `status.md` now carries the per-file
breakdown for exactly this reason. **Count by blocking cause, not by filename.**

### Pass 18's blocker was never the one written down

The `unwired` table said pass 18 "needs inference (`validateFormat` reads the
interpolated expression's type)". True, and not binding. The lexer emits an
entire `"…"` as one `STRING` token (`kg_parser::lexer::Lexer::string`) and
`Event::Token` can only *merge* raw tokens, never split one — so
`INTERPOLATED_STRING`, `INTERPOLATION` and `FORMAT_SPEC` sit in the vocabulary
and are never produced, which `kg_parser::grammar::tests::every_node_kind_is_reachable`
already asserted in so many words.

The interpolated expression **is not a node**. There is nothing pass 6 could
have typed and no `TypeKey` to ask about, so the whole-program type environment
that the table nominated as the unlock would move this pass by exactly zero.
What would move it is the *parser* learning to re-split a string token.

That is the reusable shape: **a blocker recorded as "needs pass N" may really be
"needs a different tree".** The table's entries were written by asking what the
reference reads, which gives the right answer whenever the port's tree has the
same nodes — and silently the wrong one when it does not. The pass now owns a
scanner over the token text, a transcription of the lexer's own `Frame` machine,
and decides what the interpolation's *shape* settles: an alignment containing a
`CALL_EXPR` (`Constexpr.hs`'s `eval` has no `FunctionCallF` clause, so a call
provably never folds to an `IntLiteral`), and a literal interpolation whose type
is not a value type — the exact subset `inferType` types with no symbol table,
which is why the message can carry the reference's own `showPretty` and report
`` `{uint1, uint1}` `` rather than an approximation.

### Pass 5 does not make pass 9's special case redundant, and the reason is a category error

The roadmap's one-line case for pass 5 was "a hard-coded table; pass 9 already
special-cases the same six names" — which reads as *wiring 5 lets 9 drop the
list*. In the reference it would: pass 9's guard is `tIsUndefined (typeOf x)`
(`Frontend.hs:88-96`), and by pass 9 `intrinsics` has already made that false.

**This port's pass 9 does not ask that question.** It asks four symbol-*map*
questions, because the rejection it reproduces is "`lookupInScope` found
nothing". A type table is not a symbol map and answers none of the four. Taking
the five names out of `undefined_symbols` with pass 5 wired fails **15**
assertions — eleven of them `expected:0`, i.e. eleven correct programs newly
rejected. The list stays; the two now share `intrinsics::NAMES` so they cannot
drift, and that sharing is the whole of what deduplication had to do here.

Pass 5 therefore landed **silent**, which is the correct outcome and not a
disappointment: `Type.hs:1069-1084` contains no `desugarError`. Its integration
point is also not `passes::run` — `run` receives a `TypeTable` that has already
converged, so a stamp there propagates to nothing. It is called from
`passes::types::type_table`, *before* the pass-6 fixpoint, because
`inferExpType' _ | typeResolved n = NotedExp n e` (`Type.hs:1170-1171`) freezes
an already-resolved node and that freeze **is** the mechanism. A pass whose
entire effect is its position in an ordering is one the pass list cannot hold.

### The right output for pass 3 was a file that does not exist

`reifyEnums`' numbering was ported into `scope::enum_constant_value` months ago,
with the `Frontend.hs:195-208` citation on it, because pass 19 range-checks the
values reification invents. Both of its other consumers — `Constexpr.hs:291-292`
and `checkEnumConsts` (`TypeCheck.hs:205-215`) — were already done.
`captureThis`' output is read only by `desugarLambdas`, called from exactly one
place (`Template.hs:78`, the 8th of pass 8's nine sub-passes), and contributes no
frontend diagnostic even once pass 8 lands.

So the agent assigned pass 3 wrote no code, and that is the deliverable. A pass
declared "not started" in the status table was in fact finished and filed under
another module's name. **Before porting a rewrite-only pass, find its consumers
and check whether one of them already carries it** — the port reorganises by
what reads a fact, not by which pass computed it, so a pass can arrive
pre-ported.

### Pass 17 cannot close the gap it looks like it closes

`deduceAuto` looked like the fix for the 184/1030 `auto` bindings the language
server leaves unannotated. It is not, and the reason is ordering:
`removeTemplate` is execution position **15** and deletes a template outright,
keeping only the diagnostics inside it (`Frontend.hs:298-299`). Pass 15 runs
before pass 17, so `deduceAuto` never sees a template body. The library's
unannotated bindings live in template bodies and are reached only through the
instances pass 8 builds. The hint count moves by zero.

What the pass does own is the failure arm, and it decides it **without
consulting the type table at all**. An unset key reads as `Ty::Unresolved`, so
"inference decided this cannot be written" and "inference never visited this
node" are the same answer; asking would fire on every `auto` in a lambda body or
an uninstantiated template. It reports only the subset whose answer is fixed by
syntax under any environment — `auto x;` with no initializer, and `auto` from an
initializer list. That is the same shape as the entry above this one: a port that
computes an answer where the reference merely has not computed one yet diverges
exactly there, and the defence is to decline rather than to ask.

### A note on the method

Wiring one at a time and running all three gates between each was what produced
the attribution table above; wired together, eight would have been one number.
It also caught a stale binary: pass 18's diagnostics did not appear from
`kg check` until `target/release/kg` was rebuilt, which for ten minutes looked
exactly like the crate's recurring "shipped with no caller" failure. Driving the
real binary is still the right check — but rebuild it first, or the check lies in
the direction that wastes the most time.

---

## The reference's guard was an accident, and the port optimised it away

Two skeptics attacked `templateTypeCheck` a day after it landed. Both returned
"defective", both were right, and the two defects turn out to be the same
mistake told twice: **a citation was read as being about a different function
than the one the code calls.**

### The guard nobody wrote

`templateTypeCheck` was the only diagnostic pass in `passes/` that did not call
`facts::reached_only_after_elaboration`. Nine others do. The module said why it
did not need to:

> Those decline on their own: nothing in a template body is inferred
> (`Inference.hs:60`), so their arguments have no resolved type.

That is a true statement about the *reference*. `noteType` stamps every node
`Typed TUnresolved n` (`Type.hs:973-976`); `inferExpTree`'s `go` never descends
into a template body (`Inference.hs:63`) or into either branch of a `static if`
(`:64`); so `templateArgsResolved` fails there and `check` returns the node
untouched. The reference has no guard for these regions because it does not need
one — the annotation *is* the guard.

The port had thrown that annotation away one entry earlier in this journal. The
entry above records asking `Templates` instead of the type table for
`tIsTemplate`, because a `TEMPLATE_DECL` reads `TUndefined` there. It is a good
trade and it is what makes the pass possible. It is also a **syntactic**
predicate: `names_a_template` looks a name up in a whole-program index and never
consults `TypeTable`, so it answers `true` in a region the reference's table
never visited. Every argument spelling a top-level template's name was
"resolved" no matter where it was written, and the pass walked into two subtrees
the reference had already deleted:

```
inline void main() {
    static if (false) { T1<Foo> t; }    // staticControl deleted this branch
}                                       // (Constexpr.hs:47) before pass 8 ran
```

`Error 1`, on a file the reference compiles clean. The `auto`-parameter clause
reached the same region and printed the literal word **`unresolved`** into a
user-facing message — a guard failing out loud, and the tell that should have
been chased when the pass was written.

The lesson is not "call the shared helper". It is that **replacing a
reference's predicate with a better one can delete a silence that was never
stated as a rule.** The reference is full of guards that are consequences of
evaluation order rather than of code, and a port that computes an answer where
the reference merely has not computed one yet will diverge exactly there. The
question to ask of any such shortcut is not "is it more accurate?" but "what was
the inaccuracy doing?"

### `theType` is not `typeOf`

`matchParamKind` (`TypeCheck.hs:249-251`) falls back to `theType t1 == theType
t2`. The port hard-coded a template-template parameter as matching nothing,
citing `infer TemplateF{} = TTemplate` (`Type.hs:1267`). The citation is real
and it is about `typeOf`. `theType` is a second function on top of it
(`Type.hs:458-464`):

```haskell
theType = tType . typeOf
  where
    tType (TType x) = x
    tType x | not $ tResolved x = TUnresolved
    tType _         = TError "Expected a type"
```

`tResolved TTemplate = False` (`:1002`), so `theType` of a `template <…>
typename` signature is `TUnresolved` — the same value `theType auto` has
(`infer AutoF = TUnresolved`, `:1174`). An `auto` slot in the expected signature
therefore **matches** a template-template parameter, and `Z<W>` compiles. And
`theType Typename` is not `TUntyped` either: `TUntyped` *is* resolved, so it
falls to the third clause and is `TError "Expected a type"`, which is why a
`typename` slot still does not match. The old code got that pair right by
accident.

Three of `theType`'s equivalence classes are now an enum with the derivation on
each variant, because the failure mode here is silent: every value involved is
spelled `TUnresolved`, `TUntyped`, `TTemplate` in the reference's own vocabulary
and the port's `Ty` has all three, so the wrong one type-checks.

### The finding neither skeptic could close

The second skeptic flagged, at low confidence, that an instance is resolved by
the **bare last segment** of its path while `lookupSymbol` resolves the
qualified name (`TypeCheck.hs:224`, `Symbols.hs:37-44`). Their probe was a
class-qualified call to a non-static member template, whose legality they could
not settle without a reference build — and there is none in this checkout.

The corpus settles it. `test/syntax/struct.k:22-38` is `expected:0` and reads
`static Foo::Bar<uint3, 10> b;` — a **member** template reached through its
class. Add a top-level template also called `Bar`, give the two their parameters
in the opposite order so the arity gate cannot hide the mistake, and the pass
validates `<10, uint3>` against the wrong signature and invents two errors.
No reference build needed: the shape is the corpus's own, and the collision is
the only thing added.

**A finding that cannot be closed as stated can often be re-aimed at something
the corpus already decides.** The skeptic's uncertainty was about a language
question; the defect underneath it was not.

Qualified paths are now declined outright, on both the instance and the argument
side. Declining *all* of them costs nothing measurable today — a differential
run leaves 2041/2041 and the 565-name strict set byte-identical — and the narrow
alternative (poison only the simple names a nested template also declares) buys
reach this pass cannot use until it is given the qualified-name symbol map pass
9 already builds.

### Two smaller infidelities, both toward silence, both closed

`constexprResolved (Designator _ e)` discards the name (`Constexpr.hs:388`); the
port asked `constexprResolved` of the `DESIGNATOR`'s children uniformly,
including its `NAME_REF`, which is `False` — so `Q<{0}>` reported the
`auto`-parameter clause and `Q<{.z = 1}>` said nothing. And `validate Typename`
accepted a *template* name through an undocumented disjunct, where
`tIsType TTemplate` is `False` (`tInner TTemplate = Nothing`,
`Type.hs:599-602`) and the reference says "Expected a type".

### Nothing moved, and that is the finding

Five gates, before and after: 2041/2041 decidable, 565 strict — the same 565
names — 479/479 and 355/355 corpus, 13/72 repoint, check 68.1 ms, keystroke
103.6 ms. Three false positives were removed and two silences closed, and the
scoreboard did not notice any of it.

That is the honest reading of what conformance measures. Its 1768 `expected:0`
assertions punish an invented diagnostic **only on a program the corpus
contains**, and none of these three shapes is in it: the corpus has an untaken
`static if` and it has a wrong-kind template-template argument, but never one
inside the other; it has a qualified member-template instance, but no top-level
template colliding with it. All three were found by reading the reference
against the code and then writing the program that separates them.

**A green scoreboard is evidence about the corpus, not about the compiler.**
The five gates are load-bearing for regressions and near-blind to a false
positive on a shape nobody wrote down. Six tests now hold these; each was proven
by breaking the fix and watching it go red.

## A template name has no type, and the pass that needed one asked elsewhere

`templateTypeCheck` (pass 8's one diagnostic-only sub-pass) needs
`tIsTemplate (typeOf arg)` in two places: `templateArgsResolved`'s guard for a
template-template parameter (`TypeCheck.hs:325`) and `validate`'s dispatch
(`TypeCheck.hs:243`). Both are cheap in the reference — `getSymbols` files a
`Template` under the name of the declaration it wraps and
`infer TemplateF{} = TTemplate` (`Type.hs:1267`).

Here the answer is `Ty::Undefined`. `passes::types`' `Walk` files a
`TEMPLATE_DECL` under `declared_name(node)`, which is the node's first `NAME` or
`NAME_REF` **child** — and a `TEMPLATE_DECL`'s children are a
`TEMPLATE_PARAM_LIST` and the wrapped declaration, so there is no such child and
nothing is filed. Every template name in the program reads `TUndefined`.

The obvious fix is to make `declared_name` delegate through the wrapper. It was
not taken. That map is read by eleven passes and by `ConstEnv`; giving several
hundred names a type they have never had is a change whose blast radius is the
whole frontend, and it would have ridden along inside a new pass — the exact
shape `rustfmt.toml` refuses for formatting and `CLAUDE.md` refuses for
scoreboard edits. The pass asks `deduce_template_args::Templates` instead, which
is already a whole-program index of top-level templates by simple name and which
answers *both* halves of the question at once: `tIsTemplate` and
`lookupSymbol arg symbols`, which `validateTemplate` needs two lines later
anyway.

The consequence worth writing down is that the reference's `validate Template{}
_ = argError "Expected a template specifier"` (`TypeCheck.hs:264`) turned out to
be **dead code**. Its guard can only be reached when `tIsTemplate (typeOf arg)`
is false, and `templateArgsResolved` has already required that to be true for
exactly this parameter kind. `T1<bool>` is `expected:1` in the corpus and is not
this pass's rejection — it belongs to pass 12. Reading the guard first would have
saved an afternoon of trying to make an unreachable clause fire.

**The pass costs 1.6 ms on `check` and 1.9 ms on a keystroke** — one extra
`descendants()` walk of the edited file, measured with four interleaved A/B
pairs, distributions not overlapping. That buys fourteen assertions. It is worth
recording only because the ratio is the thing to watch: pass 8's remaining eight
sub-passes are rewrites, and a rewrite cannot be paid for with one more walk.

## A benchmark that stopped measuring the thing it was named after

Three reviewers attacked the cross-module type environment. The visibility
attack found nothing — the fallback resolves exactly `findInImports`, and a
differential build with the two call sites neutered moves six assertions and
nothing else. The other two both found something, and they found the same shape
of mistake twice: **an under-approximation is only safe where the thing reading
it treats absence as absence.**

**The benchmark.** `xtask bench`'s keystroke stage fed each file its own bytes
back. That was honest for as long as `passes::run` rebuilt the type table on
every call — the stage paid for inference either way. It stopped being honest the
moment inference got a memo, because `Db::parse_module` keeps the old
`Arc<Parse>` when a reparse compares equal, `item_tree` is keyed on that `Arc`'s
identity and `infer_module` on the item tree's. Identical bytes therefore hit
three memos in a row and the fixpoint never ran. The reported 91.6→70.6 ms was
27 ms of inference leaving the *measurement*. Measured honestly — one trailing
space, alternating so consecutive passes always differ — the same change is
96.9→101.3 ms. **A keystroke got 4.6% slower, and that is the correct outcome to
report**: passes 4, 10 and 19 now have resolved types where they used to see
`Ty::Undefined` and bail, so they do more work. The win is real and it is
somewhere else: batch `check` over the corpus went 14.1→12.3 s.

The general lesson is about the shape of the invariant, not about this stage.
**A benchmark's setup encodes a claim about the memo graph, and the memo graph is
exactly what an optimisation changes.** The claim here was written down in a
comment — "so the memo is cold for this file" — and stayed true for months after
it stopped being true. It is now pinned by a test rather than a comment:
`re_entering_identical_text_leaves_the_type_table_memoized` asserts both
directions, and it is in `tests/query.rs` rather than in `xtask` because the fact
belongs to the database.

**The false warning.** `inferExpTree` hands *one* symbol map to
`evaluateConstexpr` and to `inferExpType` (`Inference.hs:37,47`). This change
gave the second half the import graph and left the first half at one file, and
`inductionVarType` (`Type.hs:1133-1137`) is the one rule that reads both:

```haskell
inductionVarType x
    | isIntLiteral x = constIndexType x                    -- clog2 of the value
    | otherwise      = try (tConst . TUnsigned) $ sizeOf x -- width of the type
```

`isIntLiteral` is true of anything the fold reduced to a literal, so for a `const`
in another module the reference takes the first branch. This port asks
`SymbolEnv::folded_int`, which reads one file, so it got `None` — and `None` fell
into the **second** branch, which now had a real width to report. `for (const auto
x : K)` with an imported `const uint32 K = 8` typed the induction variable
`const uint32` instead of `uint3` and warned about a narrowing conversion on a
program the reference accepts. `test/syntax/auto-placeholder.k:39-49` pins the
in-file case at `bitsizeof(x) == 3`; nothing in the corpus pairs an imported
constant with a range-`for`, so every gate stayed green.

The `folded_int` doc said the right thing and was read one level too narrowly:
"returning `None` where the reference would have folded costs a *type*, and an
unresolved type is quiet." True of a caller that treats `None` as an absence.
`induction_var_type` is not one — it is a **two-branch rule**, and
under-approximating the guard of a two-branch rule does not fall silent, it falls
into the other branch, and the other branch speaks. The fix is
`SymbolEnv::fold_declined`, the sibling of `ConstEnv::declines_known_constant`
one level up: an environment whose folding is narrower than its typing has to be
able to say so. Answered by walking the limit, not just its root, because the
fold is bottom-up — `y + 1` invented `const uint33` for the same reason `y`
invented `const uint32`.

The three-line alternative (take `sizeOf` only for a non-`const` limit) was
tried and rejected: a `const uint16` *parameter* is a limit the reference
genuinely does not fold, so it types the induction variable from the width and
this port already agrees. Suppressing that would have traded a false positive for
a false negative on a case that was right.

**A third finding, which no attack was pointed at.** The landing's own status
table claimed `auto` bindings annotated over the reference library went 184→199.
It did not. Driving all 480 corpus files through the language server's
`textDocument/inlayHint` handler over stdio — the exact path a user's editor
takes — gives 184 before and 184 after, and the *only* difference anywhere in the
corpus is one label: `: const E` became `: const helper.interpolated_string::E`,
which is the qualified-name row of the same table, counted twice. The fallback
does work: a synthetic `import a; auto x = MakeAa();` newly annotates. The
library simply has no unannotated binding that an import alone was blocking —
they are all under a `template <…>`, which `inferType` visits for its condition
only (`Inference.hs:60`). **A number that moves in the direction you expect is
the easiest kind to publish without checking**, and this one was in three places
before it was measured once.

**Two notes that outlive the fix.** The no-backwards-flow argument in
`passes::types` — nothing a module imports can depend on its importer, because a
cycle is a load error — is about the *import* relation, and pass 8 breaks it:
`instantiate` rewrites the template's definition node, in the declaring module's
tree, from `decidedInstances` collected over the whole file list
(`Template.hs:88,112-120`). The per-module union survives pass 6 and has to be
re-argued for pass 8, not assumed. And `SymbolEnv::method` has no caller at all
yet, so its import fallback is dead code — which is why the constructed-key
hazard it carries (`class_qualified_name ++ [member]` handed to a lookup whose
second arm strips an *import alias*) could not be demonstrated. It is guarded now,
before pass 8 wires the caller, because a guard added afterwards is a bug fix and
a guard added now is a precondition.

## The whole-program type environment is a union, not a fixpoint

`inferType` in the reference is one fixpoint over the whole program:
`inferType :: [NotedExp] -> [NotedExp]`, rebuilding `getSymbols' TemplateDecl`
over the entire file list every round (`Inference.hs:27-42`). Transcribing that
shape would have re-inferred the base library on every keystroke and thrown away
the per-module memo `Db::type_table` is built on — the memo that had just taken
`keystroke` from 1.9 s to 91.6 ms.

The factoring that avoids it is one observation. **A module's imports cannot
depend on the module**, because an import cycle is a load error
(`Parser/IO.hs:90`). So the whole-program map is the disjoint union of
per-module maps computable in dependency order, and `Program::files` — post-order
DFS, base library first — is already that order. Each module's fixpoint runs
against imports that have *already converged*, so what crosses the boundary is a
finished value (`ModuleTypes`) rather than a work list, and a finished value can
be memoized. The memo key is `(the module's item tree, the converged map of each
module it directly imports)`, both by pointer. Direct imports suffice for the
transitive ones: a change two modules away rebuilds the module in between into a
*new* map, which invalidates this one — the cascade rides on the values.

Three things this cost that were not obvious in advance.

**Post-order is not enough on its own to make a cycle terminate.** A cyclic
import still produces a `targets` entry — `walk_imports` reports the cycle, but
the callback that resolved the paths ran first — so the graph really can hold a
forward edge. The walk is therefore not recursive: it fills a map as it goes and
a module is only ever handed what is already in it. A forward edge finds nothing
and contributes nothing, which is also what the reference does with a cyclic
import (`Parser.hs:201` never reaches `updateImports`, so it supplies no
symbols).

**The environment had to be given the module's own namespace, and that is a
correction, not an extension.** `moduleDecl` wraps a file's declarations in
`scoped ident` (`Parser.hs:185-189`), so every top-level declaration of
`module a` is keyed `["@a", …]`; this port started inference at the empty scope,
which is self-consistent within one file and wrong the moment two files meet —
`struct S` in `a` and `struct S` in `b` were the *same nominal type*, because
`TStruct` carries the qualified name and both said `["S"]`. `InferFile::scope`
existed for exactly this and had only ever been passed `SymbolPath::empty()`. A
hover test had already written the divergence down — "the key is `a::Aa` and the
type is `Aa`; whichever eventually changes, this test says which one moved" — and
it moved.

**Resolving names invents work for the passes downstream, and one of them was
wrong.** `Fn<Enum[10]>(…)` with an imported `Enum` started reporting "Invalid
element access; did you forget `typename`" on two `expected:0` assertions. The
cause was three layers away: `term` tries `typ' False` **before** every value
form (`Parser.hs:844`), and `type''` gathers `many (brackets expression)` into
one `Array (Seq []) t dims` (`Parser.hs:533-538`) — so where the base names a
type, the reference never built an `ArrayAccessF` at all and `tElement TType{}`
is unreachable for that shape. This parser keeps one `INDEX_EXPR` for both
readings, so `infer` is the only place left that can tell them apart, and it now
does: a `TType` base builds the array type, appending its dimension when the base
is already an array so that `E[4][10]` composes into `Array [] E [4,10]` rather
than nesting. That was invisible for as long as the base was `TUndefined`,
because `tElement` answers `TUnresolved` for anything unresolved. Three
`expected:1` assertions that had been *passing on that error* went back to
undecidable, which is the honest score: they were being decided by an error the
reference does not produce.

Net: `conformance` 2022→2027/2027, `--strict` 584→579, and a batch `check` that
got materially faster — `xtask conformance` end to end 14.1→12.3 s, because the
memo replaced a rebuild `Db::diagnostics` was doing per call.

**The `keystroke` figure originally written here — 91.6→70.6 ms — was wrong, and
the entry below says why.** A keystroke got *slower*.

---

## An index that answered a question nobody asked

Four reviewers each attacked one documented trap in the deduction landing. All
four cleared the trap they were assigned. Three of them found a real defect
*next to* it, and the fourth found one that cannot happen. That ratio is the
finding: the traps had been written down, so they were got right; the code
around them had not, so it was not.

**A member template shadows the top-level one, and the port reached past it.**
`Templates` keys top-level function templates by their simple name, and the type
carried a paragraph arguing that this is sound: `lookupInScope` walks outward
from the call's scope (`Symbols.hs:82-87`), and *for a call written at module
scope* the walk ends exactly where the index answers. The paragraph is true. The
pass then applied the index at every scope in the file — including the ones the
paragraph excludes. Three programs, all of which the reference deduces cleanly:

```
template <typename T> inline void Foo(T x, T y) { }
class C {
public:
    template <typename T, typename U> inline void Foo(T x, U y) { }
    inline void go() { bool a; float32 b; Foo(a, b); }
}
```

`error: Conflicting template argument deduction results for parameter `T`.` —
and the fingerprint is right there in the message, because `T` is the *top-level*
template's parameter. The port had deduced against a signature the program does
not call. A member function of the same name does it too, and so does a local
`auto Foo = [](…)`: `lookupSymbol` finds a `Function` or a `Variable`, and
`deduceInstance' _ e = e` (`Type.hs:1448`) is a catch-all, not a "keep looking",
so the reference does no deduction at all.

The guard is four lines and needs no symbol map. Every key `lookupInScope` tries
before module scope is `s ++ [name]` for `s` a prefix of the call's own scope, so
a shadowing declaration is exactly one whose binding scope is an ancestor of the
call and is not the file — a question the CST answers on its own. `navigate.rs`
already had `binder` and `introduces_scope` for goto-definition, and they are the
same two functions.

The lesson is not "the index was wrong". The index is right. It was applied
outside the argument that made it right, and the argument was sitting three lines
above the code that broke it.

**`template <typename, auto> typename C` had a default argument.** The parser
emits a template-template parameter's inner `paramKind` list as *bare children*
of `TYPE_PARAM` — `TEMPLATE_KW L_ANGLE TYPENAME_TYPE COMMA AUTO_TYPE R_ANGLE
TYPENAME_KW NAME`, no wrapping node. `default_type()` is "the first `Type` child",
so it returned the inner `typename`, and `has_default` came out `true` for a
parameter with no `=` anywhere in it. Downstream that is the difference between
`sequence` throwing the whole argument list away and the port reporting a
conflict, so the program above with a template-template second parameter was
rejected — and deleting the contents of the inner `<…>` silenced it. The output
was decided by whether the inner list happened to be non-empty, which is not a
fact about defaults at all.

`template_param_list()` was `None` for the same reason, which made
`ParamKind::TemplateTemplate` unreachable and every template-template parameter a
`Typename` — so clause 15 (`Type.hs:1572-1573`) bound a `TTypeArg` for a
parameter the reference's pattern does not match. Both facts now come off tokens:
the `template` keyword and the `=`, which is what `optional (equal *> …)`
(`Parser.hs:366-368`) actually means. Wrapping the inner list in its own node is
the better fix and changes the CST, so it is not this change.

Worth keeping as a rule: a generated accessor named `default_type` is a claim
about the *grammar*, and it is only as true as the node the grammar emits. When a
production has no node of its own, every "first child of kind K" accessor over it
is quietly answering about something else.

**The one that was reported and is not real.** `reconcile`'s clause 10 is
`TError{} <- ty` — a top-level pattern — and the port wrote `ty.is_error()`,
which recurses through `tInner` (`Type.hs:626-627`). A genuine textual
divergence, and unreachable: a `TTypeArg` slot can never hold a `TConst` or a
`TInstance`, because `deduceType`'s clauses 6 and 8 strip both from the actual
(`Type.hs:1546,1550`) before clause 15 can bind it, and the only types
`reconcile` manufactures are `tSuper` of two integers and a bare `TError`. The
report proposed a unit test that builds the unreachable state by hand and a
matching change at the other end that would have made the two ends *disagree*
about something neither can see.

Rejecting it was right; leaving it alone was not. The clause is now written the
way the reference writes it — behaviour-identical by the argument above — and
`an_error_binding_is_always_a_bare_error_type` pins the reachability property
instead of the unreachable state. Breaking either strip reddens it; the two
existing error tests do not notice. A divergence that cannot be observed still
costs the next reader the derivation, and a test is cheaper than a paragraph.

**The comment about trap 22 was wrong about trap 22.** It said swapping
`reconcile`'s arguments "inverts clauses 4-7, so a covariant merge starts
narrowing". Clauses 4/5 are a mirror pair and so are 6/7: swapped, clause 6
computes exactly what clause 7 computed before, and the widen/narrow answer is
identical. What a swap actually breaks is clause 2, `reconcile x Nothing = x` —
the storing of a *first* binding. Swapped in this port, the `let … else` returns
the empty slot and every parameter in every program silently stays unbound; six
of the deduction tests redden, and the one that does not is the assertion that
expects an unbound slot and gets one for the wrong reason.

I found this by doing the swap and running the tests, which is the only way the
claim was ever checkable. The code was right and its stated reason was wrong,
which is the worse of the two failures here: house style makes the *why* the
point of the comment, and a wrong why is repeated by the next person to touch it.
It already had been, twice.

**Seventy-five citations, drifting in one direction.** `File.hs:line` is
load-bearing for review and has no gate, and the deduction region had drifted by
three to twelve lines almost everywhere — including the anchor for trap 24 (`the
+1 clause`, cited `Type.hs:1554-1555`, actually `1566-1567`, where `1554` is
blank and `1555` is the array clause). Two citations in the same function claimed
overlapping line ranges for disjoint clause groups, which is the signature of a
number copied from a summary rather than read out of the file. The citations that
carry the traps — `Type.hs:1407`, `:1414-1416`, `:1431-1432` — were exact
throughout, in every file. The load-bearing ones were checked; the scaffolding
was not.

**What the scoreboard says, and why it did not move.** Measured by switching the
pass off and back on: without pass 4 the gates read `2015/2015 decidable` and
`591` strict failures; with it, `2022/2022` and `584`. Exactly seven assertions,
and none of this change's four fixes moved either number, because all four remove
diagnostics from programs the corpus does not contain.

Seven is the honest ceiling for this pass as a *diagnostic*. `deduceTemplateArgs`
does not report; it **rewrites** `Fn_T(x)` into `Fn_T<bool>(x)`, and everything
downstream reads the rewrite. The one diagnostic it can produce is `reconcile`'s
last clause, and the corpus has very few programs whose only error is that shape.
Of the 44 remaining failures in `template-argument-deduction.k`, all of them
"expected Error 1, compiled cleanly" — never an invented one — 21 are method
calls `o.Fn(x)`, which `rewrite` reaches through a clause guarded on
`tIsClass (typeOf a)` (`Type.hs:1390-1393`) and so needs the receiver's class
type from another module; 13 need the deduced type to *become* the type of the
call so a `return` or a `static assert` can be checked against it, which is the
rewrite this port structurally cannot perform; and 6 are calls inside a template
body, which pass 6 never visits (`Inference.hs:60`) and which need pass 8. So the
"27 assertions attributed to `deduceTemplateArgs`" counts what deduction
*unlocks*, not what it *reports* — and only the seven are the pass's own.

**One operational note, learned expensively.** This workspace's Rust is not
uniformly rustfmt-formatted and `cargo fmt` is not one of the gates. Running
`cargo fmt --all` rewrites 114 files; no single config reproduces the tree,
because different files are in different styles. If you need to reformat, do it
per-file and diff before keeping it.

---

## The repoint experiment, and a gate that read 0/72 while working perfectly

The conformance harness reimplements `test/syntax/syntax-test.py` in Rust. That
buys speed and per-assertion names, and it costs the one thing a scoreboard most
needs: **a scoreboard written from a script cannot discover that it misread the
script.** Every number `xtask conformance` reports has been conditional on a
reading nobody audited.

`cargo xtask repoint` closes that. It shells out to the actual `syntax-test.py`,
with the actual per-test flags, driving `target/release/kanagawa` — which is what
`set_target_properties(kanagawa::exe …)` does at cutover. Two changes made it
possible:

- **The compat binary runs the frontend**, not just the parser. It builds a
  `Settings` from `LegacyOptions` — the reference has no manifest, so every field
  is a flag — and calls `Db::check` with the command-line files as roots.
- **A clean frontend-only run exits 0.** `--backend` defaults to `None`, whose
  help text is "produce metadata only" (`Options/CmdArgs.hs:75`), and that is
  what `syntax-test.py:103-106` invokes: all 2,516 live assertions are
  frontend-only runs expecting exit 0. Exiting 1 there is the safe-*looking*
  choice and the wrong one — it makes the binary unusable as a `kanagawa::exe`
  replacement and forfeits the check. A request for a real backend still refuses.

**Result: 13/72, and the cross-check is clean in the direction that matters.**
No file passes upstream that `--strict` calls dirty — the native harness never
invents a failure. The ten that go the other way are fully explained: nine
contain `expected:<C++ code>` assertions that `xtask conformance` books as
*undecidable* and upstream's runner cannot, and `options` requests
`--backend=sv`.

The gate's own first run reported **0/72**, and the failure was invisible.
`--kanagawa-root` defaults to the relative `../kanagawa`, and the runner is
spawned with its working directory set to a scratch tree — so the script path,
`-testfile`, `-helperdir`, *and the `${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}` expansions inside the
per-test options* all resolved against the wrong directory. Every test failed
with a `python3: can't open file` that the summary line never showed. It looked
exactly like a frontend with no passes.

What caught it was having run the same thing by hand first, in a throwaway
script, and getting 13. Without that number to disagree with, 0/72 is perfectly
plausible for a compiler this incomplete — and the gate would have been
committed broken, reading zero forever, as convincing as any real measurement.
**A new gate needs a known answer before it is trusted, and the cheapest source
of one is the ad-hoc version you wrote to see if the idea worked.**

## A language server nobody could start

`kg-lsp` is 4,400 lines with 90 tests. It answers `initialize`, publishes
whole-program diagnostics, and the VS Code client is written against it. Its
launch command, `kg lsp`, exited 2 — `kg-cli` had no dependency on it at all.
The subcommand's refusal text said "the language server lands as the `kg-lsp`
crate", which had been true once.

That is the fourth thing this session that existed and had no caller, after
`WarningSet::filter`, `Db::check` and `Db::diagnostics`. The pattern is
consistent enough to name: **a crate is not shipped until something a user types
reaches it.** Tests do not count — kg-lsp's 90 passing tests exercised the server
through its library API, which is exactly the path a user never takes.

Wiring it surfaced a second bug immediately, and a nastier one. `bin/kg.rs`
opened with:

```rust
let stdout = std::io::stdout();
let mut out = stdout.lock();
```

held for the whole dispatch. `lsp-server`'s writer thread locks stdout itself,
and `StdoutLock` is reentrant per *thread* — so the server answered nothing and
never exited. Not a crash, not an error: a hang, which an editor reports as
"language server not responding" and a developer reads as a problem with the
editor. The fix is to hold `Stdout` handles rather than locks and pay a lock
acquisition per write, which for a command that prints diagnostics is not
measurable and for `lsp` is free.

Two things this cost, both worth remembering:

- **An in-process test of `kg lsp` hangs the suite.** One existed, asserting the
  old exit 2; once `lsp` ran the real server it took the test harness's stdin and
  blocked. The whole workspace run wedged rather than failing. The replacement
  drives a real subprocess with a 30-second watchdog whose panic message names
  the deadlock, because the failure mode here is silence and silence needs a
  timer.
- **The honesty tests had to be inverted, not deleted.** `the_unimplemented_commands_exit_two`
  listed `lsp`; `build` is now the only entry. Same for `--help`, which still
  claimed `check` "runs the parser only".

## Bounding the memo, and tuning the constant to the measurement
