`Db`'s four memo tables are not alike. `parses` and `item_trees` are keyed by
`ModuleSource` and so are bounded by the program. `programs` and `symbols` are
keyed by the *set of roots asked about* — which, in a language server, is one
entry per file the user has ever opened, each pinning an `Arc<Program>` with its
module graph and its list of item trees. Unbounded in a process that runs for a
working day. Nobody noticed because until this session nothing shipped that kept
a `Db` alive that long.

The first attempt cleared the map when it filled. The `keystroke` benchmark
found the cliff immediately — which was satisfying, because the comment I had
just written said "if profiles ever show it thrashing the answer is a real LRU,
not a bigger number". It showed thrashing within the minute.

The replacement is FIFO, not LRU: an LRU wants an access stamp written on every
*read*, which puts the write lock on the hot path of a cache whose whole purpose
is to be read. Eviction here is cheap to be wrong about — a miss costs one
`program::load`, and that load's inputs are still memoized per module, so an
evicted entry re-resolves a module graph and re-parses nothing.

**The bound costs 7%** in the benchmark: 112 → 120 ms. A/B'd by raising the cap
to 4096, which recovers exactly the 112, so the cost is the eviction and nothing
else. The benchmark sweeps all 479 corpus files in sequence — every entry is
evicted before it is asked for again, which is the pattern most hostile to any
bounded cache and one no editor performs.

So the constant stays at 64. Raising it until the benchmark went green would
have been tuning the constant to the measurement: the number that gets faster is
the one workload built to defeat the bound, and the thing traded away is a server
that does not grow without limit. Worth writing the A/B into the comment, because
the next person to see a 7% line in a profile deserves to know it was bought
deliberately.

## An `Option` that modelled a state the reference does not have

`Settings::target_device` was `Option<String>`, defaulting to `None`, and
`import_search_path` skipped the device half of the search entirely when it was
unset. A test pinned that: `no_target_device_means_no_device_dirs`.

The reference has no such state. `targetDevice :: String` with `= "mock"`
(`Parser/Options.hs:29,47`), and `Parser/IO.hs:110` is
`map (</> "device" </> targetDevice opt) (importDir opt) ++ importDir opt` —
unconditional. There is no way to ask for "no device"; there is only a device
whose name you did not type.

The consequence for a user is total and silent: a `kanagawa.toml` that declares
`import-dirs` and does not mention a device — the common case, not an exotic one
— cannot see `library/device/mock/hardware/config.k`, so `mini-base` fails on a
re-exposed module and the standard library is invisible. This is the *same* bug
that produced 2,088 false conformance failures when the rooted harness first ran;
it was fixed there by setting the field explicitly and left in place everywhere
else.

The type is now `String` with `DEFAULT_TARGET_DEVICE`, so the state cannot be
expressed. The test now asserts the opposite of what it did, with the citation —
the second time this session a test has turned out to encode a wrong expectation
(after `!~x`), and both were found by checking the claim against the reference
rather than by anything failing.

**An optional field is a claim that the value can be absent.** Worth checking
that claim against the thing being modelled before writing the `Option`, because
`None` then propagates as a legitimate answer through every consumer, and no
type error ever appears.

## Profiling the keystroke, and three allocations that were not needed

Wiring the language server to the frontend made a number matter that had never
been measured: what one edit costs. `xtask bench` grew a `keystroke` stage — a
rooted `Db` with the base library warm, one file re-entered as though typed, the
whole program re-checked. **131 ms** on the corpus's worst file.

The old headline had been reporting the parse: 6.2 ms, "within a 16 ms frame",
"the editor-latency ceiling". That was true while the server published parse
errors and became a comfortable fiction the moment it stopped. A 20x gap sat
behind a line of output nobody had reason to doubt. Same shape as the `worst`
statistic that hid `Doc::drop`, and the same fix: correct the instrument first.

Then `sample(1)` on the running benchmark, three times, fixing the top entry
each time. All three were the same mistake — work done eagerly for every node
and used by almost none:

- **`Walk::node`, 14%.** `Declarations::of` computed each node's type
  (`type_of_node`, a *deep* `Ty` clone — it owns `Vec`s and `BTreeSet`s) and its
  interned name (a `String` allocation) *before* the `match` that decides
  whether either is wanted. Most nodes are neither declarations nor named. Moved
  into the arms that use them.
- **`count_unresolved`, deep clone per node.** It cloned a whole `Ty` to ask
  `.resolved()`. `TypeTable::is_resolved` peeks instead.
- **`count_unresolved`, called twice per round.** The outer loop in
  `type_table` recomputed the measure that `infer_program` had just returned in
  `InferOutcome::signature` — a second full-tree walk per round for a number
  already in hand.

131 → 111 ms, and `check` 1.9 → 3.0 MiB/s across the session. Conformance
unchanged throughout.

What the profile says now is structural rather than local: ~40% of a keystroke
is rowan cursor allocation and free — `first_child`, `next_sibling`,
`Preorder::next`, `nanov2_free`. rowan's red nodes are allocated per navigation
step, and the check walks the whole tree several times over (lowering, the
declaration map, each inference round, each pass). The next real win is fewer
walks or an incremental reparse, not another micro-fix; both are bigger than a
sitting.

## The two front doors were still looking at a bare parse tree

`kg_db::Db::check` and `Db::diagnostics` had been wired to the semantic passes
for a while. Neither of the things a user actually touches was calling them.

`kg check` called `kg_syntax::parse_file` directly and printed *"parse only —
name resolution and type checking are not implemented yet"*, which had stopped
being true. `kg-lsp` did not depend on `kg-db` at all: `publish_diagnostics`
rendered `Parse::errors`, so the editor gutter showed syntax errors and nothing
else — no unresolved import, no type error, none of what a person opens an
editor to be told.

`Db::diagnostics`'s own doc says it is "the language-server answer, one
`textDocument/publishDiagnostics` payload". It had no callers.

Both are wired now. What the work actually consisted of, in both cases, was
deciding what the *inputs* are:

- **`kg check`'s paths are program roots, not the unit of work.** `Db::check`
  follows imports and the implicit base, so a diagnostic can land in a file the
  user never named — worth saying in the help, because the alternative is a
  confusing phantom error at the import site. A missing `base.k` is now reported
  rather than silently checked against an empty world, which is what the
  reference does (`Parser/IO.hs:83`) and which promptly invalidated a test
  fixture that had been declaring `import-dirs` with no base library.
- **The server keeps one `Db` per project root**, sharing its `Vfs` through
  `Db::with_vfs` so an unsaved buffer is what the frontend sees. Keyed on
  `Settings::root` because that is the unit a program resolves against: two
  files under different manifests have different import paths and cannot share a
  memo. Every edit invalidates the file in *every* database, not just its own —
  a header under `library/` is reachable from several roots, and the stale memo
  in the root nobody is editing is the one nobody would catch.

The fallback in `publish_diagnostics` is deliberate: `frontend_diagnostics`
returns `Option`, and `None` falls back to the parse rather than to an empty
list. Publishing `[]` for a file with no database would clear the gutter as
though the file were clean, which is the same failure as a warning switch that
parses and does nothing — an absence that looks like an answer.

The regression test is the point. It opens a file that **parses cleanly** and is
still wrong (`bool b = !a` on a `uint8`; `tNot` has no integer clause,
`Type.hs:571`) and asserts the server reports it — plus an edit that fixes it,
so the memo cannot answer from the previous text.

## Every `--W` flag worked, and none of them did anything

`kg_diag::WarningSet::filter` had **no callers anywhere in the workspace**. Every
`--Wno-shadow`, every `[warnings] shadow = "allow"`, parsed correctly, resolved
correctly, was stored on `Settings` correctly, and was then never consulted. The
CLI, the language server and the conformance harness all published the full
diagnostic list.

Nothing failed, and nothing could have: a disabled warning that still fires looks
exactly like a warning. The only reason it surfaced is that an audit went looking
for functions with no callers — which turns out to be a much better smell than it
sounds, because a *feature* with no callers is invisible from every direction
except that one.

The filter now runs inside `Db::check` and `Db::diagnostics` rather than at each
call site, so the three consumers cannot disagree about which warnings exist. It
is worth a line in the strict scoreboard: 593 → 592.

There is an uncomfortable footnote. The commit before this one had claimed, of
the per-test conformance flags, that "`no-warning` disables `shadow`" — which was
true of the parsing and false of the effect. The flags were being read into a
setting nothing honoured. Parsing a flag and *obeying* it are two separate
claims, and only one of them had a test.

## Two passes, two symbol maps, and the same fixpoint run twice

`pass $ inferType` appears **exactly once** in `desugarPasses`
(`Frontend.hs:69`). Its two consumers — `passPar $ cata typeErrors`
(`Frontend.hs:65`) and `validateProgram symbols` (`Frontend.hs:56`) — are later
passes that read the annotations it left.

This crate had it the other way round. Pass 10 and pass 19 each built a
`TypeTable` from empty and ran the whole fixpoint into it. A profile put
`kg_ty::infer::infer_program` at **57% of `check_source`**, split near-evenly
between the two callers — so about a quarter of every check, and of every
keystroke through `Db::diagnostics`, was the same work done twice.

The interesting part is why it could not be fixed by caching. **The two
environments disagreed**, and only one was right. Pass 19's map keyed on
qualified names and resolved with `lookupInScope` (`Symbols.hs:83-87`). Pass
10's keyed on *simple* names and admitted only names the file declared exactly
once — a restriction its own doc justified by saying `kg_ty::infer` threads a
scope that "deepens only at `class`/`struct`/`union`/`enum`, not at a function
body's `$`".

That is not what the traversal does. `Round::visit_function` builds
`param_scope = scope.child(name)` and `body_scope = param_scope.child("$")` and
hands the body the latter, transcribing `Parser.hs:414-424`. The premise was
false, so the restriction bought nothing — while costing every file that
declares one name in two functions.

Both fixpoints now live in `passes/types.rs` as one `type_table()`, built once
in `passes::run` and handed to both consumers. 215 lines of the simple-name map
are gone.

- `check` throughput **1.9 → 2.5 MiB/s**; the worst file **160 → 114 ms**.
- Conformance **unchanged**: 2014/2014 decidable, and `--strict` still 593.

The unchanged scoreboard is worth stating rather than glossing. It would have
been easy to write this up as a correctness fix, since one of the two maps was
demonstrably wrong; the corpus says otherwise. The win is a quarter of the
check, and one environment where there were two that disagreed — which is the
kind of thing that produces a bug later, not now.

**How the duplication survived review:** each pass's doc argued convincingly for
*its own* environment, and pass 19's even explained why pass 10's was wrong. Two
correct-looking local arguments, no reader positioned to see that both ran. The
tell would have been the profile, which is the same lesson as the `Doc::drop`
allocation: the measurement is what makes an architectural mistake visible.

## `None` meant two different things, and the safe reading was the wrong one

An audit lens over the new whole-program layer turned up an `Error 1` the
reference does not produce:

```
const uint32 s = bitsizeof(uint8);
inline void main() { uint32 x; auto z = x << s; }
```

`ERR Invalid shift left. Result type exceeds maximum bit width.` Nothing in the
corpus catches it, and nothing was going to.

The mechanism is a guard doing its job backwards. `inferExpTree` is
`staticControl . unfix . evaluateConstexpr symbols . unfix . inferExpType symbols`
(`Inference.hs:47`) — **fold, then infer the parent** — and the literal-specialised
inference rules are *weaker* than the generic ones. The reference folds `s` to
`8`, takes `tShiftLLiteral` (`Type.hs:770-771`) and widens to `uint40`; this
toolchain does not fold, so `s` arrives as a 32-bit operand and hits the generic
`tShiftL`, whose `tWidth y >= 20` clause (`Type.hs:894-896`) rejects outright.
`fold_divergent` exists precisely to suppress the diagnostic when that happens.
It decided by *trying* to fold and concluding "no divergence" when the fold
failed.

**The two most common things the reference folds and this door cannot are
exactly the things that make the fold fail.** `FileScope::bit_width_of` and
`bit_offset_of` return `None` unconditionally, so `bitsizeof`, `bytesizeof`,
`bitoffsetof` and `byteoffsetof` never fold here and the guard reported clear in
the one case it was built for. It looked safe because `= 8`, `= cast<uint32>(8)`,
`= clog2(256)` and enum constants all *do* fold — every constant anyone had
thought to test with was foldable.

The root cause is an overloaded return value. `Folded::Unresolved` means "not a
constant, or not yet", and an incomplete environment produces it for a third
reason: *I cannot answer that*. Those are not the same claim, and one of them is
about the environment rather than the program. `ConstEnv` now separates them —
`declines_known_constant` — and `kg_const::declined_by_environment` answers the
guard's actual question: not "did this fold?" but "would the reference have
folded it where I did not?"

Two things worth carrying forward:

- **The bug was one level up from where it fired.** The shift expression
  contains no `bitsizeof`; the divergence is in the *declaration* of `s`, three
  lines away. A first fix that looked only at the failing subtree passed the
  reviewer's minimal case and still left the bug in. The environment had to be
  asked, because only the environment knows which of the names it declined were
  constants.
- **A guard biased the wrong way is worse than no guard.** Getting
  `fold_divergent` wrong toward `true` costs a missed diagnostic, which the
  scoreboard already books as undecidable. Getting it wrong toward `false`
  invents an error the reference does not have — the direction that breaks an
  `expected:0`. Where a guard cannot be exact, it should fail toward silence.

The regression test pins all four unfoldable initializers, the foldable control
that hid the bug, and a genuine shift error — verified red by reverting the fix,
because a test that has never failed is not known to test anything.

## The oracle is per-test, and the temp file is not where it looks

Wiring the conformance harness to the rooted `Db::check_snippet` should have
been plumbing. It produced **2,088 failures**, then 62, then 0 — and each drop
came from reading the reference's own build system rather than from writing
code.

**2,088 → 62 was `--target-device`.** It appears on no command line in the
corpus, because `mock` is the *default* (`Parser/Options.hs:47`). The import
search is `map (</> "device" </> targetDevice) importDir ++ importDir`
(`Parser/IO.hs:110`), so without it `library/device/mock/hardware/config.k` is
invisible, `mini-base` fails on a re-exposed module, and every assertion in the
corpus reports the same false error. A default that is never written down is
harder to find than a flag that is.

**62 → 0 was the discovery that there is no single compiler configuration.**
The harness had one `Settings` built by hand. The reference has seventy-three,
one per `add_syntax_test` call: a default `set(OPTIONS …)` block
(`CMakeLists.txt:39-44`), then whatever that call appends, then two more flags
from `syntax-test.py:106`. Thirteen cases override something, and the overrides
decide outcomes — `imports` adds `--import-dir=<test/syntax>/imports`, without
which nineteen `a1.*` imports fail; `custom-base` swaps the base library;
`no-warning` disables `shadow`; `all-warnings-as-errors` promotes every warning.
The harness now parses the flags out of CMake and applies them, so an upstream
change to the defaults shows up as a diff here instead of as silent drift.

**The third finding never showed up as a failure at all**, which is why it is
the one worth recording. `add_test` sets
`WORKING_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}` (`CMakeLists.txt:71`), so
`syntax-test.py` creates its subfolder in the **build** tree. That directory
holds nothing but `syntax_test_temp_file.k`. The harness had been placing the
snippet in the *source* tree's `test/syntax/imports/`, which contains the `a1/`
fixtures — and `Parser/IO.hs:107` searches the importing file's own directory
*first*. Every `import a1.b1.b1` would have resolved through a directory the
reference cannot see. That is the false-**green** direction: the emptiness of
the build subfolder is load-bearing, and copying it means using a path that is
never created on disk at all. Nothing is written; the path is interned and given
a VFS overlay, so the read-only corpus stays read-only.

Validated by injection, as ever: teaching the parser to ignore
`--import-dir=…/imports` brings 70 failures straight back.

Result: **2014/2014 decidable, 908 undecidable**, up from 1958/1958 and 964.
Under `--strict` the gap fell 711 → 593 failures, and the warning column went
**33 → 1** — that column was almost entirely the missing module graph, not
missing passes.

## The fuzzer that could not fail

`xtask fuzz` mutates real corpus files rather than generating random soup. That
choice is the whole point: random tokens hit an error in the first few tokens
and spend the rest of the run in recovery, whereas a real file with one brace
deleted gets six hundred lines in before anything goes wrong — which is where a
recursive-descent parser's interesting state lives.

3,000 mutations, 9,000 stage checks, all green. Which proved nothing, because a
detector that has never fired is not known to work.

So a bug was injected: drop a `;` that follows a `}` in the formatter's output.
The fuzzer came back **clean**. The flaw was mine, in one line:

```rust
let Ok(once) = kg_fmt::format_file(input, &config) else {
    // Refusing to format broken input is correct behaviour.
    return Ok(());
};
```

`format_file` has two failure modes and they mean opposite things.
`Unparseable` is correct behaviour — a file with syntax errors should be
declined rather than laid out on a guess. `Verification` means *the formatter
produced a different program* and caught itself doing it. Treating both as "fine"
meant kg-fmt's own safety net was silencing the fuzzer: the net exists so the
corruption is not written to disk, not so nobody hears about it.

With the two variants separated, the same injected bug is caught in 26
iterations, and the shrinker reduces a 400-line corpus file to:

```
module a.a{module a.a}import a.a
enum o:t{B};inlinevoid t(){a<0>a;}
```

with the diagnosis `token 21 changed: (SEMICOLON, ";") became (IDENT,
"inlinevoid")` — the dropped semicolon had merged `inline` and `void`.

**Always test that the detector detects.** A green fuzz run is evidence only
once the fuzzer has been shown to go red. Ten minutes of injecting a fault is
the cheapest insurance available against a suite that reports success by
construction.

One detail worth keeping: shrinking insists on the *same* `Failure`, not merely
on some failure. Without that, delta debugging happily converges on whatever
different bug the smaller input happens to trip, and hands back a reproducer
for something else entirely.

## A benchmark that hid the thing it was built to find

`xtask bench` reported the formatter's worst file as the **maximum** across its
five passes. That is a statistic with no stable value: a max-of-N grows with N
and tracks scheduler noise rather than the code. It read 109 ms ± 5 ms, which is
wide enough to hide most real changes.

It hid one immediately. `Doc::drop` was allocating a fresh `Rc<DocKind::Nil>`
for every node it dismantled — `mem::replace` needs something to leave behind,
and the obvious thing to leave behind allocates. Tearing a document down
therefore cost exactly as many allocations as building it. Cloning a shared
thread-local sentinel instead is a refcount bump.

A warm-cache profile showed that plainly (lowering 34 ms → 28 ms), and the
benchmark showed nothing: 108.4 ms before, 108.6 ms after. The instrument was
wrong, not the optimisation. Switching `worst` to each file's own **median**
across passes made it 108.4 → 104.0 with a ±0.2 ms spread, and aggregate
formatting throughput 2.3 → 2.5 MiB/s.

Two things worth carrying forward:

- **The measurement was the deliverable.** The allocation fix is four lines; the
  reason it was findable at all is that the benchmark stopped reporting
  variance. A benchmark nobody can trust is worse than none, because it is used
  anyway.
- **The obvious guess was wrong.** Before profiling I was confident the cost was
  `trivia`'s `prev_token`/`next_token` walks — rowan's are O(depth), and they
  are called per token per node as lowering descends. Stubbing all three out
  saved ~10% of lowering. It was the allocator. Measuring first cost ten minutes
  and saved a refactor of the wrong thing.

`cargo test -p kg-fmt --release --lib -- --ignored --nocapture profile` is kept
as the per-stage stopwatch that found it.

## The semantic layer, and two accessors that were dead from birth

`kg-resolve`, `kg-const` and `kg-ty` landed behind `kg_db::check_source`, taking
conformance from 1832/1832 decidable to 1924/1924. Nothing in
`xtask/src/conformance.rs` was touched to move that number, which is the whole
reason the seam exists.

**Finding: generated code can be dead and silent.** `cargo xtask codegen` emits
an accessor for whatever `kanagawa.ungram` describes, whether or not the parser
builds that shape. Two accessors were wrong from the day they were generated:

- `EnumDecl::base_list()` and `EnumDecl::enum_variants()` — the ungram claimed
  `'enum' Name BaseList '{' EnumVariant … '}'`, the parser emits `':' Type` and
  nests the variants in a `DeclList`. Both returned nothing on **every enum in
  existence**. `BASE_LIST` was already asserted unreachable by kg-parser's own
  `node_kind_coverage` test — the ungram was describing a node nothing built.
- `Attr::name()` — same shape of error, `None` for every attribute.

Nothing failed. No compile error, no red test. The tell was social rather than
technical: *three separate consumers had independently written the same
workaround*. kg-db and kg-lsp each had "try the typed accessor, then fall back
to walking the untyped tree", and kg-ty's carried the comment "accept either".
Three workarounds, one cause, and nobody looked up.

The ungram was corrected rather than the parser — the parser is the artifact
validated by 479/479 losslessness and 355/355 acceptance. Deleting
`base_list()` then made the compiler point at every dead call, which is how the
workarounds got removed instead of left to rot.

**The lesson generalised into a test.** The real defect was that nothing
exercised the generated layer, so `crates/kg-syntax/src/ast/mod.rs` now has
tests that reach a real enum's base type and variants, an attribute's name and
argument, and a class body's items. An accessor that returns nothing on every
input now fails a test rather than being silently worked around.

## Why `FRONTEND_COMPLETE` is still `false`

`--strict` scores exactly as if the flag were `true`, and reports 711 failures.
The decomposition is exact:

- **678** `expected:1` snippets that compile cleanly — 834 total, minus the 156
  now decided (1924 passing − 1768 `expected:0`);
- **33** assertions naming a specific warning — 79 warning assertions, minus 39
  spelled `warning:0` and 7 spelled bare `warning:`, both of which pass
  vacuously.

The blocker is structural, not a matter of writing more passes.
`kg_db::check_source` is handed one text and no file system, so the module
search of `Parser/IO.hs:37-110` cannot run: `import helper.foo` resolves to
nothing and every base-library name is invisible. Pass 9 (`undefinedSymbols`,
`Frontend.hs:82-155`) is therefore unwireable at this seam *in principle* — its
job is to reject names absent from the whole-program symbol map, and running it
against a single file would reject every base-library name and break the 241
assertions the reference defers to the C++ backend. Passes 4, 8, 10, 11 and 12
sit behind the same wall.

**The next unlock is one change**: a `check_source` variant that takes a VFS
root, so `kg_resolve::ModuleGraph` can resolve imports against `test/syntax/`
and the base library.

## The conformance oracle, and a file nobody runs

There is no reference binary in this environment — no GHC, no cabal — so the
oracle had to be the `expected:` assertions embedded in the corpus itself.

> **Superseded 2026-08-12.** Half of that was wrong for the whole project. The
> reference's *executable* links a C++ backend; its frontend *library* does not,
> and ghcup was already installed. `oracle/` now builds all 26
> `Language.Kanagawa.*` modules in about two minutes. The corpus assertions
> remain the conformance oracle — that part stands — but they are no longer the
> *only* oracle. See "The constraint that was half true" below.
`xtask conformance` reimplements `test/syntax/syntax-test.py`'s semantics
natively: accumulate snippets, match the first `Error (\d+)` and the first
`[--Wno-x]`, fail on `Call Stack:`.

Two things fell out of reading that script closely.

`test/syntax/basics.k` — the largest file in the suite at 406 assertions — is
never registered with `add_syntax_test`, so upstream's live oracle is 2,516
assertions, not 2,922. The harness runs it anyway and labels it, because a test
that exists and is never run is worth knowing about.

More useful: `syntax-test.py:103-106` invokes the compiler with **no
`--backend`**, and the reference's default is `backend = None`, which its own
help text calls "produce metadata only" (`app/Options/CmdArgs.hs:75`). Every
one of those 2,516 assertions is a frontend-only run. **The repoint experiment
therefore does not need the backend** — at the end of Phase 3, pointing
`kanagawa::exe` at this binary should make `ctest -R '^syntax\.'` green using
upstream's own runner. That is a far stronger check on `xtask conformance` than
the harness can give itself, because it tests the scoreboard against the thing
the scoreboard was written from.

## Four parser bugs, and why the gates found them

The parser reached 355/355 acceptance only after four fixes, three of which
were mine and none of which a unit test would plausibly have caught. Recorded
because each is a trap the next person could re-introduce:

- **`Input::from_lexed` compared raw adjacency.** The lexer's `glued(i)` flag
  compares a token to its immediate raw neighbour, which is trivially true in a
  contiguous stream — so `int<2> == 2` saw `>` glued to `=` and refused to close
  the angle. Fixed to compare adjacency to the next *non-trivia* token.
  Conformance 1815 → 1823.
- **Template-argument follow-set.** `assert(pos < v.size && v.size > 0)` really
  does close at angle depth 0. An allow-list of what may follow `>` was tried
  first and broke `bitsizeof S<uint6> - 2`, which is a template instance used as
  an operand; inverting it to a deny-list fixed both. 353 → 355.
- **`at_decl` did not skip `inline`/`noinline`**, so a nested function
  definition in statement position fell through to expression parsing. 334 →
  353.
- **A bare `template` qualifier** routed to `items::item`. `templateQualifier`
  is `try (L.symbol "template" <* notFollowedBy langle)` (`Parser.hs:646`), so
  the disambiguator applies precisely when `template` is *not* followed by `<`.

**The pattern worth keeping**: every one of these was found by a corpus gate,
not by a test someone thought to write. The gates were built in Phase 0, before
any grammar existed, which is why the 0 → 355 progression is measured against a
scoreboard the parser could not influence.

## `!~x` — a spec that contradicted itself

`docs/spec/grammar.md` §3.12 stated that two prefix operators at the same
precedence level cannot stack, and then offered `!~x` as an example that works.
Both cannot be true: `!` and `~` are both level 2 (`Parser.hs:923-926`) and
megaparsec's `Prefix` is not chainable.

Verified against the parser — `!~a`, `~!a`, `-~a` rejected; `!-a`, `~-a` parse
— which is the real rule: a prefix operator may stack onto a *tighter* level,
never twice within one level. Worth keeping straight: `!!x` and `~~x` fail in
the **lexer**, because `operator o` is
`try (string o *> notFollowedBy (oneOf (o ++ "=")))` (`Parser/Lexer.hs:262`),
while `!~x` lexes cleanly and fails in the **precedence table**. Same outcome,
different mechanism.

A test had encoded the wrong expectation. It now pins all five cases plus the
rejections, with citations.

## Two files, one module, one exit code

`kg check a.k b.k` rejected a valid program. Both files said `module m`; `a.k`
declared `const auto Ten = 10`, `b.k` said `static assert(Ten == 10)`, and pass
9 reported `Symbol name not in scope: `Ten``.

The symbol was in the map the whole time. A declaration inside `module m` is
filed under the mangled key `[@m, Ten]`, and pass 9's `is_known` probed two
*exact* keys — the bare name and the name as written. Neither is `[@m, Ten]`.
The reference does not probe; `lookupInScope` (`Symbols.hs:79-87`) walks
outward from the referring module's own namespace, which reaches the key on the
first step.

The tell was in the pass's own output. It printed **"Perhaps you meant: `Ten`
defined in m"** alongside the error — and that hint is generated by searching
the same map for exactly the key the probe had failed to ask for. The pass knew
the answer well enough to suggest it and still called the program broken.

Two things worth keeping:

**The door with the tests was not the door with the bug.** This is unreachable
from the language server, which roots each program at a single file, so the
multi-root path had no user until `kg check` started taking several. Every test
of pass 9 went through the one-root door. The regression test added for this
uses two roots, and I confirmed it goes red when the walk is removed rather
than trusting that it would.

**A fix that only silences is not a fix.** The same test asserts the other
direction — a name declared nowhere still errors — because widening a lookup
until the error stops is indistinguishable from deleting the error, and the
gates cannot tell those apart either: an over-wide lookup loses `expected:1`
assertions, which the strict run books as failures rather than flagging as
suspicious.

## A pattern match that sees through a name

`kg check -W all` warned on this, and did not warn on the same loop written
`: 256`:

```
const uint16 K = 256;
inline void V(uint8 x) { }
inline void main() { for (const auto i : K) { V(i); } }
```

    warning: Narrowing conversion from `const uint16` to `uint8`

The rule is `inductionVarType` (`Type.hs:1131-1137`):

```haskell
inductionVarType x | isIntLiteral x = constIndexType x
                   | otherwise      = try (tConst . TUnsigned) $ sizeOf x
```

and `isIntLiteral` (`Type.hs:1087-1090`) is three lines of pattern match on an
`IntLiteral` constructor. `K` is not a literal, so the port took the `sizeOf`
branch and got the *declared* width, `uint16`. The reference takes the other
branch and gets `clog2 256 = uint8`. Passing `uint8` to `uint8` warns about
nothing.

The port's leaf was not wrong. It was reading a different tree.

`inferExpTree` (`Inference.hs:47`) is

```haskell
staticControl . unfix . evaluateConstexpr symbols . unfix . inferExpType symbols
```

and `evaluateConstexpr` is a **rewrite**, not a query: it replaces a
`NamedValueF` whose declaration is a `const` with an int initializer by that
literal, cast to the declared type (`Constexpr.hs:284-288`). By the time
`inferExpType` runs, `K` *is* the node `IntLiteral 256`. A three-line pattern
match sees through a named constant because something upstream already
substituted it.

This port implements only the `inferExpType` third, on a lossless CST that is
never rewritten. So the equivalent is to **ask** where the reference **matches**:
a new `SymbolEnv::folded_int`, defaulting to `None`, which `kg-db` answers with
the `ConstEval` it already owns.

Three things worth keeping:

**The direction of the default is the safety argument.** Returning `None` where
the reference would have folded costs a type, and an unresolved type is quiet.
Returning `Some` where it would not have folded invents a type, and an invented
type invents diagnostics. The default is `None` and the implementation declines
anything `declined_by_environment` marks, so the failure mode is a missing
warning — which the scoreboard books as undecidable — rather than a false one,
which breaks an `expected:0`.

**A test that only proves the warning stopped is a mute button.** The regression
test pins the *value*: `K = 256` gives `uint8` and `K = 512` gives `uint9`, so a
rule that merely stopped consulting `sizeOf` fails it. The end-to-end check does
the same from the other side — with `K = 256` a `uint7` parameter still warns,
and the message names `const uint8`, which is the width being computed rather
than suppressed. Both tests were run against the unfixed code and confirmed red.

**Six more sites read the same unrewritten tree.** `uint<N>`, array bounds,
`fan_out<N>`, `[[latency(n)]]` and the literal-specialised binary-operator rules
all pattern-match for a literal where the reference sees a folded one, and the
corpus pins all six (`constexpr.k:1322`, `basics.k:1504`, `basics.k:1176`,
`function-constants.k:276`). They are not done here: each one *adds* diagnostics
— folded array bounds make `uint2[-2]` reachable, folded attributes make two
function types stop comparing equal — so each needs its own gate run. Closing
just this one moved the decidable count 2014 → 2015 and strict failures 592 →
591, and cost 1.5 ms of a 93 ms whole-corpus check.

## The fourth crate with no caller

`crates/kg-lsp/src/fmt.rs` opened with:

> `kg-fmt` — the comment-preserving formatter over the CST — is owned by
> another crate that does not exist yet.

It exists. It has 403 files of corpus coverage, a verifier that refuses any
edit that would change the program, and `kg fmt` has been calling it from the
CLI for phases. `crates/kg-lsp/Cargo.toml` carried a note explaining that a
path dependency on the missing directory would fail the workspace.

So "Format Document" was greyed out in the editor for a formatter that worked.

This is the fourth instance of the same failure — after `WarningSet::filter`,
`Db::check` and `Db::diagnostics`, all of which existed, were tested, and had
no caller. The rule stands: **a crate is not shipped until something a user
types reaches it, and tests do not count.** Three edits, exactly the three the
module's own doc comment predicted, and the capability lit up on its own,
because it was already gated on a runtime `available()` rather than hard-coded
off. The seam was built correctly; nobody walked back through it.

Worth keeping from the wiring itself:

**An empty edit list is a real answer, and it is the right one twice.** Once
when `kg-fmt` refuses — it declines a file that does not parse, and
`format_range` additionally declines an edit it cannot prove is the same
program. And once when the file is already formatted: a no-op edit list still
marks the document dirty, pushes an undo entry, and can retrigger
format-on-save. Both now return no edits, for different reasons.

The declining matters more in an editor than in a batch run, because
format-on-save fires against a buffer that is mid-edit. `void f(` is a syntax
error for the tenth of a second it takes to type the parameter, and a formatter
that guessed would rewrite it.

**The obsolete test was corrected, not deleted.**
`formatting_answers_with_no_edits_while_there_is_no_backend` asserted the old
contract and had to go red. It became
`formatting_round_trips_through_the_real_formatter`, which asserts the handler
reaches the real formatter and returns exactly what `kg fmt` would — so the two
front doors cannot drift apart, which was the original reason for putting the
formatter in its own crate.

Three stale claims went with it: `infer.rs` said `kg_const::ConstEval` "is
still `todo!()`, so calling it would panic" in three places. It is fully
implemented, and the previous entry is about calling it. A comment that
describes a wall which is no longer there is worse than no comment — it stops
the next person from trying the door.

## Four semantic features, and the one that was already lying

`kg-db` gained `Db::definition_at(roots, file, offset)` — a cursor position in,
a located declaration out — and the language server gained goto-definition,
hover, find-references and inlay hints on top of it.

The reason it lives in `kg-db` and not in the server is a theorem. Pass 9
(`undefined_symbols`) answers "is this name in scope?" and `definition_at`
answers "which declaration is it?", and if those two ever disagree the editor
says *undefined* over a name the compiler accepts, or jumps to a declaration the
compiler says does not exist. So `definition_at` reuses pass 9's sources 2-4
verbatim, and narrows them in exactly two places — it probes only the written
prefix, never the bare leading segment, and it requires a *unique* import hit
where pass 9 accepts any. Both narrowings decline. Every source is therefore a
subset of pass 9's, which makes "a name pass 9 rejects is never one this query
jumps to" a property rather than a hope, and a test asserts it at every offset
pass 9 reported across five fixtures.

Pass 9's source 1 could not be reused: it is a flat set of every name declared
anywhere in the file, because a yes/no answer never needs to know *which*
declaration. That coarseness is exactly where locals and parameters live, which
is most of what anyone points at in an editor, so the scope walk had to be
built — a CST ancestor walk, innermost first, because `ScopeData` stores each
scope's *end* state and records no source extent, so there is no offset → scope
map to read.

**`document_highlight` had been lying since it was written.** Its doc said name
resolution "does not exist yet" and it matched by spelling. So eight `x`es in a
function with a shadowed binding all lit up together — telling the reader that
assigning to the inner `x` changes the outer one — and every `class` keyword in
the file lit up, which is a fact about the lexer and not about the program. It
now runs through the resolver, and the shadowing test asserts the two sets are
disjoint *and* that together they account for every `x`, so neither query can
quietly lose an occurrence to the other.

That fix cost something real and worth naming: struct fields are not lowered
(`Symbols.hs:48-49`), so they no longer highlight at all, where before they
highlighted textually. A usefulness regression chosen over a correctness one.
A hardware programmer points at fields constantly, and the honest answer is that
the feature is off for them until fields are lowered — not a textual guess
dressed up as resolution.

**The overflow nobody was looking for.** `convert::offset` computed
`line_start + character` and clamped afterwards. "End of line" has no spelling
in the protocol, so clients send a huge column instead — and `line_start +
u32::MAX` overflows on every line but the first. Debug panics; release *wraps*
to a small number that then survives the clamp and reads as a plausible offset
near the top of the file. It was found by an agent writing a test helper for a
different feature, reported as "a real bug it does not own", and confirmed here:
the first test written for it passed, because it probed line 0, where the line
start is 0 and nothing can overflow. Moving it to line 1 panicked immediately.

Worth keeping: a test that exercises the boundary of the *wrong* dimension is a
test that passes for free. The bug needed a non-zero line start, and line 0 is
the one every test reaches for.

## Right, and unusable

Pass 4 landed with every gate green: 961 tests, clippy clean, conformance up
seven assertions, strict down seven. It also made `check` on
`test/library/processor/risc-v.k` take **1.9 seconds instead of 95 milliseconds**
— a twentyfold regression on the number an editor waits for, on a keystroke.

Nothing in the correctness suite could see it. Conformance snippets are a few
lines each, so the pass looked cheap there; the implementer measured the
template index at 2.7% of the conformance run and reported that in good faith.
It was a true number about the wrong thing — the index build, over inputs too
small for the pass *body* to matter.

The cost was the shadow guard, which is the part that was most carefully
reasoned about. It asks each enclosing scope "do you bind this name?" and
answered by walking that scope's subtree. So the cost is (calls) × (size of each
enclosing scope), and the shape that hurts is many calls sharing one *large*
ancestor — a class full of methods. The outermost ancestor's subtree is most of
the file, re-walked once per call inside it.

The relation is the same one computed the other way round: walk the file once,
and for each `NAME` record the scope that binds it. The lookup becomes one hash
probe per ancestor. 1894 ms → 96.94 ms, against a pre-pass-4 baseline of 94.81 ms,
so the pass now costs about 2 ms of a check.

Two things worth keeping.

**A profile reads differently from a benchmark.** The benchmark said "check is
slow". The profile said `pass_4_deduce_template_args` was 4815 of 6769 samples —
71% of a check, in a pass that had existed for one commit. That is not a number
anyone would have guessed from the code, which looks like a linear walk over
call expressions; the quadratic part is one function call deep inside it, in the
guard rather than in the loop.

**A timing test was written as a guard, and then deleted.** It passed with the
quadratic code as readily as with the linear code — 0.09 s against 0.02 s, both
far under any bound loose enough not to flake on a slow machine. A fixture large
enough to separate them is too slow to be a unit test. Keeping it would have
been worse than having nothing: a green test named
`many_calls_under_one_large_scope_stay_linear` asserting that it is. The rule
this project already applies to correctness tests — break the code, watch it go
red — applied to a performance test and it failed, so it went. The benchmark on
real files is the guard, and `CLAUDE.md` now says so.

## Two loops where the reference has one

`check` spent 42% of itself in `type_table`, and `type_table` was a fixpoint
wrapped around a fixpoint: rebuild the symbol map from the current annotations,
run `infer_program` **to convergence**, and repeat while the unresolved count
fell.

The reference is one loop (`Inference.hs:31-37`):

```haskell
loop prevSig p
    | prevSig == sig = inferred
    | otherwise      = loop sig inferred
  where
    symbols = getSymbols' TemplateDecl p
    inferred = parallel (inferExpTree symbols) p
```

`symbols` is in the `where` of `loop`. It is rebuilt every round, and that is
the whole reason the loop exists — a round that resolves a declaration's type is
what lets the next round resolve its uses.

The port had split that into two, and the cost of the split was exactly a factor
of two. Instrumenting the rounds showed the inner loop running **exactly two
iterations, every single time**: it can never stop after one, because its exit
test needs a round that changes nothing to confirm stability
(`Inference.hs:29` — `loop []` guarantees it). So every symbol-map rebuild paid
for two full walks of every file where the reference pays for one. The outer
loop's last iteration was worse: a whole convergence run that improved nothing,
by definition, since that is what ended it.

The seam comment had described the fix without naming it as one: *"the rebuild
is `kg-db`'s to trigger between rounds; the loop shape below is what it hooks
into."* There was no hook. `SymbolSource::rebuild(&TypeTable)` is it, and the
outer loop is gone.

check 86.15 → 66.73 ms, keystroke 111.78 → 95.06 ms, and 2022/2022 and 584 both
unchanged — which is the result to want here, because this changed the shape of
a fixpoint and the corpus agreeing at both ends is the evidence it converges to
the same place.

Cumulative for the session's performance work: check 94.81 → 66.73 ms (−30%),
keystroke 119.72 → 95.06 ms (−21%).

**The plan said the next performance item was incremental reparse.** The profile
says parsing is 9% of a check. Even a perfect incremental parser — one that costs
nothing at all — buys less than a tenth of what the frontend costs, and the two
changes that did land were worth 30% between them. The plan was written before
there was a profiler to argue with; the item stays open, but it is not next.

## The formatter parses the file four times

`kg-fmt` had been the slowest stage in the toolchain for the whole project —
about 104 ms on `library/numeric/float32.k`, against 70 ms for a *full check* of
the same file — and nobody had ever profiled it. The roadmap's entry said only
"nobody has looked. That is the whole reason it is on the list."

The profile:

| | |
|---|---|
| `align::realign` | 30.4% |
| `lower::Lowerer::source_file` | 27.3% |
| `verify::check` | 20.8% |
| `parse_file` (top level) | 7.6% |
| `reattach` | 6.6% |

and then the part worth knowing — **40.5% of `realign` is itself `parse_file`,
and 26.3% of `verify::check` is too.** Formatting one file parses it four
times: once at the top, once in each of `realign`'s two passes, and once more in
the verifier. Roughly a quarter of formatting is parsing, and three quarters of
that is re-parsing.

Two of the four were avoidable and are now gone. `realign` runs two passes — code
anchors (`=`, `as`) first, then comments, because padding the first shifts the
second — and each re-parsed the output to find where the anchors landed. The
second pass only needs a fresh tree if the first actually moved something, so the
parse is threaded through and re-taken on demand. Separately, both passes read
the *input* tree, which neither of them changes, so its anchors are now gathered
in one walk rather than one per pass.

104.2 → 99.6 ms, 2.5 → 2.7 MiB/s. About 4.5%.

**That is a modest number and it is the honest headline.** The remaining cost is
structural, and each part of it earns its place: lowering builds the `Doc`, which
is the actual work; the verifier re-parses the output and compares token streams,
which is the only reason anyone can trust a formatter that rewrites comments; and
the two surviving parses are of two genuinely different strings. There is no
large win hiding here — the formatter is slow because it does the job three times
on purpose, and the third time is what makes it safe.

The useful correction is to the roadmap's framing rather than to the code. "The
formatter is the slowest stage" invited the reading that something was wrong with
it. Nothing is. It is slower than a type-check because it is doing more passes
over the text than a type-check does, and the profile is the evidence for
leaving it alone.

What would actually move it is a faster parser — 39 MiB/s, and it appears here
four times. That is a different project and it would pay off in `check` and
`keystroke` too.

## Six fold sites, zero assertions, and a note that lied

The roadmap carried an item called "close the remaining constexpr-fold sites",
and its authority came from a doc comment in `kg-ty` that read:

> **Six callers of this function still do not** [ask] … The corpus pins all
> six — `constexpr.k:1322`, `basics.k:1504`, `basics.k:1176`,
> `function-constants.k:276`, and `constexpr.k:1405`/`:1414`.

Both halves of that are wrong, and it took surveying every site before touching
any of them to find out.

**"The corpus pins all six" — it does not.** Every assertion named is an
*accept* (`expected:0`) that was already passing. They pass because an
unresolved type is silent, and they pass after folding because the folded type
is legal. They are guardrails: they tell you if you break something. They pin
nothing, and no assertion anywhere moves when the sites are converted.
Conformance held at 2049/2049 and `--strict` at 557 across all four
conversions — not approximately, exactly.

**"Six callers" — there are eight**, and one of them must never be converted.
`deduce_int` matches a literal against a template *formal*'s written extent.
Folding there binds a template argument the reference leaves unbound, and
`reconcile` answers a conflicting binding with a `TError` (`Type.hs:1500-1505`)
while the instance mangling changes underneath it. That is two separate ways to
invent an error on a correct program, and it had been sitting in a list labelled
"still to do".

Two more stay literal-only for a subtler reason: `infer_binary`'s guard and
`infer_mux`'s selector test things a `ConstInt` cannot express.
`isUntypedIntLiteral` (`Type.hs:1092-1095`) distinguishes `4` from `4u8`, and a
`ConstValue::Enum` must not select a mux arm where `ConstInt` would flatten it
into one. Those need a value-returning companion to `folded_int`, not
`folded_int` itself. Reaching for the tool that was already there would have
computed wrong widths, and widths are what the conversion warnings are derived
from.

### So what did the four conversions buy?

Nothing on the scoreboard, and the honest framing is that the scoreboard was
never the point — it just looked like it was, because a note said so.

What they bought is that `uint<FOO>` now produces `Invalid member access on
type` where it was silent, that a hover over `uint32[N] a` says `uint32[4]`
instead of nothing, and that every rule downstream of a resolved type —
subtyping, initializer arity, `auto` deduction, template argument checking — is
reachable on programs where it was previously skipped. For a project whose whole
thesis is developer tools first, a type the editor gets *right* is the deliverable
even when no assertion counts it.

### The rule this leaves behind

Fold sites are asymmetric in a way that is easy to get backwards. Folding
*narrower* than `evaluateConstexpr` costs a type and produces silence, which the
scoreboard books as undecidable and which is honest. Folding *wider* invents a
diagnostic on a program the reference accepts. So the tests that matter most
here are the ones asserting that something does **not** fold — a mutable `auto`
in a width, a `static for` induction variable — and both are load-bearing
against the specific mistake they describe: dropping the `const` guard in
`scope::const_inner_type` turns the first red, and registering an induction
variable as a constant turns the second red.

### The benchmark, because pass 4 earned that habit

Four new sites now run a constant evaluation on every fixpoint round, which is
exactly the shape of the pass-4 regression. Interleaved A/B over the whole
corpus, three pairs: **1410 / 1412 / 1418 ms with the folds against 1441 / 1418 /
1431 ms without.** The distributions overlap, so the honest reading is "no
measurable cost" rather than "slightly faster" — though a fixpoint that resolves
more per round having fewer rounds to run is a plausible reason it did not get
slower. Worst-file keystroke is unchanged at ~110 ms either way.

And the meta-rule, which is the expensive one: **a TODO note is a previous
session's claim, not a fact.** This one had a specific corpus citation for every
item, which is exactly what made it credible. The citations were real; the
conclusion drawn from them was not. Survey before you schedule.

## Provenance is a copy, not a mapping, and the roadmap had the reference backwards

Roadmap 1d closes by asking for this entry: a proposal for **(b)**, a lowered IR
that may be rewritten, with the provenance representation named, because that is
the decision the rest of the frontend inherits. The representation is named
below. It is `Src` — the reference's own type, transcribed — and arriving at it
meant disproving the sentence that made the problem look hard.

Three designs were written against 1d independently and three reviewers graded
them. All six re-derived the same correction, which is the strongest signal
available in a checkout with no reference build.

### 1d is wrong about where the reference points, and wrong in the easy direction

The roadmap says, and the brief repeats: *"an error inside `Foo<int32>` must
point at the instantiation, not at the template body — and the reference gets
this for free because its copies are distinct nodes with distinct ranges."*
Both halves are false, and it takes five files to establish:

* `makeInstance` copies the body with `desugarWithNote n rewrite instanceDecl`
  (`Template.hs:127`), where `n` is the note stored in `decidedInstances` —
  `note $ unfix e` of the `TemplateInstance` node, i.e. the instantiation site
  (`Template.hs:96`).
* `desugarWithNote n f = para f'` with `f' e' (Note n' e) = NotedExp (n' <> n)
  (f e' e)` (`Desugar.hs:92-94`). `n'` is the **copied body node's own** note;
  the instantiation's note is the right operand.
* `instance Semigroup Src` is a stack push whose head never moves:
  `a <> b = SrcStack a b`, `a <> (SrcStack b c) = SrcStack a (SrcStack b c)`,
  `(SrcStack a b) <> c = SrcStack a (SrcStack c b)`
  (`Parser/Syntax.hs:623-626`).
* Every consumer reports the **head**: `fixErrorOffset (SrcStack a _, e) =
  fixErrorOffset (a, e)` (`Error.hs:182`), `offset (SrcStack a _, e)`
  (`Error.hs:201`), `symbolOffset`/`symbolLoc` (`Error.hs:104,111`), and
  `srcFile (SrcStack a _) = srcFile a` (`Error.hs:197`), which is also the key
  `makeErrorBundles` *groups* by (`Error.hs:169`) — so even the file the bundle
  opens in is the template's.
* The tail is rendered, not discarded: `fixError (SrcStack a b, e)` runs
  `expandErrorStack 0 e b` (`Error.hs:176-178`), and `addErrorContext` turns each
  remaining frame into a nested bundle whose message is the literal string
  `"while compiling"` (`Error.hs:192-194`), printed as `"note: " ++
  errorBundlePretty x` (`Error.hs:70`).

So the reference emits a C++-style instantiation backtrace: the primary error
lands in the template body, in the template's file, with one `while compiling`
note per instantiation frame. The clincher is that it could not do anything
else. `desugarError = ErrorF . fancyError (-1)` (`Error.hs:139-140`) and
`fixErrorOffset (Src o _ _ _, FancyError (-1) e) = FancyError o e`
(`Error.hs:183`): a desugar-inserted error carries **no offset of its own** and
takes the note's head. Every pass-8 error is of that shape. The reference's own
context helper says the same thing out loud — `errorMsgWithContext n msg
(NotedExp n' _) = NotedExp (n' <> n) $ desugarError msg` (`Error.hs:151`).

The consequence is large and good. Roadmap 1d calls the synthetic-range mapping
"the entire difficulty"; there is no synthetic range to invent. Non-instantiation
synthesis goes through `newNote e (NotedExp n _) = NotedExp (Typed TUnresolved $
untype n) e` (`Type.hs:983-984`), which hands the new node a **donor's** `Src`
verbatim, and every one of the five rewrites picks a donor that is already the
right thing to show a user: `abbreviatedFunctionTemplate`'s synthetic
`typename x$T` donates from the `auto` parameter (`Function.hs:296`),
`closureCalls`' cast donates from the callee (`Closure.hs:23-25`, `new = flip
newNote b`), `addLambdaWrappers` donates from the argument (`Function.hs:375`),
`moveFunctions` keeps the node's own note (`Function.hs:105-118`).
**Provenance is not a mapping problem. It is a copy.**

1d's *conclusion* survives intact — five sub-passes add declarations nobody
wrote, and no key-space trick does that. It is in fact stronger than 1d knew.
`resolve` (`Template.hs:159-163`) replaces a decided `TemplateInstance` node with
its mangled name, and the fixpoint applies it as `desugar (instantiate . resolve)`
(`Template.hs:58`). That is a rewrite, it is inside `decidedInstances`' own
convergence argument, and virtual instantiation cannot express it either.

### The representation: `Src`, with the tail interned

```rust
// crates/kg-base/src/src.rs — kg-base, not kg-hir. See the cost note below.

/// `Src` (`Parser/Syntax.hs:610-621`), transcribed. A non-empty stack of real
/// source ranges: `head` is where a diagnostic is reported
/// (`Error.hs:182-184,197,201`), `via` is the instantiation chain
/// `expandErrorStack` renders as `while compiling` (`Error.hs:186-195`).
#[derive(Copy, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Debug)]
pub struct Src {
    /// The head of `SrcStack`. **Always a real range in a real file.** A
    /// synthetic node copies a donor's (`newNote`, `Type.hs:983-984`), so no
    /// node ever invents one.
    pub head: FileRange,
    /// Whether `head` is this node's own text or a range it was *given*.
    /// **Not in the reference**, which cannot tell them apart and does not need
    /// to. Here it is the difference between an index an editor may answer a
    /// position question from and one it may not.
    pub written: Written,
    /// `SrcStack`'s tail, interned. `Expansion::ROOT` is a bare `Src`.
    pub via: Expansion,
}

#[derive(Copy, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Debug)]
pub enum Written {
    /// `head` is this node's own text, and `(head, kind)` is a valid `TypeKey`.
    Own,
    /// `head` came from a donor. No position question may be answered from it.
    Donated,
}

#[derive(Copy, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, PartialOrd, Ord, Debug)]
pub struct Expansion(u32);

/// One link of `SrcStack` (`Parser/Syntax.hs:618`). Pushed **only** by
/// instantiation (`desugarWithNote n`, `Template.hs:127`); the other four
/// rewrites copy a donor's `Src` unchanged, because that is what `newNote` does.
#[derive(Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Debug)]
pub struct ExpansionData {
    pub site: FileRange,
    pub instance: InstanceId,
    pub parent: Expansion,
}
```

Two constructors, and the distinction between them is the part a previous draft
got wrong in a way that silently emptied the whole LSP story:

* `expanded(node, site, instance)` keeps `node.head` and `node.written` and
  pushes a frame. An instantiated copy of a body node **is** the user's own
  text, so it stays `Own`. It is the `n' <> n` of `Desugar.hs:94`, specialised
  to the only shape `instantiateTemplates` uses.
* `donated(donor)` copies `head` and `via` and sets `Donated`. This is
  `newNote`.

`written` is set at every construction site and is never derived from which
constructor was used, because `copyNote`, `renote` and a bare `NotedExp n` all
reuse a note under a *different* variant — `moveFunctions` builds
`NotedExp n $ SeqF (init b ++ init c ++ [NotedExp n $ IfF …])`
(`Function.hs:110-118`), a `SeqF` wearing an `IfF`'s note.

`Src` alone cannot build a `TypeKey`: that is `{ file, offset, end, kind }`
(`kg-ty/src/infer.rs:317-332`) and `kind` is load-bearing, not decoration —
divergence #21 records that dropping it makes a cross-module lookup a collision
rather than a miss. So `NodeData` carries the originating `SyntaxKind` beside its
`Src`, and the pair `(head, kind)` is a legal key **iff** `written == Own`.
Four bytes, and without them the hover census below cannot be built at all.

One detail worth keeping because it is free and correct: `resolveTypeParam`
substitutes with `argAt = unNote . unfix . (args !!)` (`TypeCheck.hs:333-336`),
which unwraps exactly one `Note`, and `desugarWithNote`'s `para` never visits the
spliced children. So in the reference an argument subtree keeps its own `Src`, in
the *instantiating* file, with no frame pushed. Reproduce that literally — splice
the argument's subtree unchanged. It is the one case where a pass-8 diagnostic
already lands in the user's own buffer.

### What a diagnostic points at, and what three instantiations produce

`emit` is `Diagnostic::error(src.head, message)` followed by one
`with_label(frame.site, format!("while compiling `{}`", …))` per frame — the
transcription of `Error.hs:176-195`. `kg_diag::Diagnostic` already carries
`labels: Vec<Label>` with `Label { range: FileRange, message }`
(`kg-diag/src/lib.rs:96-100,120-131`), so the chain needs no new model.

**One instance gets one frame, not one per use site.** `decidedInstances` is
`Map.unionsWith Map.union` over the per-module maps (`Template.hs:88`) and
`Map.union` is left-biased, so `Vector<uint8,4>` written at fifty sites keeps
exactly one note and the reference shows exactly one "required from here" — the
first in program order. That is the rule, it is user-visible, and it is a
determinism hazard: the fold over per-module lists decides the winner, and
`in_program_order`'s own comment says why hash order cannot be allowed to decide
anything (`db.rs:660-666`). `InstanceData` therefore keeps `site` (the first, in
`Program::files` order, pinned by a test) for the faithful chain, and `sites:
Vec<FileRange>` for the editor.

Two doors, one core. The `kanagawa` compat binary renders what the reference
renders. `Db::diagnostics(roots, file)` **re-aims**: if the primary is not in
`file` and a frame is, the outermost such frame becomes the primary and the body
location becomes a label reading `` in the body of `Vector<T, N>` ``. Without
that, a user who writes `Vector<Bad, 4>` gets a squiggle in
`library/data/vector.k` and nothing in their own buffer, because
`crates/kg-lsp/src/handlers/diagnostics.rs:42` filters by file and documents why.
Re-aiming is invisible to conformance, which reads the exit code and the first
`Error N` and never a location (`Parser/IO.hs:114`, `syntax-test.py:113-118`).

Three instantiations failing at the same body node produce three diagnostics in
the reference: `nub $ errors $ unnoteType desugared` (`Main.hs:81`) compares
`(Src, ParseError)` and `Src`'s derived `Eq` covers the whole stack, so equal
heads with distinct tails survive. Compat emits three. The editor merges to one
with three labels, keyed on **(primary range, diagnostic identity)** — not on
message text, because messages interpolate types (`kg-ty/src/convert.rs:324-331`)
and a text merge would never fire on exactly the width errors this compiler
exists to catch. New row in `known-divergences.md`.

Two wiring items make the difference between a provenance chain and a fifth
module with no caller: `related_information: None`
(`kg-lsp/src/handlers/diagnostics.rs:57`) drops every frame before it reaches the
client, and `kg-diag/src/render.rs:76-78` prints `note: {label.message}` and
throws `label.range` away, where the reference prints a full located sub-bundle.
Both are small. Neither exists. And `Sink` is *not* the sole `Diagnostic`
constructor — `kg-ty/src/convert.rs:268,331,359` and `kg-const/src/eval.rs:340`
build them directly and live in crates forbidden from depending on `kg-db`
(`kg-db/src/lib.rs:8-10`). That is why `Src` goes in `kg-base`: every constructor
that can fire inside an instance has to take one.

### What the LSP answers inside a template body

Goto-definition, references, document-highlight and rename **never see an
instance**, because they never see the IR. They are name questions answered off
the CST and the symbol map, and an instance's name is `Foo<|@uint8$int@4|>`
(`Mangle.hs:26-28`) — not something a user can type or wants to see. This also
keeps `navigate::tests::a_name_pass_9_rejects_never_resolves` a theorem rather
than a coincidence.

Hover answers the **template body's** type, which is what the user is looking at,
plus a census: `instantiated 3×: uint8 · uint16 · uint32`, distinct types only,
capped. Inlay hints appear **only when every instance agrees**; otherwise
nothing, per `inlay_hints.rs`'s own rule that a missing hint reads as "not
inferred", which is true, while a wrong one reads as a fact about the code. Both
are backed by one reverse index over IR nodes with `written == Own`, which is
precisely why the flag exists.

And here is the part that must not be buried, because it is the difference
between a payoff and a rounding error: **every LSP handler roots at the open
file** — `&[snap.file]` at `hover.rs:69`, `inlay_hints.rs:98`,
`definition.rs:60` — and `Program::files` is the import closure *downward*. A
template's instances are decided by the files that **import** it, which are not
in that program at all. Open `library/numeric/float32.k` and the census is empty:
`InstanceSet` has nothing in it, hover says what it says today, and not one of
the 846 unannotated `auto` bindings moves. The IR is not what unblocks that; a
rooting change is (root at the workspace, or at the reverse-import closure), and
that is a separate decision with its own cost. It should be taken deliberately,
with the number in hand, rather than discovered at merge.

### The queries, the keys, and what a keystroke costs

```rust
fn body_ir(&self, roots: &[FileId], m: ModuleSource) -> Arc<ModuleIr>;
fn module_instances(&self, roots: &[FileId], m: ModuleSource) -> Arc<Vec<Instance>>;
fn instances(&self, roots: &[FileId]) -> Arc<InstanceSet>;
fn instance(&self, roots: &[FileId], key: &InstanceKey) -> Arc<InstanceIr>;
```

`Db::instance` is `makeInstance` and nothing else (`Template.hs:125-139`), which
really is a pure function of `(templateDecl, args)`, keyed on
`InstanceKey { template: SymbolPath, args: ArgList }` — a **value** all the way
down, for the same reason `TypeKey` is a value (`infer.rs:304-306`, "the tree is
rebuilt between rounds"). It is deliberately *not* "makeInstance plus the nine
sub-passes": the nine read a whole-program symbol map over the **rewritten**
program (`Template.hs:82`, `withSymbols` at `:66-81`), so a memo keyed on the
declaring module alone would go stale when a callee three modules away changed —
exactly the failure `db.rs:42-52` refuses.

`InstanceIr` owns its own nodes. `ExpId` is an arena index and an arena index is
an address, never a key; a retained memo holding `u32`s into a dropped arena is
not a crash, it is a silently wrong node. Cross-body references go through a
`DefId`-shaped handle, the way rust-analyzer's `Body`/`ExprId` do.

The honest framing, in the shape `db.rs:517-521` already uses about pass 6:
**say which whole-program shape you are refusing to reproduce.** The reference
rebuilds `getSymbols' TemplateDecl` over the entire program every inference round
(`Inference.hs:36-37`) and runs the nine sub-passes over the whole program every
outer round (`Template.hs:60`). That is not reproduced on the keystroke path at
all. **Pass 8 is whole-program and batch-ish**; what is incremental is the
*copy*, not the fixpoint. `Db::diagnostics` keeps returning parse-stage plus
`frontend_diagnostics` on `didChange`, and pass 8 publishes on idle — which means
a snapshot taken *outside* `global_state.rs:246-253`'s `dbs` lock, because a
background computation holding that lock has not left the hot path, it has moved
the stall to the next keystroke.

Both new whole-program memos go in a `Bounded` with their **own** constant and a
comment saying why 64 is wrong here: `db.rs:114-119` justifies eviction as cheap
because a miss costs one `program::load` whose inputs are still memoized, and a
miss here costs a whole-program pass 8. `Bounded::insert` hard-codes
`MAX_ROOT_SETS` today (`db.rs:158`), so a second bound is a small refactor, not a
constant.

### The instance key

The reference's key is the `Seq args` node itself, and `Eq`/`Ord` on `Note`
ignore the annotation (`Parser/Syntax.hs:594-599`) — so it is pure structural
shape. Two facts fix what "shape" means: the key is taken **after**
`evaluateConstexpr`, which rewrites a `const` reference to its literal
(`Constexpr.hs:286-293`), so `Foo<K>` and `Foo<4>` are one entry; and after
`deduceTemplateArgs` filled the list to full length with deduced arguments and
written defaults (`Type.hs:1406-1428`). `ArgList` is therefore the argument
subtrees' shape — kinds and token text, trivia elided, with the fold applied —
interned so `Eq`/`Hash` are a `u32`, in a `BTreeMap` so `Map.toList`
(`Template.hs:120`) has a deterministic order.

**Not the mangled name.** An earlier draft proposed keying on it and folding
`deduplicateInstances` into the key. `mangle (FunctionType x y z) | isClosure =
""` (`Mangle.hs:42-43`) drops a whole argument when the template is
`data.closure.core.Closure` — the one template the closure machinery instantiates
most — so mangling is non-injective *by construction* and `Mangle.hs:21`'s
comment is an aspiration, not a spec. The reference's backstop is
`deduplicateInstances`' `nubBy`, which keeps the first in `Map.toList` order
(`Template.hs:144-156`); folding that into the key changes which instance
survives a collision, i.e. which arguments get substituted into a body. Keep the
key structural, mangle separately, and keep `deduplicateInstances` as its own
step.

Of the four rules at `Template.hs:90-108`, rules 3 and 4 — `StaticIfF`
contributes only its condition, `TemplateF` only its parameters — are
`facts::reached_only_after_elaboration` (`facts.rs:35-51`) with one arm added:
`decided _ (Note _ StaticForF{..}) = forLimit` (`Template.hs:106`) restricts a
`static for` too, and `facts.rs` has no `STATIC_FOR` case. Reusing it verbatim
under-restricts, in the false-positive direction, which is the one direction
constraint 2 forbids. Add the arm and a test. (`facts.rs` walks `ancestors()`;
`decided` is a descent, so the IR version is a fold, not a query.)

**Rule 1 is the one to get right, and the literal port is wrong.** `all Map.null
x && templateResolved` is not the static property "nothing nested inside me": it
is true only because `resolve` replaced the inner instance with a mangled name on
the *previous* round. A port whose tree is never rewritten will find
`optional<fixed<I, F>>` still nested on every round, `all Map.null x` false
forever, and the outer instance never decided. A grep over the corpus finds 424
argument lists containing another user template instantiation across 87 of 469
files — `optional<fixed<I,F>>`, `from_array<optional<uint8>>`,
`HashFunction<uint32, index_t<Depth / Associativity>>` — so this is not an edge
case, it is the library. Since the IR *is* rewritable, do `resolve` literally,
and restate the guard as "arguments resolved and every nested instance already in
the decided set", iterating.

Rule 2's `indirectInstances` needs a separation the reference gets from
laziness. `resolveTemplateParam` is `inferType' . desugar resolveTemplateInstance
. templateTypeCheck . inferType' . desugar (resolveTypeParam …)`
(`TypeCheck.hs:367-372`) — it **runs `templateTypeCheck`, a diagnostic pass**, and
keeps only a Bool; the rewritten parameter is consumed by `para decided` and
thrown away, and its errors never reach `hasErrorSymbol`, which is taken from
`getSymbols program'` (`Template.hs:82-83`). Speculative diagnostics must go to a
discard sink that is never shared with the materialized instance pipeline.
Sharing one memo between them publishes errors about arguments the reference
never accepted — diagnosing earlier than the reference, out of a cache, which is
the hardest kind to notice. The same family: `| hasErrors' = (program',
hasErrors')` (`Template.hs:55,84`) means a program carrying an error symbol
instantiates *nothing*, and pass 8 needs that gate the way `Db::check` already
reproduces the parse gate.

### The first slice, and the gate that proves it

`crates/kg-hir`: the arena, `Src`, ~90 `Exp` variants mirroring `ExpF`
(`Parser/Syntax.hs:280-584`), the structural interner, a `lower(&ast::SourceFile,
&TypeTable, &ItemTree)` that lowers every `PATH` to `Exp::Path(Unsorted)` and
sorts nothing, a pretty-printer, `Db::body_ir`, `Db::module_instances` +
`Db::instances` implementing rules 1, 3 and 4, and `kg dump ir` / `kg dump
instances` beside the existing `kg dump ast|cst|tokens`. Nothing wired into
`passes::run`. Nothing new diagnosed.

`cargo xtask ir`, over all 479 corpus files:

1. **Totality** — every file lowers with zero `Exp::Unsupported`.
2. **Round trip** — `lower(parse(pretty(lower(parse(f)))))` structurally equal to
   `lower(parse(f))`. Not byte-for-byte; the IR carries no trivia. This catches a
   lowering that drops a field, which is the failure mode a variant-per-construct
   IR actually has.
3. **The provenance invariant** — every `Src::head` resolves to a live CST node,
   and every `written == Own` node has a CST node at exactly that range whose kind
   matches. Assert it on *synthetic* nodes specifically, with hand-built fixtures,
   so it can fail now rather than in the slice that wires the rewrites.
4. **The differential oracle.** `passes/template_type_check.rs:222-296` already
   implements `templateResolved`/`templateArgsResolved` as `Cx::instance`. Rule 1
   tests the same predicate. Restricted to the shapes that pass already handles,
   the two sets must be equal over all 479 files — two independent readings of one
   Haskell predicate agreeing over the whole corpus, runnable before a single
   instance body exists.
5. **Computing `Db::instances` emits zero diagnostics**, so the speculative
   `templateTypeCheck` leak shows up on day one.
6. **Nothing moved**: 2049/2049, 557 with a byte-identical name set, 479/479 and
   355/355, 13/72, `bench` inside the A/B noise band. **The predicted assertion
   delta is exactly zero**, stated in advance so it is a prediction rather than a
   disappointment.

Then break one lowering field and watch (2) go red; point one `head` at a donor
without setting `Donated` and watch (3) go red. A gate not proven load-bearing
pins nothing.

The strongest gate available is not code. `--dump-source` prints the fully
instantiated, desugared program (`Options/CmdArgs.hs:103`, `Main.hs:90-91`), and
diffing `kg dump ir` against it would grade pass 8 against the oracle rather than
against our reading of it. There is no GHC, stack or cabal in this checkout and
`compiler/hs` has never been built here — the same absence that stopped a skeptic
settling a question two entries ago. A day of toolchain work would pay for itself
before the second slice lands.

### What this makes hard

**Inference has to move, or there will be two of them.** `kg_ty::infer` is 4,579
lines of `SyntaxNode` walking and the two `inferType` sub-passes need it over
`ExpId`. A second implementation is the failure this codebase has refused twice
in writing (`passes/types.rs:13-24`, `lib.rs:42-49`). The honest end state is
that inference moves onto the IR entirely and `Db::type_table` becomes a
projection back through `written == Own`. That is a much larger change than pass
8 and it is the single most likely thing to blow the estimate.

**The scope boundary in 1d is wrong by at least three passes.** "Only pass 8 and
its downstream consumers move" does not hold: `higherOrderFunctions`
(`Frontend.hs`, execution position 2) rewrites `inline void F(() -> void cb)`
into a `TemplateF` with a `Closure<…>` parameter (`Function.hs:313-363`), which
is the template pass 8 instantiates and the closure type sub-pass 7 tests
(`tIsClosure $ typeOf b`, `Closure.hs:19-20`); `captureThis` (position 3) is what
puts `ThisF` into `lambdaCaptures`, consumed by `Function.hs:157,407-409`; and
`trimExternClasses` is position 7, before pass 8. `passes/higher_order.rs` is 61
lines and diagnostic-only. All three end up on the IR.

**An IR-resident symbol map is a missing component about the size of the one
specified here.** `SymbolMap n e = HashMap QualifiedName (NotedExp n e)`
(`Symbols.hs:27`) — the value is the declaration *node in the tree being
rewritten*, and callers splice subtrees out of it: `addLambdaWrappers` pulls the
callee's parameter list into a synthesized lambda (`Function.hs:390-404`),
`moveToParentScope` builds one over a subtree (`Function.hs:33`) and inlines a
const member's initializer into the use site (`Function.hs:55`).
`Db::global_symbols` is `SymbolPath -> DefId` over CST item trees and cannot
answer for a declaration pass 8 itself created — which, from round two on, is
most of the program.

**Whole-program, with no import-order firewall.** `Db::type_table`'s speed rests
on an argument this journal already spells out: a module's imports cannot depend
on the module. Pass 8 breaks it — a downstream module decides an instance of an
upstream template — and `instantiate` splices the copies into the *declaring*
module's tree (`Template.hs:112-120`). The per-module memo does not survive; the
`(template, args)` instance memo recovers the copy and nothing else.

**Memory in a dimension the corpus has never paid.** The arena is bounded by
instances × body size, and the `instance` memo's key stream is keystroke-generated
(`Foo<uint`, `Foo<uint8`, `Foo<uint16`) — invalid entries never looked up again
and never freed without a bound.

**Two renderings that must agree about which diagnostic exists while disagreeing
about where it points**, and only one of them is under a conformance gate.
**Two already-passing passes must move with zero net change** —
`templateTypeCheck`'s 14 assertions and six documented declines (#21), and
`deduceTemplateArgs`' reporter half — and a refactor whose success condition is
"the scoreboard does not move" is the hardest kind to validate in a project that
has already written down that a green scoreboard is evidence about the corpus.

**~90 hand-written variants that nothing keeps in sync with the grammar.**
`xtask codegen` generates the AST from `grammar/kanagawa.ungram`; `Exp` mirrors
`ExpF` and the two deliberately disagree at the `PATH` sort (#22), so only the
totality gate will notice a grammar change. Sorting a `PATH` is a genuine
capability the IR unlocks and a genuine way to invent diagnostics — #22 exists
because guessing wrong fires on `S1<Foo>` for every struct in the corpus.
`Path(Unsorted)` is the escape hatch, spelled in the type, and slice 1 uses
nothing else.

### What is still unknown, and what would settle it

**How many instances the corpus actually has, and what they cost.** Everything
about the memo bound and the memory ceiling is arithmetic once the number exists.
`kg dump instances --stats` in slice 1: distinct instances per template, total
body nodes, arena bytes.

**Whether mangling collides on the corpus, and if so which instance wins.** Build
both maps per template — structural and mangled — and on every collision check
whether the survivor is the one `Map.toList` + `nubBy dup` would have kept
(`Template.hs:120,144-156`). Cardinality alone detects the collision and misses
the divergence, which is the part that changes a body.

**Whether the inlay-hint payoff exists at all under the current rooting.** Count
the library's unannotated `auto` bindings that sit inside a template with a
written instantiation reachable from the program rooted at *their own file*.
Measured the way this journal already insists — all 480 files driven through the
