   `static if` took (`dependent-template.k::8`), `c.c1s.Foo<uint32>(x)` on
   an array (`member-function-template.k::20`). Now the loop's, at the
   name. A `Closure<…>` that `desugarLambdas` made is undefined only with
   no base library, where `make_captureN` is pass 9's first and stops the
   reference — and neither `Own` nor `Donated` tells it from a method
   template's name, which the lowering donates its `NAME_REF`. The text
   does: the verdict is a `CopiedName` with its pass, admitted where the
   identifier's range spells the name and otherwise dropped (pass 9's
   counts toward the flag; pass 12's says nothing).
3. *A template in a copy carries the copy's note.* In a copy the
   declaration's note is a `SrcStack`, rendered after the verdict's own
   (`Error.hs:185-189`): `A<bool>::A2_t<2, 3>` is noted at `A2_t`'s text
   and then at `A<bool>` (`template-instance-identifiers.k::7`). Given at
   the text; inside a copy, where the verdict's own frames follow, the
   interleaving is unmeasured and only the declaration's text is given.
4. *An instance a rewrite minted* is noted past the capture list's `[`
   (`lambdas.k::13`'s `Closure<…>` arguments), as the copies' verdicts
   already were (`capture_list_note`).

**After:** 25 programs apart, every one the reference's for the loop — the
CST's "Too many arguments" lacked the reference's note, and the CST arms
never judged a runtime or `auto` argument the loop's "Unresolved argument"
names. A `template` keyword before an instance is no part of its note
(`template Go<bool>` at `Go`).

## Pass 2 on the loop: a verdict the corpus never asks — 2026-10-10

*Sprint W3 step 1. `kg_hir::rewrite::higher_order::HigherOrderFunctions::
refused`, `kg_sem::elaborate::Elaborated::higher_order`,
`TextPass::HigherOrderFunctions`.*

`passdiff` read nothing: no corpus program writes a non-inline function
that takes a function, so the CST pass gave no verdict and the comparison
is vacuous — the reading is recorded, and every behaviour rests on probes
(`kg-oracle --errors`) and rooted-door tests instead. The probes found the
CST pass wrong three ways, each now the loop's: the note is the function's
first token (`void Run(…)` at `void`, `[[async]] void Pipe(…)` at the `[[`),
not its name; a parameter typed through an alias is a function too
(`resolvedFuncParams`, `Function.hs:133-141`), which the CST could not
resolve; and an error in a `static if` branch pass 6 deletes is deleted
with it. The last is the general rule worth keeping: the reference prints
the `ErrorF`s left in the *final* tree (`Error.hs:85`), so a verdict a pass
raises early is lost if a later pass removes the node that holds it. The
loop's rewrite leaves the refused function as written, so the check reports
a refusal only where a function at that text still stands at the end.

Two pass-1 differences turned up beside it, the CST's and left: a local
function in a class's method is a free function to the reference ("Free
functions must be declared `inline`") and clean here; and a free function's
note is its first token (`[[pipelined]]`), here its name.

## The CST's passes 2, 6, 12 and 16 deleted, and what the deletion found — 2026-10-10

*Sprint W3 step 1. `passes::run_through_8`, `run_from_10`, `FromLoop`.*

**What went with them.** Beside the four modules (2463 lines): the judge
that ran a moved pass's CST code on a copy of the sink (`judge_text`) —
no CST pass sits behind one now, so `passdiff`'s `PROBED` is empty and a
move of passes 4 and 8 brings it back; the CST run's shared constant
folder, whose errors were pass 6's; the dead `static if` branches only
pass 12's arms read; and the index of every `template <…>` declaration
only their "Undefined template" asked — a walk of every root's
declarations on every CST run, once priced at 80 ms of a `risc-v.k`
keystroke before it was narrowed to declarations.

**The LT verdict pass 4 keeps.** Pass 4's CST code decides "Could not
deduce all arguments" where the argument list is decided, and its own
flow reads that verdict: a call that has one gets no closure check. So
the decision stays and its output is dropped after pass 8 — pass 12 is
the loop's, which says it where the reference does. Deleting the
emission alone would have run the closure check on every such call.

**Tests that only the CST door could see.** Every test the four modules
held, and every test elsewhere that read their verdicts through the text
door, now reads the rooted door. Two read differently there, and the
reference sides with the rooted door both times: a name declared `auto`
is typed — `auto x = 3; uint1 y = bytesizeof(x)` is "bytesizeof is
undefined for a type with bit size of 2", where the CST table could not
be trusted for an `auto` and stayed silent; and an LT verdict on
`Show(clog2(x))` is the reference's first error of two, the second pass
11's "Unresolved argument" on the runtime `clog2`, which has no version
at a module's text yet (only the folded `clog2`'s). `scope.rs`'s tests of
`FileScope`'s fold read their `static assert`s at the rooted door: what
they pin now is the loop's fold. `FileScope` itself is read only by
passes 4 and 8's argument folds and the CST type table.

## Passes 4 and 8 on the loop: the census asks every `validateArg` clause — 2026-10-10

*Sprint W3 step 1. `kg_sem::census::{refusals, template_mismatch,
pretty_param}`, `TextPass::TemplateTypeCheck`.*

**One judge for two CST passes.** The CST reported pass 8's verdicts from
two places: its pass 8 (`validateArg` on an instance written with its
arguments) and its pass 4 (the closure check on a call it deduced, and a
conflicting deduction). Neither reads the sink, so both run together in
pass 8's place as the CST side of one `TextPass`, whose loop side is the
census's refusals and a round's conflicts at a module's text — before the
same checkpoint, so admitting pass 4's verdict at pass 8's place changes no
output. The LT verdict pass 4 decides stays dropped (pass 12's).

**What the census lacked, measured before it was ported.** The first
reading left 12 programs unsettled, every one a clause the census never
asked: it validated only the first argument it refused, skipped
template-template parameters and an initializer list for `auto`, compared
only literals it named (no float), and could not resolve `Foo<10, 10>` over
`<typename T, T X>` at all — `resolveTypeParam` puts the *argument's node*
where `T` was (`TypeCheck.hs:334-339`), so `X`'s kind is typed `uint4` and
its `theType` is `TError "Expected a type"` (`Type.hs:458-464`), which is
resolved; the reference refuses both arguments, the second against a type
it spells "Expected a type". Two more followed once those landed: a zero
width is a *type* — `infer (ParamIntF x)` takes `fromIntegralConstexpr`,
not the natural the fold asks (`Type.hs:1246`, `Constexpr.hs:300-303`) —
so `int<N>` under `N = 0` wants `int0`, and a literal is re-stamped only to
a width above zero (`:281`); and a template-template parameter's wanted
kinds are substituted too (`template <T> typename TT` under `T = uint32`
wants `<uint32>`). A refusal stops the census instantiating the instance,
so each clause could have moved what the loop decides on a correct
program; `loop-left` 321/321, `ptdiff` 2422 and `backend` 3267 say none
did.

**Spelling a parameter list.** `validateTemplate`'s message is `showPretty`
of both lists (`PrettyPrint.hs:159-177`): kinds (`typename`, `auto`,
`uint32`) against parameters (`bool B`, `bool B = true`). Where a list
holds a shape the port cannot spell — a template-template kind, a named
type, a default that is not a literal or a built-in type — no refusal is
made, as before: an instance the reference refuses is then instantiated,
the census's old behaviour — the program is still rejected, by whatever its
copy then says, which may not be the reference's first error.

## Passes 4 and 8's CST code deleted; three census gaps its tests found — 2026-10-10

*Sprint W3 step 1. `passes::templates`, `template_type_check::
resolved_instance_args`, `kg_sem::census::{refusals, template_mismatch,
pretty_param}`, `instances::standalone`.*

**What is left, and why.** The CST passes 4 and 8 are gone; two pieces of
them are not. The `template <…>` index (`passes::templates`) is what the
parser's own checks ask — a template named without its arguments, a type
or constant used as a value, the parse-time table's member templates —
with the scope walk that keeps an index keyed by simple name honest. And
the guard pass 8 ran behind, `templateResolved`, stays as
`resolved_instance_args`: `cargo xtask ir`'s differential grades the
second census's IR reading of the same predicate against it, so it goes
when W3.7 deletes the second census, not before. Everything only the
validation read went: the CST run's fold environment, the other modules'
tables, the loop's names for a message, the program's inference in the
CST context. The memo counters show it (`tests/memo.rs`): the same
misses, fewer asks.

**The tests found what the corpus could not.** Pass 8's 36 tests moved to
the rooted door, where the loop's census answers them; three went red
against the census and green against the reference, none of the three in
the corpus (`passdiff` had read 0 unsettled over every program):

- `S1<S2>` for a `typename` parameter, `S2` a template: the census asked
  `tResolved` of the argument before "Expected a type", and `TTemplate`
  is not resolved (`Type.hs:1002`). `validate Typename arg` has no such
  guard (`TypeCheck.hs:236-238`); what reaches it is what
  `templateArgResolved` let through, a template's name among them.
- A template-template parameter in either list went unspelled, and an
  unspellable list refused nothing — the instance was decided. It is
  `"template" <+> angles (commaSepList a) <> line <> pretty b`
  (`PrettyPrint.hs:159`): the kinds on one line (the `group` fits them in
  80 columns), then a hard break, so `kg-oracle --errors` prints
  `<typename X, template <typename>` and `typename Y>` on two lines. The
  CST pass had collapsed it to one, a divergence its module docs owned.
- Once spelled, an `auto` slot mismatched a template-template parameter
  the reference matches: `matchParamKind` compares `theType`, and
  `theType` of `auto` is `TUnresolved` (`infer AutoF`, `Type.hs:1174`),
  as is a template's `TTemplate` under `tType`. The census read the
  wanted `auto` as `kind_type` reads one inside a function type, `TAuto`.

So a test written against the CST pass, ported, is a probe of the loop
the corpus never made — worth porting before deleting, not after.

**Seven tests corrected, each the text door's premise.** The text door
runs no loop, so it ran no pass 9, 11, 12 or 19 and no closure library: a
call to an unknown name was clean there and is pass 9's "Symbol name not
in scope" here; `Foo<bool>(a, b)` with `b` a `float32` was clean and is
pass 19's conversion; a lambda as a function-typed template argument is
pass 11's "Unresolved argument"; a short argument list the CST declined
(its silence 1) is completed with the default and refused; a local `S1`
shadowing the template is rejected by the reference's parser and by pass
12 here (divergence #7). A callback's closure type needs the
`data.closure` modules the reference's base library imports; the tests
load two stubs (`tests::closured_errors`), under which the probes give
every message the CST tests asserted.

**`instances::standalone`'s gate was the text door.** `kg dump instances
-` and the census's unit tests gated `hasErrors'` on `check_source`'s
errors, which lost pass 8's own refusals with this deletion (and each
moved pass before it): `F4<4>` over `template <typename T>` decided an
instance. It gates on the base run now, as `Db::instances` does.

## What an edit keeps of the loop: 5d-0 — 2026-10-10

Sprint W7.5d step 5d-0, the measurement the owner asked for before D1
(`loop-across-edits.md` §5; the numbers are in its "Measured 2026-10-10"
passage, made by `cargo xtask loop-rounds`). D1 is to be built. What a
later reader needs:

**Positions are an input, and the reading first written missed it.** The
comparison as planned — the copies decided into a module, spelled with
nothing a run interns — says D1 would keep 62% of the library's time
across an edit, and 8–13% of a body edit's on `risc-v.k`, `array.k` and
`hash_table.k`. Every one of those differences is a moved range: a root
edit above a request moves the request's site and its argument subtree,
and `instantiate` carries both into the library module with their `Src`.
With the old run's positions in the edited file carried through the
edit first (`xtask/src/edits.rs`, `Splice::start` and `end`), it is
95.5%. A design keyed on what the computation read is keyed on positions
too; D1 relocates, or it keeps little where it matters.

**Pooled and per-edit disagree, and the pooled figure is the one to
read.** As written, the median edit keeps 95.8% of its library's work
and 91% of edits keep more than half — the letter of §5's rule, met
without relocation — because most corpus roots are small and ask for
their copies above the edit. By time it is 62%, and the slow programs, the
ones a keystroke budget is about, keep almost nothing. A rule about "most
edits" is read by the time-weighted figure.

**The instrument checks itself twice.** Each root measured twice without
an edit must keep every library round with every state equal (348/348);
an interned id spelled into an input fails it. `ExpId`'s `Debug` carries
its arena's stamp, which every run mints anew, so the state hash strips it
(`unstamped`); a mutant that leaves it in is red. And a module the copies
keep whole must end as it ended: the first full run found
`library/test/unit.k` ending otherwise after signature edits, where its
copies had all agreed. `fixture<TestN>` calls `TestN::run` through the
symbol map, and a class's type holds its fields, not its methods, so the
copy's key does not move when `run`'s signature does — §3's (3), which
the copies cannot see. The fourth reading followed: each module's whole
state hashed at every census, a round kept only while it agrees. (3)
changed state on 44 of 1123 edits (signature and import only), 0.6 points
of the library's time — rare, so step 2's read door will rarely refuse a
key, but not absent, so it is needed for exactness.

**The clock is `KG_LOOP_PROFILE`'s, read by a program.**
`kg_sem::profile::record` runs a closure with the clock on and an observer
shown each round's census (one call in `elaborate.rs`); every visit
carries its round, and inference's walk of each module is now a visit of
its own — `inferType walk`, inside `inferType`'s whole-program time and
left out of `KG_LOOP_PROFILE`'s total. Trace only: identity 304/304
against `cea5957`, `infer-identity` 304/304. The measurement costs 335 s
and 4.8 GB with six workers, most of it the per-round state hash
(`risc-v.k` alone 11 s without it, 158 s with); `--filter` or `--every N`
for a look.

## The editor answers twice: four rounds, then the fixpoint — 2026-10-10

*Sprint W7.6, W7 item 6; the owner's answer of 2026-10-10 (sprint §8).
`kg_sem::elaborate::{elaborate_layered, Stopped}`, `kg_db::layered`,
`Db::{diagnostics_layered, diagnostics_first, looped_first}`,
`PassBudget::Layered`, `kg-lsp`'s `Tier::First`.*

**The seam: an observer, and a fork.** The round-four answer is the
fixpoint run's own first four rounds — read, not assumed: `max_rounds` is
read nowhere in `elaborate_opts` but the check that stops the loop, so up
to the bound a bounded run and a fixpoint run are one computation. The
loop now hands a view of its state to a callback as it passes the bound
(`Stopped`), and `Stopped::answer` forks every module — arena and type
map — and ends the fork as the bounded run ends itself: `deduplicateInstances`
over it, the bound reported, `left` counted, the trajectory so far. The
run goes on from the state it never left. A resumable elaboration, the
other design, would have stored the `Program` between calls; it borrows
the interner and the expansions and carries its incremental units, maps
and snapshots, and keeping it in a memo is the self-referential struct
Rust refuses. The fork is graded where it can be: `infer-identity`'s
incremental run is now the layered one, so its last answer against the
whole walk also says taking the first leaves the run as it was, and each
first answer is compared with the loop bounded at four — 159 of 304
roots run past the bound, all identical. The kg-sem unit test pins the
fork piece by piece; `deduplicateInstances` on the fork is the one piece
nothing pins — no corpus program has a duplicate at the bound (its
mutant survives the test and `infer-identity`), kept because it is the
bounded run's own ending.

**Why the loop has a thread of its own.** The loop ran on whichever
caller asked first, and a second waited for it (`Db::looped`'s in-flight
cell). Layered, that caller would hold the run to the fixpoint — and
after an edit three callers race for it: the diagnostics lane, inlay
hints and code actions on the request pool. An inlay hint that won the
race would wait 2.2 s on `risc-v.k` for what four rounds answer in 0.9.
So under `PassBudget::Layered` the loop belongs to no caller
(`kg_db::layered`): the caller that starts it lowers the program, the run
gets owned modules and shared interner and tokens, and each reader waits
for the answer it wants — the first or the last — and goes. The answers
come back as elaborations; the first reader to want one builds its
`Looped` (`looped::finish`, which reads the database), once, detached
from its request since others wait on it. The batch path keeps the
inline loop untouched: `scripts/identity.sh` against `cea5957`, 304
roots identical.

**Which answer the other features read, and why the first.** While the
fixpoint runs on, hover, inlay hints, signature help, navigation and code
actions read the newest answer ready (`Db::looped_first`): the first,
which is the current text's and is exactly what they answered before
the fixpoint was run at all — the same answer at the same latency — and
the last once it lands. The last completed loop, W3.4's policy for a
broken buffer, is the previous text's and answers nothing about what the
edit wrote; a buffer that stops parsing still reads it (`editor_loop_ready`,
where the first answer, being memoized, is the newest loop too).
Completion still never waits. A template's list of instances read off
the first answer says it may be short ("had not reached its fixpoint").

**Cancellation needed a second token.** The run answers to the database's
token, which the server raises as it queues an edit. But the database's
token is lowered by the very change it announced, and a run no reader
holds the database for — a hover took its first answer and left — could
miss a raise that brief and run on over a stale program. So each run has
its own token too, which every input change raises
(`Db::retire_flights`) and nothing lowers; the unit test with no reader
waiting goes red without it. A cancelled run writes no memo; the first
answer, already built, keeps its own — it finished, and is a correct
answer at its bound. A waiter unwinding on a cancelled run held the
stages' lock as it unwound and poisoned it for every other waiter — the
mutant that made the waiter deaf found it; the lock is released first
now, and read past poison.

**The new row found the first answer gaining an error.** The plan said
the round-four answer "may miss a diagnostic, never gain one".
`edit-identity`'s editor row checks it, every step: on its first run,
`test/library/control/async.k` and the two `rendezvous` tests showed
"Undefined template `fork`" / "`join`" at four rounds and nothing at the
fixpoint — `fj.fork<0>(…)` on a `ForkJoin<…>` the next round makes, whose
member template no lookup can find yet. The editor showed these until
today. Pass 12's undefined-template verdict is not judged on a truncated
loop now (`kg_sem::check`); the batch path never truncates. The same
verdicts were most of main's four-round cost on `risc-v.k`: each was
placed by a scan of the whole module (`capture_list_note`), 0.45 s a
keystroke of `looped`'s own time — which is why the first answer is
faster than main's four rounds below. Measured, not inferred: with the
verdict judged again on a truncated loop, the first answer on `risc-v.k`
is 1317 ms and `looped` 0.44 s a keystroke, main's own figures; the
fork, the thread and the second build cost the first answer nothing
measurable beside them.

**Measured** (2026-10-10, two interleaved A/B runs against `cea5957`,
load 7–31, so upper bounds; `cargo xtask bench --filter keystroke-phases
--recorded`, seven keystrokes, a trailing space):

| | main, four rounds | first answer | last answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| `risc-v.k`, recorded settings | 1325–1353 ms | 926–942 ms | 2156–2171 ms |
| `array.k`, recorded settings | 213–232 ms | 239–243 ms | 875–907 ms |
| `risc-v.k`, the keystroke stage's settings | 387–423 ms | 416–421 ms | 543–548 ms |
| `array.k`, the keystroke stage's settings | 209–241 ms | 238–249 ms | 863–868 ms |
| `float.k`, the keystroke stage's settings | 331 ms | 346 ms | 705 ms |

The fork costs 25 ms a keystroke on `risc-v.k` and 7 on `array.k` and
`float.k` (the `first answer's fork` phase); a body edit's rows in
`--filter phases` agree (`risc-v.k` 0.91–0.93 s first, 2.05–2.25 s last;
main 1.35–1.37 s and 2.09–2.75 s). The corpus-wide `keystroke` row's
worst moved from `risc-v.k`'s 424 ms to `float.k`'s 486 ms in one run,
the `fixpoint` row 904 ms; `float.k`'s own A/B above is +15 ms, so the
rest is that run's load. **Memory:** the editor's peak footprint over
the recorded keystrokes of both files is 0.82 GB on main and 1.29–1.33 GB
now — the fixpoint's own state, not the fork: a batch run of `risc-v.k`
to its fixpoint alone peaks at 1.24 GB (`bench --filter cancel`).
`edit-identity` whole: 148 s, 7.1 GB footprint on main; 141 s, 7.3 GB
with the editor row. `bench --filter cancel`, the editor's lane: worst
6.5 ms from the raise to the return.

**Driven over stdio** (`kg lsp`, a Python client, `Down<120>` with 300
statements a copy — the e2e tests' fixture, 121 rounds): version 1's
first answer, empty, 51 ms after `didOpen`; a hover on `x` inside the
body 10 ms later, from the first answer, saying the list may be short;
version 1's last answer, the error, at 1.41 s. An edit to version 2 is
answered first at 59 ms, and a second edit while version 2's fixpoint
runs is answered at 105 ms with version 3's one answer; version 2's last
answer never arrives. The publishes, in order: (v1, 0), (v1, 1), (v2, 0),
(v3, 1).

**The resilience gate grades the last answer.** A mutant's clean file
has its diagnostics run to the fixpoint before the mutation lands — an
editor's state once the user paused — and a buffer opened broken has its
own loop run to its last answer before it is asked anything, since the
first answer it would otherwise read races the run. The fixpoint's loop
has more instances than four rounds': `copies` 135 → 141 hovers
(`this-capture.k`'s `Go`, a second instance), and eight completions in
one fuzzed `higher_order_functions.k` buffer list the same candidates
with other types — their `ir-only` keys change, which the ratchet reads
as eight newly failing items until blessed. Two runs, identical ledgers.

**Not done.** The first answer's `Looped` is built in full — tables, the
copies' check — when the diagnostics need only its verdicts and a hover
its trees; building it lazily would save CPU, not latency (it runs beside
the continuing fixpoint). The fork copies every arena whole; a fork of
only what the dedup touches is possible and was not worth its
complication at 25 ms.

## Memory watched per use case — 2026-10-10

The owner accepted D1's cost the same evening: the editor keeps a second
copy of a program between edits. Their words were: "The extra memory
cost is acceptable. We can document that and keep an eye on memory usage
across use cases, but if we are efficient with our memory usage, then
duplicating it during editing isn't rough."

Until now nothing kept that eye. Peaks were read off `/usr/bin/time -l`
by hand, and the only memory bound was the gates' own (`bounded.rs`), at
8 GB a child.

`cargo xtask mem` (`xtask/src/mem.rs`) now measures five programs under
three use cases each, one fresh process per case:

- `kg check`'s `Db::check`;
- the editor's check of a file just opened;
- the same after five edits.

Each runs under the program's recorded compile settings. The measured
child is xtask itself, not `kg`, because `kg check`'s flags cannot state
every recorded setting. For example, `risc-v.k` under the bench's rooted
settings is a program the reference rejects.

The peaks are held to `memory-budgets.json` at the workspace root, each
its blessed peak plus a quarter. A fifth was tried first, but `risc-v.k`'s
after-edits peak read 1391–1522 MiB on one tree, which left 9% headroom on
the second run. The file sits at the root so a bless does not stale the
ledgers' tree fingerprint. `scripts/gates.sh` runs the check after
`bench`, and it fails the run when a peak exceeds its budget.

The first reading is in `docs/plans/performance.md` §12. Its finding is
that the editor's memory grows with edits:

- A four-line program keeps +16 MiB after one edit and +83 after 200, and
  is still rising at 200.
- `array.k` keeps +302 MiB after 20 edits.
- `risc-v.k` goes from 907 MiB at open to 1522 after five edits.

This was measured before D1 holds anything. Some of the first edit's rise
is by design, since the old program is served while the new run builds.
A rise that is still going at 200 edits is not by design, and it is the
next item on memory.

## One engine: the CST inference engine deleted — 2026-10-10

Sprint W3.7 (M6). The CST inference engine — `kg-cst-infer`, the
per-module fixpoint over the lossless tree that typed every module for
the CST passes before W3 and for the editor after — is deleted, and with
it the CST constant evaluator (`kg_const::ConstEval`), the one-file
constant environment (`FileScope`), the type table (`kg_ty::TypeTable`)
and the second census. The program-wide loop is the one engine: the
backend walk, the checks and the editor read it alone. What a later
reader would otherwise have to rediscover:

**What parity was, measured before anything was deleted.** The
resilience gate graded the loop's answers against the CST engine's on
140 broken buffers. Its `ir-silent` total — 764 hovers, 375 completion
lists on main — read as "the loop is behind", and it was not: classifying
each silence (`xtask/src/resilience.rs`, `silence`) put 736 of 748 hovers
and 96 of 189 lists in **redefinitions** — a declaration, or one it is
written in, that redeclares a name its scope holds. The reference's parser
rejects the file there (`parseSymbol`, `SymbolTable.hs:200-201`), so no
program holds it and the loop keeps one declaration per name; the CST
engine typed it because it typed text, not programs. The snippet
accumulators redeclare `main` once a snippet, which is most of it. Seven
hovers and 66 lists were **text edited since the loop the editor reads**,
which the next loop over a parsing buffer answers. The rest, 5 hovers and
27 lists, sit in code the reference rejects. So parity is defined as:
*the loop answers wherever the CST engine did, except in a redefinition
no program holds and in text edited since the loop ran*. The editor gives
those up, and a buffer opened broken gets no member list, completion
detail or inlay hint until a loop runs (a hover runs its own) — recorded
in the plan's W3 entry with the counts.

**One real gap the classification found.** A declaration a rewrite
rebuilt — `main` minted again by `moveFunctions` round a class it lifted
out (`Function.hs:88-119`), a method `desugarLambdas` rebuilt — wears its
old node's `Src` as `Donated`, and the `Own` node lowered from the text is
no longer in the tree: the position index, which took `Own` nodes alone,
had no answer at all (`test/syntax/export-class.k`). It now indexes the
reachable `Donated` declaration standing at a `(range, kind)` where an
`Own` node of its constructor was lowered and no reachable `Own` node
claims it (`kg_hir::position`). Restricting it to declarations matters:
the first draft indexed any such node and answered an attribute's `Seq`.

**The parser's checks needed the parse, not a type table.** The last CST
readers of the engine's table were two checks the reference makes while
parsing: a type written where a value goes (`Parser.hs:823-828`) and a
member template on a receiver whose class has none (`:766-770`). Both ask
what the parser built — `isType`, `resolveTypeName` — which the sorted
lowering already records (`kg_hir::sort::is_type`, the unsorted reasons),
so `kg_db::parsed` reads it off the loop's sorted tree; the member check
confirms against the loop's types at the text, since the sort alone read
three programs apart (each rejected elsewhere first) and the loop alone
missed `member-function-template.k::22` (`c2s[1].c`, which the loop types
unresolved). `passdiff` grew probes for them, reading the reference's
`PARSE-ERROR` as the verdicts: 3099 programs identical on each.

**`check_source` is a `Db`.** It had been the "text door" — passes of its
own over one text — long after every type-reading pass moved to the loop,
which only a `Db` runs, while its callers (`xtask bench`'s `check` stage,
`xtask fuzz`) read it as the frontend. It is a `Db` over the text alone
now. The bench's `check` stage therefore measures the loop too: its
numbers before and after 790b9ab are not comparable.

**The resilience gate grades the editor alone.** With no second engine
there is no `agree`: every answer the editor gives is in `answered`,
`key = answer`, so a lost or changed answer is a named regression, and
why the editor says nothing is a histogram by reason and declaration
kind. What it cannot see any more is whether an answer is right; that is
the loop's, graded on whole programs by `conformance`, `errors`,
`ptdiff`, `backend` and `output`.

**Two divergences closed by deletion, and the tests that pinned them
corrected.** #19 (sibling command-line roots did not share types — the
price of the CST engine's per-module memo) and #20 (one-file constants
beside an import-closure type environment) were the engine's, not the
port's: the loop merges the roots as `Main.hs:70,76` does and folds and
types with one map. `two_roots_in_one_namespace_do_not_see_each_others_types`
pinned the silence as deliberate; it is `…_see_each_others_types` now,
read off `kg-oracle --errors`.

**Kept, deliberately.** `kg_const::fold_binary_values` and `CastTarget`
(the IR's fold reads them; the binary table's tests moved onto the
function); `kg_ty::TypeKey` (what an IR node's `Src` names);
`Looped::instance_named`, listed as dead and given its caller —
`kg dump instances` files a member template's instances by the class
instance's note, never by cutting the mangled name at `<|` (the first
draft did, and `xtask lint`'s `mangled-text` counted it). Tests that went
through the rooted door moved with their names (`tests/constant_fold.rs`,
`tests/rooted_types.rs`); the memo tests that pinned the CST engine's
interface firewall pin the loop's memo now, each red with `Db::looped`
served whatever the program.

## The editor's memory is the allocator's: purge eagerly — 2026-10-10

What the editor seemed to keep across edits, in `cargo xtask mem`'s first
reading, is not data.

A counting allocator in the measured child gave `array.k`'s live heap as
133 MiB after every one of twenty edits. Over the same edits the resident
set climbed from 414 to 668 MiB and then held.

Two things account for the difference:

- **On macOS the resident set counts purged pages.** `vmmap` found
  mimalloc's regions 631 MiB resident and only 379 MiB dirty. The rest
  had already been given back, and the kernel takes such pages only under
  pressure. `xtask mem` now grades the footprint on macOS.
- **mimalloc returns a freed page a second after the free** (its
  `purge_delay`), and only while it is allocating. An idle server
  therefore keeps whatever its last check freed.

Setting the delay to 0 took the footprint after twelve edits from 380 to
199 MB, and the peak from 490 to 385 MB. The cost was 1.1% more
instructions; on `risc-v.k` the editor's peak fell ~10% for 1.3%.

- A forced `mi_collect` after each check reached the same 199 MB but did
  not lower the peak.
- Neither `MIMALLOC_PAGE_RECLAIM_ON_FREE` nor running the loop on the
  calling thread changed the shape. The calling thread was tried because
  each editor run is a new thread, which suggested abandoned per-thread
  pages.

`kg-alloc` is now the one place the allocator is chosen. It also holds
`purge_eagerly`, which `kg lsp` and the `kg-lsp` binary call before they
serve.

- The option's number (15) is written into an `extern` declaration
  rather than taken from `libmimalloc-sys`'s `extended` bindings, which
  need a crate this checkout does not have. Its test reads mimalloc's
  1000 ms default back through that number, so an upgrade that moved
  the option goes red.
- `kg check` keeps the default delay: 6% of its peak is not worth 1.6%
  more instructions in a process that returns everything when it exits.
- The `kg-lsp` binary had been on the system allocator all along.

The numbers are in `docs/plans/performance.md` §12.


## The loop kept per round, and the shadow that checks it — 2026-10-10

*Sprint W7.5d, D1 step 1 (`loop-across-edits.md` §6, "Built
2026-10-10"). `kg_sem::snapshot` (`Recorder`, `Rounds`, `Key`, `Splice`,
`Shadow`), `kg_db::snapshot` (`Kept`, `Db::{set_snapshot_shadow,
take_shadow_report, snapshot_size}`), `elaborate_layered_recorded`, the
`shadow` ledger of `cargo xtask edit-identity`. No round is reused yet.*

**A round is a log, not a copy.** Every write in place goes through
`ExpArena::node_mut`, which already logged the index (the entry "The
loop's floor"); with a log open it now also keeps the node as it was,
and `TypeMap::write` and `rollback` keep the entry as it was. A round
then costs its length, its root and what it wrote over, and the state
after round *r* is the final arena cut to its length with the later
logs undone newest first (`ModuleRounds::restore`). Three economies:
a node the round appended is cut, not undone, so a log has a floor and
writes above it are not kept; round 0's log is not kept at all, since
no state before round 0's end is ever restored; a type write is kept
only where it changes the entry *strictly* — by `Ord`, since `==`
ignores a parameter's name (`Type.hs:126-129`) and a write that renames
one must be undone too.

**The key gained what `resolve` renames.** The design keyed a round on
the copies decided into the module; the build adds the module's own
mentions (the occurrences the census met there, 5d-0's third reading,
at most 1.3 points of reuse) and a copy's site where its frames carry
one other than the occurrence's head (`instance_site`, the last name
past a qualifier) — positions the copies' frames hold and the key did
not. Neither moved a corpus number; both close a hole one can name.

**The shadow compares nodes, not hashes.** 5d-0's state hash formats
every node (`Speller::final_state`) and took `risc-v.k`'s run from 11 s
to 158 s. The shadow compares, at a round's end, only what either run
changed in it — the arena's own write log, both runs' type logs, the
nodes appended — once the round before was equal; round 0, a round
after an unequal one, and the end of both runs are compared whole, the
end with no log on either side, so a log that missed a write cannot
hide behind itself. A node is the same when its expression is, each
child by index (`Exp::same_but_stamps`), its kind and provenance are,
its head relocated is the new head, its expansion's frames are
(instance, site relocated, round, iteration), and its type is, by `Ord`.
`edit-identity` with it: 134 s, against 141–148 s without (W7.6's
entry; load unmeasured).

**Relocation: 5d-0's rule, and what its edges cost.** The database
finds the edit as the one splice between the kept text and the new
(`Splice::between`); where the inserted text repeats what is beside it —
`xy` to `xyy`, a parameter typed after one ending in its letter — the
edit could be at either place, and the splice covers both. The first
unit test typed `/* moved */ ` before `using C = …` and the shadow called
the round unequal: the declaration's node had taken the comment, so its
start stayed where 5d-0's rule moved it. A rule giving the edges no
place was tried and lost a line typed above a request — the request
starts at the splice's edge. It is not needed: the edited module is
never followed, and any other holds positions of the edited file only
through what its key spells, where a wrong guess parts the key and
costs reuse — **except through a read across the boundary**, below.

**What no key holds: (3), seen as reads.** Over all 348 roots every
unequal round is a signature or import edit and its undo — 46 edits, 94
modules: `library/test/unit.k` 48 (`fixture<TestN>` calling the edited
`run()`, as 5d-0 found), `library/data/closure.k` 18 and six modules
more under a removed import, `library/test/runner.k` 8 and four more
under a signature edit. One of the four is `library/data/array.k` under
a signature edit to `library/data/function.k`: its arena held, at round
0, *a parameter list of the edited file*, copied in by
`resolvedFuncParams` (`Function.hs:133-141`,
`ExpArena::deep_copy_from`). A read carries positions as a copy does,
so step 2's read door must hold its answers' positions aside and
relocate them as the keys'. Until it lands the ledger books the 94
(`unequal`, a fail set) beside the 1808 steps whose every followed round
agreed (`kept`, a pass set); "every restored state equals the actual"
holds on body and library-body edits, 397502 rounds of 397502.

**A sampled run is held to its roots' items.** `fast.sh loop` runs a
quarter of `edit-identity`; a ledger written from a quarter would read
every other root's item as lost. So a sampled run writes none and is
compared with the baseline restricted to the roots it ran
(`ratchet::enforce_sample`). The mutants were proved that way, against
the baseline the lead is to bless, read through `KG_RATCHET_BASELINE`
rather than written into `baseline.json`: a type write left out of the
log, red on 1215 items; a node write, 588; every round keyed by round
0's key (a copy's round left out), 326; a node restored a round early,
586; relocation skipped, 314 — each of the sample's 87 roots, 40 s.

**What recording costs the keystroke.** The undo logs cost nothing a
profile sees (`KG_LOOP_PROFILE`'s `snapshot ends`, 0.000 s a run). The
keys cost `risc-v.k`'s run 117 ms of 1.85 s at first, and the first A/B
said so: the last answer 116–135 ms behind main's, the first unchanged.
`sample` put half of it in resolving every symbol of every type the key
spells — needless where both runs intern into one database — and most of
the rest in spelling the same types again; with symbols left numbered
and each type and expansion spelled once per census (a type by strict
value), 48 ms (`array.k` 100 → 40). What is left is the types' `Debug`
renderings; a structural hash would take it, and step 3, which reads the
key before running a round, is where it will be felt. The run also freed
the program it replaced before publishing its last answer; it frees it
after now.

**Measured** (two interleaved A/B runs against `b4ee408` in one build
directory, sources touched and rebuilt each turn, load 15–33, so upper
bounds; `cargo xtask bench --filter keystroke-phases --recorded`, seven
keystrokes; `kg check -I library -I test/library`):

| | main | step 1 |
|---|---|---|
| `risc-v.k`, first answer | 997, 1024 ms | 1016, 954 ms |
| `risc-v.k`, last answer | 2290, 2370 ms | 2467, 2284 ms |
| `array.k`, first answer | 274, 274 ms | 263, 256 ms |
| `array.k`, last answer | 1056, 1052 ms | 1103, 1004 ms |
| the editor's peak footprint, both files | 1.36, 1.33 GB | 1.78, 1.80 GB |
| `kg check risc-v.k` | 2.46, 2.47 s; 824, 824 MB | 2.63, 2.33 s; 841, 841 MB |
| `kg check array.k` | 0.91, 1.09 s; 313, 312 MB | 1.56, 0.94 s; 292, 311 MB |

`kg lsp` over stdio on `risc-v.k` (a manifest importing the reference's
library, six keystrokes, two pairs): the same answers within 0.15 s, the
server's peak footprint 1.37–1.48 → 1.87 GB. The editor holds 0.45 GB
more at its peak — the run before's program, kept to the next fixpoint
where main freed it at the next first answer — and beside the program it
shares, the snapshot itself is 5.8 MB on `risc-v.k` (1.71M nodes; logs of
8923 nodes and 233950 types; keys of 77763 positions) and 2.1 MB on
`array.k`. `cargo xtask mem`, which landed on main beside this step,
agrees (two interleaved runs against `df4b8b5`, peak footprint): `check`
main's on every program, the editor after five edits `risc-v.k` 1194–1214
→ 1586–1610 MiB, `array.k` 437–439 → 540–557, `float.k` 497–498 →
550–559 — and `risc-v.k`'s resident set, 2087–2137 MiB, over its budget of
1910: the accepted cost, for the lead to bless. **The owner accepted it the same day**, on the condition of
efficiency: "if we are efficient with our memory usage, then duplicating
it during editing isn't rough" (`loop-across-edits.md` §7); `cargo xtask
mem`, added on main, keeps it visible. One number this step does not
account for: the `kg` binary's batch check of `risc-v.k` peaks 17 MB
higher in every run (824 → 841 MB; `array.k` unchanged, the time main's),
though its batch path is the same code but for two structs a field
larger, and mimalloc's peak pages are the same where its pages over the
run are more (7.8K → 10.1K); `xtask mem`'s `check`, the same query in
one process, reads main's 770–771 MiB footprint as 767–772.

## W4 after one engine: what the copies had become — 2026-10-10

Sprint W4 (`single-source-of-truth.md` D1/D2), taken up after W3.7 deleted
the CST inference engine. The plan's rows were written on 2026-09-25
against three engines' worth of code. A survey read every open row again in
the code before anything changed (`f93d6f0`), and the rows' "Replaces"
columns became "Copies today". Nine commits followed (`7940167` …
`7bc82b8`), every one exact on every gate but the two that change what a
program outside the corpus gets (`6b57574`, `1c92997`). What a later reader
would otherwise have to rediscover:

**Most copies had gone with the engines, not with W4.** Of the eleven open
rows, D1.2 had landed with W1.1 (2026-09-27) and D1.8 with the CST engine.
Every copy D2.1, D2.2 and D2.5 listed had been deleted by M4's `81452c6` or
W3.7's `b56fd7b`. With those copies went the drift D2.1–D2.4 were written
against:
- the three dated template-index bugs;
- the homonyms;
- the re-export;
- `Shadow` binding a variable before its declaration ended;
- the census's literals-only `static if`.

A plan row naming copies is a claim about the tree on the day it was
written.

**What W4 found instead was code the twin's deletion left alive-looking.**
Five pieces had no effect on any program, yet still compiled, were tested
and read like owners:
- the twin's static control in `kg_hir::rewrite`: `static_control`,
  `static_control_with`, `static_control_before_templates`, the
  `fold`/`for_twin` arms and `const_index_width`. None has had a production
  caller since `81452c6`; only its own tests called it.
- the sorted lowering's twin door (`find_in_twins`, `named_template`) and
  `SymbolMap::base`, behind maps and an `Option` that every constructor
  left empty or `None`;
- `InstanceSpec::known`, which every spec was built with as `Vec::new()`;
- the walk's `extern_classes`, built for every walk and emptied by
  `trimmed_already` before it was read;
- `kg_ty::convert::check_conversion` and `classify`, the very owner D2.6
  planned, which nothing ever called: pass 19 on the loop decides under
  guards of its own. This is the recurring failure (`CLAUDE.md`) seen from
  the other side: a tested module that no caller reaches is not an owner,
  however well it reads.

What to grep for after a deletion milestone: a field or parameter that
every construction site fills with `Vec::new()`, `FxHashMap::default()`,
`None` or `false`, and a `clear()` called before the first read. Each of
the five was one of those.

**Measured, not argued, before deleting a fallback.** Three of the walk's
decisions and one of `instantiate`'s looked dead by reading. An
instrumented `ptdiff` over its 2422 programs counted each (the probe was
never committed):
- **The walk's `static if` fold: 0 firings.** It went (`6b57574`). A
  `static if` still standing is pass 16's error, so the walk declines it,
  as it declines one anywhere else.
- **The walk's `set_node_type` fallbacks** (`written_integer_type`, the
  literal arms, `local_type`, `operand_type`) **and `deduced_type`'s
  folded-literal branch: 0 firings.** They stay, in the register, as
  insurance: a node the loop leaves untyped aborts the backend, an error on
  a program the reference compiles, and nothing counts their firings yet.
- **`t_arg`'s `written_builtin`: 2 firings, so not dead at all.** Both come
  from `template.k`'s `Bar<uint6, 101>` over `Foo<T, 100> N`:
  - the census mints the argument of the indirect instance
    `Foo<uint6, 100>` afresh (`Mint::exp_from_type`, a `newNote`, so
    `TUnresolved`);
  - the reference substitutes the written argument and keeps its `TType`
    note (`resolveTemplateParam`, `TypeCheck.hs:334-339`).

  The fallback papers over that difference. It ends when the census mints
  its arguments typed.

**The plan's direction for D1.6 was impossible.** It had
`kg_const::LiteralType::minimal` delegate to `kg_ty::width`, but `kg-ty`
depends on `kg-const`, never the reverse. So the value domain owns
`inferIntLiteralType`, and `kg-ty` maps it into `Ty`.

**One small rule hid a real drift.** Of the five readings of
`isAbbreviatedTemplate`, `kg-sem/src/check.rs`'s also took `const auto`.
Every check that skips an abbreviated template therefore skipped
`F(const auto x)`. The reference does not make that a template
(`isAuto . paramType`, `Parser/Syntax.hs:706-707,722`), and rejects it with
"Could not deduce type" (`kg-oracle --errors`). No corpus program writes
one, so no gate saw it (`1c92997`).

**What stays two, and why.** The register lists each pair with the gate
that compares it:
- the walk's spelling of pass 19's two tree rewrites: pass 19 reports them,
  but the loop's tree does not carry them (`ptdiff`, `backend`, `output`);
- the walk's typing fallbacks, and `written_builtin` (both above);
- the census's substituted `kind_type`: `resolveTemplateParamType`
  computed without building the substituted tree;
- `abbreviated.rs`'s firing guard, and its per-node summary in
  `kg-hir/src/facts.rs`;
- the CST parse-time readings: `Templates`, `visible_through_imports`,
  `Binders`, `innermost_declaring_scope` and `facts::innermost_declaration`.
  They answer the parser's `findSymbol` at a position, and no post-parse
  structure carries that question.

Moving the parser's template checks onto the sorted lowering's own facts
would delete `Templates`, `visible_through_imports` and `Binders`. That
changes verdicts, so it is a D2 item of its own and has not landed.

## References and rename across the project — 2026-10-10

Until today find-references searched the programs the open buffers root,
and rename refused a file-scope declaration whenever an unopened `.k` file
under the import directories imported the declaring module. Both now
search the project. The design question was written down in the history's
"Later" ("Workspace-wide references, and the rooting question under it");
this is the answer, measured.

**Search more files, each rooted at itself.** Rooting once at the whole
workspace makes one program of every file, and every file with no `module`
header shares one namespace there (`Main.hs:70,76`, `Symbols.hs:37-41`):
each would resolve the others' names without importing them, divergence
#19's shape. A rename built on it edits a file that never named the
declaration. So each file is searched under the program it roots, as an
open buffer always was. `a_file_that_does_not_import_the_declaration_holds_none_of_its_uses`
pins it: `other.k` imports `extra`, spells `twice`, and is left alone; with
the cursor's file and `other.k` rooted together it is reported (red).

**Which files.** Every file of the project — under the import directories,
and under the manifest's root (a test bench beside the library it imports
need not sit in either import directory) — that spells the name and roots
a program holding the declaring module:

- *Spells the name* is a substring test on the text, before anything is
  parsed. Every use is an identifier token spelled as the name
  (`occurrences`' needle argument), and a token's text is part of its
  file's, so the test is exact as a filter and costs one read.
- *Roots a program holding the declaring module* is
  `Db::program(&[file]).contains(..)`, the loader's own answer. A name
  resolves within the program its file roots, so a program without the
  module holds no use of it.

That replaces the rename's textual import scan rather than copying it, and
it answers the transitive question the scan got wrong. A module re-exposes
an import whole with `module facade { module helper }`
(`SymbolTable.hs:158-166`, `filterImported`/`reExposed`), so `user.k`,
which imports only `facade`, names `helper`'s `twice`. And a member needs
no import at all: `v.f` names `f` through `v`'s type, which can arrive
through any function's return. In the corpus `test.internal.assert` is
imported directly by one file, `test/unit.k`, which re-exposes it; 36 other
files use its `assert_equal`. The old scan would have found `unit.k` alone.

**What `occurrences` needs per file.** For a name no `.` can reach (not a
member), name resolution only: the program and its symbol map. A member's
uses through a receiver (`v.f`) need the program-wide loop's type of `v`.
So a selector is skipped outright when the target is no member —
`definition_at` answers a selector only with a member the receiver's type
declares — and the loop is asked for lazily, at the first selector that
needs it. A file nobody has open gets a loop of its own (`Db::loop_once`):
the fixpoint, on the request's thread, memoized nowhere. `Db::looped` would
keep it (8 entries, each pinning every module's final tree), and under the
editor's layered budget start a run that goes on after its reader has gone.
A file's program is forgotten as the search leaves it (`Db::forget_roots`),
so the search holds one at a time and none after.

**Measured** in-process, on the reference's `library` and `test/library` as
one project under the `mock` device. The declaring file is opened and its
diagnostics run, as the editor does on open, and then each request is
timed. The project is a scratch manifest beside links to the two
directories, since a manifest governs only the files under it and the
reference is read-only.

```
KG_REFERENCE=../kanagawa /usr/bin/time -l target/quick/deps/workspace_cost-<hash> --ignored --nocapture
(cargo test -p kg-lsp --profile quick --test workspace_cost -- --ignored --nocapture)
```

Measured 2026-10-10 under load 6–28 (two other agents' gates), the
declaring file open. Each figure is a reference list cold, then warm (the
second reads the parses the first left), and a rename after its
`prepareRename`:

| declaration | kind | spell it / hold its module | loops | references | heap at peak / left | rename |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `assert_equal`, `test/internal/assert.k` | template function | 37 / 37 | 0 | 484 uses in 37 files, 0.27 s / 0.20 s | +13.5 / +9.4 MiB | prepare 0.24 s, rename 1 ms |
| `next`, `data/random/lfsr.k` | method | 27 / 12 | 11 | 44 uses in 12 files, 7 s / 6 s | +499 / +24.5 MiB | prepare 10 s, rename 0.2 ms |
| `increment`, `data/counter.k` | method | 23 / 23 | 6 | 3 uses, 0.55 s / 0.49 s | +57 / +7.7 MiB | prepare 0.48 s, rename 0.1 ms |
| `is_valid`, `data/optional.k` | field | 37 / 37 | 36 | 272 uses in 20 files, 13 s before the bound; with it, 92–258 uses, 10–14 s | +950 / +82 MiB | refused (`optional.k:142`), 5 ms |
| `imem_write`, `processor/risc_v.k` | method | 4 / 3 | 3 | 2 uses, 0.51 s / 0.50 s | +97 / +3.8 MiB | refused (`mmio.k:235`), 0.5 s |

The heap columns are `kg_alloc::Counting`'s live heap above what was live
before the request: at its peak, and left after it. The peak is one
program's loop, since the search holds one at a time. Of `is_valid`'s 36
loops, `test/library/processor/risc-v.k`'s program took 2.8 s and makes
most of the peak. What is left is per module: the parse of each file read,
and the sorted lowering of each file a loop ran over. A second request
leaves nothing more (+0.0–0.1 MiB). The test binary's peak footprint over
all five cases was 1070 MB without the bound and 988 MB with it
(`/usr/bin/time -l`).

**A bound, and why it is partly a clock.** A file without a loop is ~7 ms,
and a count bounds that well. A loop costs what its program costs, and
over `is_valid`'s 36 files that was 26 ms to 2.8 s. The program's module
count ran 33–50 and tracked the time not at all, so neither a count of
loops nor a size proxy bounds the latency. So `references::Bound` is 512
files and a clock: 10 s for a reference list, which is partial past it and
says so in the log (`window/logMessage`, naming the first file not read),
and 60 s for a rename and its `prepareRename`, which are refused past it.
The price is an answer near the boundary that can differ under load. A
reference list says so; a rename turns it into a refusal, never into a
smaller edit. Tests use the count, which is deterministic. Under load
12–28, `is_valid`'s list stopped at the clock twice, with 92 and then 108
of its 272 uses, each time logging the files it had not read. The last
loop it starts can overrun the clock: one run stopped at 14 s.

A rename's search also stops at the first use it cannot place
(`Bound::until_unsure`), since the rename is refused on it whatever else
turns up. One in an open buffer is found before any file is read, so
`is_valid`'s refusal went from 13 s and 16 s to 6 ms and 5 ms.

`prepareRename` makes the same search as the rename, so that its refusals
are the rename's. It keeps the search for the rename that follows while the
database revision, the open buffers, the declaration and the bound are
unchanged (`rename::Remembered`), so the pair pays one search, not two.

**Found on the way, all three pre-existing:**

- **`importable()` never held for a module with a header.** It asked for
  the file's own scope, and a declaration inside `module m { … }` is in the
  module's (`ScopeKind::Module`, `Parser.hs:185-189`). So the rename's
  refusal never fired for any declaration of any importable module, and the
  rename edited the open programs alone. Now read off the parent chain, an
  enum's constants included.
- **The exposure list was not renamed.** `module helper { twice }` names
  the declaration (`checkSymbols`, `Parser.hs:216-223`), but
  `definition_at` resolved nothing there. A rename left "`twice`: undefined
  symbol" in the declaring file. It resolves now
  (`ModuleGraph::exposed_definitions`, the rule `check_exposed_modules`
  and `exposed_ambiguities` already applied, now in one place), so
  go-to-definition and hover answer on an exposure-list name too.
- **The textual import scan missed re-exports**, as above.

**Left, and where a rename still refuses.** These are not searched: a file
outside both the import directories and the manifest's root, a file under
another manifest, and, with no manifest, anything but the open buffers'
programs. A sibling there can still `import` the declaring file through its
own directory (`Parser/IO.hs:103`), and a rename does not see it. That hole
was there before, since the old scan read no directory without a manifest
either. It is the owner's to choose between refusing such renames and
reading the declaring file's ancestors.

Member renames across the corpus mostly refuse, and rightly: a receiver
inside a lambda or behind an abbreviated template's `auto` parameter is
typed by no loop at the text (`.is_valid` at `data/optional.k:142`,
`.imem_write` at `processor/risc-v/mmio/mmio.k:235`). Each such use is
outside a `TEMPLATE_DECL`, so it is refused rather than skipped. Reading
them is the loop's work.

Commits `c0fd42b`, `e4a4be9`, `3577281`, `63e27a8`. The run over stdio
(`target/quick/kg-lsp`, the same project) answered `assert_equal`'s
references with 484 locations in 37 files in 276 ms, `prepareRename` in
201 ms and the rename, reading the search its prepare kept, with 484 edits
in 2 ms.

**Gates** (`scripts/fast.sh --lint loop`, this tree): all green, clippy 0.
`resilience` is +8/−0, blessed from main (`a61a48b`): hover now
answers on an exposure-list name, eight sampled in the fuzzed library
headers (`numeric/float32/operator.k`'s `add`, `sub`, `mad`, …).

## The fuzzer's silent buckets: the parser's table, and the copies' passes — 2026-10-10

*`cargo xtask fuzz --differential --seconds 300 --jobs 4 --reduce 300
--seed 20261010` at `dc145e3`: 171 disagreements in 50 buckets, three
of them false alarms in one bucket and 29 ours-silent in 18. Each fix
below was reproduced from its bucket's `reduced.k`, probed against
`kg-oracle --errors` with variants of its own, and committed alone with
its evidence and a mutant-proven test. The same seed re-run partway
through, without reductions, read: false alarm 3 → 0, ours-silent 29 →
12, message 22 → 3, both-differ 21 → 8, agree 1643 → 1687 — and its
remaining mutants found four more, fixed the same way (below).*

**The one false alarm was declaration order.** `import a1.a1 as Foo`
and `Foo::a1<10> Foo;` in a block was "The import qualifier 'Foo'
conflicts with the name of symbol defined at" the local being declared.
`findInScopes` (`SymbolTable.hs:254-256`) sees only what `parseSymbol`
has registered, and a local, a parameter or a function is registered once
parsed whole; a struct's field never is (`memberVariable` is `noted`, not
`symbol`); a class's variable is from the class's first line, since
`class_` seeds the scope. Our `findSymbol` port took any nested
declaration as found, wherever it was written. It now walks on past one
the table does not hold yet (`innermost_in_parse_table`), and the same
order decides a module-scope one: a declaration not yet held leaves the
lookup to the imports, where two answers are the ambiguity (`c1<>` inside
`inline void c1()`), and one held under a `module` header is unique and
conflicts with an import aliased to its name — which the old code skipped
outright. A module-scope *template's* parameter is keyed by its bare
name without a header, so an import exposing it is ambiguous too.

**The parser's rejections need not be placed where the reference places
them.** Where the reference's parser fails with a grammar error and a
pass here rejects, the `errors` gate books the pair to divergence #7, and
the fuzzer reads it `booked-7`, not a finding. So each of these is a
pass-0 or parse-time check, reporting at the token that is wrong — in an
expression, also where the reference's lands:

- `x<>` over a name the table holds as no template: a comparison with no
  right operand. The local being declared is not in the table inside its
  own type (`static x<int32, -10> x;` in `inline void x()`).
- A type position naming what the table holds as a value: `Class Class;`
  over a parameter, `D D = {…}` in a class. The sort already knew
  (`ValueInTypePosition`) and said nothing.
- `(x)[i]`, `f()[0]`, `(s).a`, `(f)(1)`, which the reference's grammar
  never reaches: `access` follows a name only (`Parser.hs:803-819`).
  Divergence #13's claim that a later pass rejects them was false.
- A method template on a receiver the parser resolves no type name for:
  `resolveTypeName` reads one only off a `Variable`, and asks
  `findSymbol` at the method (`Parser.hs:736-762`). A parameter, a
  template's value parameter, a variable whose class is declared further
  down. This closes `c.Foo<uint32>(1)` over a parameter exactly, the
  reference's message and position, with the `async.k` / `fork_join`
  guard kept: a parameter whose written type has arguments the parser
  could have failed on counts only where the loop types it a class.
- A `const` variable as an assignment's base (`s.Do = Do;`): `namedLValue`,
  ahead of pass 9's "Undefined member".
- A type as `decltype`'s operand, which is an `expression`: `decltype(main)`
  inside class `main`'s method `main`, where the method is not in the
  table and the name is the class.

**In the copies, pass 10 had no version at all.** `cata typeErrors`
runs over the program with its instances in it; ours judged the module's
text only. The entry on moving pass 10 said so, and left it. Now:

- `!x` in `Foo<uint32>`'s copy of a member nothing calls is "Expected a
  boolean operand" at the template's text, framed (`copy_type_errors`).
- Pass 16 reports a width a copy folds to no positive integer (`c1<0>`
  over an imported `uint<N>`).
- `checkVarDecl`'s function-type clauses judge a copy's variables
  (`() -> void bar1;` in `Foo<bool>`).

The rest of `validateProgram` still judges the text only.

**`errorMsg` replaces the node whole, and that runs both ways.** The
port's `replaced` sets carried one direction: what an earlier pass
reported silences a later one inside it. `errorMsg = renote . const .
desugarError` (`Error.hs:147`) is also the other: a later clause that
reports *at* a node replaces whatever `ErrorF` an earlier pass left
inside it, so the earlier verdict never reaches the bundle. Three clauses
do it here now, each dropping pass 10's verdicts inside what it replaced:

- `staticAssert`: `static assert(!0xff);` is the assertion's "did not
  evaluate to a boolean constant" at the operand, not pass 10's. That
  was six buckets' messages. It is found by
  `DiagnosticKind::StaticAssertUndecided`.
- `checkArraySize`: `uint32[p || 1]` gives the dimension's error alone
  (`Cx::replacing`).
- `checkEnumConsts`: `F = !F` and `E1 = 1 + true` are the constant's
  "doesn't evaluate to an integer constant", raised over the earlier
  error (`Cx::raise_replacing`).

Every clause written `errorMsg … x`, over an `x` that can hold an earlier
pass's error, has this shape; a port of one should ask which way it runs.

**Smaller, each a rule the reference states.**

- A written `decltype` the fold never replaced is "Couldn't deduce type
  of the expression" at its operand (`TypeCheck.hs:53`; `decltype(x) x;`).
- An enum constant the fold finished to a `bool`, a float or a string
  "doesn't evaluate to an integer constant". It had been claimed only for
  a set left unfolded.
- A call never folds: `evaluateConstexpr` has no arm for one.
- The fold's absorbing identities are four — an integer literal beside
  `&`/`|`, a boolean one beside `&&`/`||` — not any of those operators;
  and operators over literals alone, left standing, never fold.
- A redefinition lands where the reference notes the symbol: a parameter
  or an enum constant at itself, not at its owner, and an enum past its
  name, at the `:` (`enum = do ident <- …; symbol (Enum …)`).

**What stays.** [38] is the reference's own reading: in `Foo<bool>`'s
copy, `decltype(Foo)` over a local `Foo` inside the function template
`Foo` is the function (in a plain function, or over a local `Baz`, it
accepts). [40], [41]: a local named as its type (`foo foo; return foo;`)
is typed `unresolved` by the reference's inference — its `TypeIdentifier`
keeps the use's scope, where the variable answers — and as the struct
here; an inference change, not made. [27], [39] and the position buckets
[12], [14]: an operand in parentheses is noted from its `(` (`parens`,
`Parser.hs:845`), which `kg_db::looped`'s `paren_note` applies to pass 6's
and pass 10's verdicts at the text only — a copy's pass 10, pass 16's
static assert and pass 19's conversions are one column on. `looped.rs`
was another agent's this round. Booked as `known-divergences.md` #39–#41.


**Afterwards, on main (2026-10-11).** `754e5f2`'s `decltype` clause fired
under the editor's first answer: a loop stopped at four rounds leaves
standing a `decltype` whose operand a later round types —
`multi_word.k`'s `using sum_t = decltype(p.first);` over an instance the
next round makes — so `edit-identity` read 347/348 (the first answer
showed what its last did not). `fast.sh loop` samples a quarter of the
roots and missed it; step 2's full run found it. The clause now keeps
every leftover verdict's rule, `!self.truncated`: under a latency bound
the gutter may miss a verdict, never gain one (`1ecf658`). A new clause
about what the loop *left standing* is a leftover verdict — check it
against `Cx::truncated` before it lands, and run `edit-identity` whole,
not the fast tier's quarter.

## The read door: what a round read across the boundary, keyed — 2026-10-10

*Sprint W7.5d, D1 step 2 (`loop-across-edits.md` §6, step 2, "Built
2026-10-10"). `kg_sem::reads` (`Door`, `Pass`, `Asked`), the reads' key in
`kg_sem::snapshot` (`ModuleRounds::reads`, `ShadowReport::{read_parted,
read_parted_equal}`), `kg_ty::hash_strict`, `Exp::hash_shape`,
`ResolveInstances::logged`, `TypeMap::{before_entry, writes}`. Still no
round reused.*

**Inference already had a door.** It reads another module only through
`Cx::snap_{exp,ty,is_set,src}` and its two lookups, which the incremental
walk built to know what to walk again; the read door is those six, each
read shown once a walk, the lookups from the list the walk already keeps.
The rest is spread over five passes — `addLambdaWrappers`,
`deduceTemplateArgs`, pass 1's `redundantNameScope` and
`resolvedFuncParams`, pass 7, and `instantiate`'s `resolve` — and each now
shows the door what it reads. Two are facts the whole program decides:
whether any module declares an alias a parameter can resolve through
(pass 2 resolves through one only then), and the `extern` classes.

**An item is spelled where it was written, not by its id.** A body edit
renumbers every node of the root after it, and the copies in the library
read the root's declarations all the time (`fixture<TestN>` reads
`TestN::run`). Keyed by index, every such module would part at every body
edit; keyed by where the node was written — its module's name, head,
frames, kind, provenance — with its expression's shape and its children's
identities, it parts only where what it read moved inside the edit or
changed. Positions are held aside and *ranked*: the key is the round's set
of items with each position named by its rank among the round's distinct
positions, beside those positions in order, and relocation, which keeps
order within a file, carries it whole. Two nodes can be written alike — a
rewrite's donations share their donor's head and kind — and are then one
identity; what tells them apart to a reader is their expressions, which
items hold.

**A set, and why that is enough.** Within an inference iteration every
module reads the others as the iteration found them, so a read is one item
however often the iteration makes it, and a second if a later iteration
answers it otherwise. Two runs whose module read the same set ran the same
walks of it — a unit is walked again only when something it read changed —
and a sequence would part a module whenever another needed one iteration
more.

**What a rewrite read counts only where it rewrote.** The first build kept
every read, and the shadow went to zero unequal at once — but parted 1864
module-rounds on their reads alone, 1774 of them equal all the same. A
probe of which (pass, kind) of item differed named two culprits, nine in
ten: a later round's `deduceTemplateArgs` re-reading the signature of a
template whose call it had already rewritten, and `resolve` asking the
round's decisions about a template no module decided any more (an import
removed). Neither read moved anything. A deduction or a wrapper is now
tried with its reads held (`Door::tentative`) and they are kept only where
the module changed — its arena's length or writes, its types' writes —
and `resolve` keeps only the matches it makes, by walk and mention: what
left a module alike moved nothing, and a run that left it alike ran the
same, whatever it read. Partings fell to 228, 138 of them equal; step 1
followed 692278 module-rounds with 926 unequal, step 2 follows 690288 with
none.

**What it costs.** First built, the door was 4.9% of the loop's samples
on the recorded keystroke bench, and the A/B read the last answer 60–100
ms later on `risc-v.k`. Five things brought it to 1.9% (the passes' shares
beside main's, +1 point): a hasher of its own — a folded multiply, the
seed fixed, not SipHash, whose resistance to chosen collisions a key does
not need; identities numbered once a run, an item naming them by number
and the round's end ranking their positions once; the walk's lookups
shown once each at its end, from the list the incremental walk already
keeps; a template's signature spelled once while its module stands
(`Door::declaration`, keyed by the module's write counters) and only for
a deduction that changed something; and a tried rewrite's reads held in
one buffer, a stack of where each began, cut off where it changed
nothing. A per-pass set to skip lookups already spelled cost more than
the spelling it saved, and a per-round set to keep each item once was the
key's own deduplication over again: both went. Held beside the program: the reads' keys' positions,
median 1160 a snapshot, at most 14918 (`risc-v.k`) — 179 KB;
`cargo xtask mem` reads no difference.

**What proves it.** The shadow: zero unequal over every root, and over
half of them the reads unkeyed bring 48 modules back unequal, inference's
reads of another module left out 20. Every other site left out alone
survives on the corpus — what it read that moved a module, inference read
too (step 1's `array.k` case is parted with either `resolvedFuncParams`'
reads or inference's left out) — and they stay, each a read the round
makes: a key may hold more than the corpus needs, never less. Unit tests
hold what the corpus does not: a read across the boundary parts a module
its copies do not, with its positions carried and ranked; a rewrite that
changed nothing read nothing; a strict hash tells a parameter's name.


## The prefix pass reused, and where the keystroke is — 2026-10-11

*Sprint W7.5d, D1 step 3, its first pass (`loop-across-edits.md` §6, step
3, "The prefix, built 2026-10-11"). `kg_sem::reuse` (`Reuse`,
`ReuseReport`), the snapshot's prefix boundary (`ModuleRounds::{prefixes,
reads_before_prefix, prefix_lineage}`, the node log split at the prefix's
end), `ExpArena::{parallels, translate, adopt, mints, id_at}`,
`ExpansionInterner::find`, `Db::{set_reuse, take_reuse_report}`.*

**A pass that reads its module alone is reused by what it found.** The
prefix (`round_prefix_in_place`, round 0's `pipeline_tail_in_place`)
reads nothing across the boundary and only appends, so a module that
stood where the kept module stood when its pass began gets the kept pass's
output. Where it stood is the keys again: every round before agreed, and
the door's key taken at the pass's start — what the round read before it,
`addLambdaWrappers`' reads — agrees too. Then the nodes the kept pass
appended are taken in as the pass left them, which the node log, now split
at the prefix's end, restores even where inference later wrote one in
place.

**An id is part of the node.** A child is named by stamp and index, and a
rewrite compares whole expressions (`out == rw.arena[id].exp`), so a node
taken in must name its children as the run's own pass would: an ancestor's
stamp where the lowering or a fork minted the child, the module's own
where the pass did. `ExpArena::translate` maps a kept id through the same
place in the same chain of forks; re-stamping every child as the module's
own would have been a node equal by index and unequal as a value. An
expansion is found, not interned: the pass appends nodes under their
donors' frames, all interned already, and interning afresh would shift
every later id.

**Types carried, not kept.** The first build kept each appended node's
type as the pass left it, and `cargo xtask mem` read `risc-v.k`'s editor
45–60 MiB larger after five edits: the kept types held alive every type
inference later replaced. The pass's `(new, original)` pairs replay
`carry_types` on the module as it stands, which is the kept module as it
stood, and only the pairs that gave a type: after five edits the editor
reads 1415–1423 MiB against main's 1396–1398.

**Checked, not trusted.** `edit-identity` turns on a check that runs every
reused pass on a fork as well and compares the two node by node — the
gate's evidence that the keys' "agreed" means "the same input" for this
pass, independent of the shadow. 700250 passes reused over every root,
none unequal.

**And no keystroke won.** On `risc-v.k` the prefix is 0.167 s of a 1.62 s
loop, 0.146 s of it the root's — the module a keystroke edits. Taking in
the library's 21 ms costs about what it saves, and the interleaved A/B is
main's. The library's time is elsewhere: inference's walk 0.375 s,
`instantiate` 0.098, `deduceTemplateArgs` 0.085, `addLambdaWrappers` 0.037,
`closureCalls` 0.021 (`KG_LOOP_PROFILE`, `kg check`). `closureCalls` reads
its module alone and could be taken in as the prefix is, for as little;
every other reads other modules, and a later run can know a pass's reads
are the kept run's only by asking the kept run's questions of its own
state — the door's items made re-askable, a lookup kept as its question, a
read as a place in a followed module. That is the next reuse, and
inference, reading inside a program-wide fixpoint, the last. What the prefix leaves is the machinery
they need: the boundary in the snapshot, the pre-pass key, taking nodes in
across runs, and the check.

## Salsa, and the ceiling of carrying the library — 2026-10-11

Discussed with the owner at the pause; recorded in full in
`loop-across-edits.md` §8, the owner's questions in `sprint-parity.md` §8.
What a later reader would otherwise rediscover:

**The two questions are one.** The keystroke's next lever, the read door's
items made re-askable, is salsa's revalidation — keep the questions a
computation asked, ask them again after the edit, reuse the result if every
answer reads the same. So whether to adopt salsa becomes concrete exactly
there, and the answer recommended is to borrow the algorithm, not the
crate: the loop is a whole-program fixpoint rewriting mutable arenas in
place, and the round a copy is made in is observable, neither of which
salsa's pure, equality-compared queries fit. Salsa would not solve
positions (relocation is needed whatever the substrate) nor reads outside
a query (the class of bug moves, it does not go). What it offers that we
lack is a vocabulary contributors already know — taken instead by one
internal primitive for "a memo keyed by the reads it recorded", which
`SortedMemo`, `ImportsRead` and the door each spell their own way today.

**Carrying the library has a ceiling.** On `risc-v.k`'s root edits the
library is 41% of the loop (5d-0), so even perfect reuse leaves roughly
0.5 s for the first answer and 1.2–1.3 s for the last (arithmetic, not a
measurement). The bench's 400 ms is met on its smaller program; the real
project's needs step 4, parallel rounds (W5.6 — the loop runs on one core)
or reuse inside the edited module too, and 100 ms needs the last. Whether
the reference's round order binds after parity is the owner's fork: if it
does not, a demand-driven design opens, and that is where salsa would pay.

## The reference runs on every core; a whole build is the backend's — 2026-10-11

`scripts/vs-haskell.sh` timed the reference frontend through
`oracle/driver`, which never sets the runtime's capabilities, so the
Haskell side ran on one core. The shipped compiler sets one per processor
(`app/Main.hs:62-68`) and runs its passes per module in parallel
(`Template.hs:57-78`), which a full `kanagawa --verbose` compile gave away
— `float.k` 111 s of CPU in 28.6 s of wall time. The script now times
three columns, interleaved: the reference on one core (`+RTS -N1`), on
every core (`+RTS -N`, as shipped), and `kg check`. Per core we are 12–46×
faster; against the shipped compiler as it runs, 8–16×. The figure
published at the morning's pause (12–45×) was the one-core column,
unlabelled; `performance.md` §11 and the handoff now carry both. On every
core the reference also holds 2.1–2.8 GB on every program, a 128 MB
allocation area per core.

**A whole build is the backend's.** With the build's defaults (3000
placement iterations), the C++ backend is 92–98% of `kanagawa`'s time and
costs the same whichever frontend feeds it: its `Middle-end (inclusive)`
timer encloses all of its work, and stage by stage ours and the
reference's agree within the backend's own noise. That noise is large on
`cache.k` — two dead-code passes swing 1.7–4.8 s and 0.9–2.5 s between runs
on both sides — so a single A/B of two whole builds says nothing about the
frontends. Our build is 1.5–2× the reference's speed, not the frontend's
8–46×.

**By round.** `KG_LOOP_PROFILE` now prints the loop per round as well,
and `KG_PHASES` the frontend per phase (`performance.md` §9, §13). The
rounds show two shapes: `risc-v.k`'s time is in its middle rounds, a third
of it the root module's; `array.k` and `float.k` spend half their loop in
a tail of cheap rounds, each rebuilding the symbol maps and re-running
deduction for the few copies it adds. The triage that follows is in §13.

## The backend surveyed: one thread, a pass that does nothing, an order by address — 2026-10-11

Read and measured only (`plans/backend-survey.md`; profiles in
`measurements/2026-10-11/backend-profile/`). Three findings a later reader
would otherwise rediscover, each re-read in the code:

- **`GlobalDataPropagation` is a no-op under the default options.** Its
  cost test multiplies by `--mem-to-reg`, whose default is `0.0`, so every
  candidate is skipped after the analysis has run (`lower.cpp:3011`): 2.4 s,
  a fifth of `array.k`'s backend, computes nothing. Upstream tests the pass
  only with `--mem-to-reg=100000`.
- **The liveness work list is ordered by heap address**
  (`std::set<BasicBlock*>`, `data_flow_work_list.h:28`). That is why
  `RemoveUnusedGlobals` and `RemoveDeadOperations` take 2–3× longer on some
  runs than others, on either frontend, while every other pass holds: a
  whole-build A/B on `cache.k` measures the heap, not the change. Compare
  backend stages, never two whole builds, until that is fixed.
- **Our backend library runs the consistency checks**: `kanagawa-build`'s
  `BUILD_CHANNEL` is empty, and only `release`/`nightly` define
  `KANAGAWA_SKIP_CONSISTENCY_CHECKS` — a round trip of the whole design's
  MLIR through text, and a location check after every global optimisation.
  Every backend time recorded here includes them (a few percent).

`risc-v.k`'s backend, watched for four minutes, is at 10.5 GB by 100 s and
spends its time from the first minute in `BitConstantPropagation`'s data
flow, whose facts are maps of maps per register per block. A Rust rewrite
of the backend was weighed and not recommended: the hot spots are
algorithms, fixable in C++, and upstream is active exactly where a port
would have to follow it, in the CIRCT output.

## Publishable: the submodule, the backend built here, `kg doc` — 2026-10-11

At the owner's request the repository was made publishable. What a later
reader would otherwise rediscover:

**Upstream's CMake cannot build the backend alone.** Its configure step
